short_description: Renal exploration, not necessitating other specific procedures Notes: (For laparoscopic ablation of renal mass lesion(s), use 50542)
lay_term: The provider examines the kidney for diagnostic purposes, without any curative surgical intervention, such as inspection for hemorrhage, urinary leakage, or tissue damage due to trauma. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin over the kidney. He isolates the individual renal arteries and veins with vessel loops to allow for immediate vascular control. To get access to the retroperitoneum, he lifts the transverse colon out of the abdomen. He then dissects the soft tissues. He incises Gerota's fascia, drains the perirenal hematoma, and dissects the perirenal fat to expose the kidney. Once the kidney is exposed, the provider explores the kidney to know the extent of injury. He washes the surgical wound and may place the drain as needed. He then closes Gerota's fascia and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Gerota's fascia: The fascia present just above the surrounding kidney space; also known as renal fascia. Hematoma: A collection of blood or blood clot in the tissues, usually caused by damage to blood vessels. Hemorrhage: Bleeding, typically used to refer to active or significant bleed. Nephrectomy: Surgical removal of the kidney. Perirenal: In the area around the kidney. Renal: Referring to the kidney, one of a pair of organs that produce urine; also nephric. Retroperitoneum: Behind and outside the peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdominal cavity that attaches various organs to the abdominal wall. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Transverse colon: The part of the large intestine that runs across the upper abdomen, between the ascending and descending segments of colon. Vessel loop: A piece of suture, wire or other material that can be placed around a vessel to close off circulation while a procedure is performed. Tips Use 50010 when there's no other procedure. For example, if the provider explores the kidney and determines that it must be partially removed, report only that procedure, 50240, Nephrectomy, partial, which would include the exploration. guidelines: Surgery Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Nephrolithotomy is the surgical removal of stones from the kidney, and pyelolithotomy is the surgical removal of stones from the renal pelvis. This section of the guidelines refers to the removal of stones from the kidney or renal pelvis using a percutaneous antegrade approach. Breaking and removing stones is separate from accessing the kidney (ie, 50040, 50432, 50433, 52334), accessing the kidney with dilation of the tract to accommodate an endoscope used in an endourologic procedure (ie, 50437), or dilation of a previously established tract to accommodate an endoscope used in an endourologic procedure (ie, 50436). These procedures include the antegrade removal of stones in the calyces, renal pelvis, and/or ureter with the antegrade placement of catheters, stents, and tubes, but do not include retrograde placement of catheters, stents, and tubes. Code 50080 describes nephrolithotomy or pyelolithotomy using a percutaneous antegrade approach with endoscopic instruments to break and remove kidney stones of 2 cm or smaller. Code 50081 includes the elements of 50080, but it is reported for stones larger than 2 cm, branching, stones in multiple locations, ureteral stones, or in patients with complicated anatomy. Creation of percutaneous access or dilation of the tract to accommodate large endoscopic instruments used in stone removals (50436, 50437) is not included in 50080, 50081, and may be reported separately, if performed. Codes 50080, 50081 include placement of any stents or drainage catheters that remain indwelling after the procedure. Report one unit of 50080 or 50081 per side (ie, per kidney), regardless of the number of stones broken and/or removed or locations of the stones. For bilateral procedure, report 50080, 50081 with modifier 50. When 50080 is performed on one side and 50081 is performed on the contralateral side, modifier 50 is not applicable. short_description: Drainage of perirenal or renal abscess, open Notes: (For percutaneous image-guided fluid collection drainage by catheter of perirenal/renal abscess, use 49405)
lay_term: The provider drains an abscess from the kidney (renal) or the area surrounding the kidney (perirenal) with an open approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized, the abscess site is cleaned with an antibacterial solution or sterile water. The provider then makes a left flank incision below the 12th rib into the upper pole of the left kidney. To get access to the retroperitoneum, the provider lifts the transverse colon out of the abdomen. The provider cuts perirenal muscles and dissects perirenal fat and surrounding fascia overlying the kidney to reach the abscess site. The retroperitoneum is opened and fluid is drained. The kidney is carefully mobilized and explored, pus is broken up, and all debris, which may contain pus, blood, and necrotic tissue, is cleared out. The abscess site is then copiously flushed with antibiotic solution until all loose material has been cleared from the abscess pocket. The provider then places multiple drains in the abscess cavity and sutures the ends of the drains to the skin. Finally, the provider covers the wound with gauze pads to help the wound to heal. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus surrounded by inflamed tissue. Percutaneous drainage: The act of drawing off fluid through the skin from a wound. Renal abscess: A collection of fluid or pus in the kidney caused by bacteria or any severe infection. Retroperitoneum: The anatomical space found between the peritoneum and the posterior abdominal wall. Tips For percutaneous abscess drainage with image guidance, report 49405, Image–guided fluid collection drainage by catheter (e.g., abscess, hematoma, seroma, lymphocele, cyst); visceral (e.g., kidney, liver, spleen, lung/mediastinum), percutaneous. short_description: Nephrostomy, nephrotomy with drainage
lay_term: The provider incises the kidney and creates an opening from the kidney to the outside of the abdomen when a blockage prevents urine from draining from the kidneys. Common causes of such a blockage are ovarian cancer, colon cancer, kidney stones, and pyonephrosis (infection of the renal collecting system). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized with 1% lidocaine solution and under ultrasound guidance, the provider places a needle into the kidney. A small amount of dye is injected through the needle to the kidney and urinary system. The needle is then replaced with a catheter called a nephrostomy tube, which is about the same diameter as an intravenous tube, that stays in the kidney. The other end of the catheter remains outside the body to drain urine into a bag. The catheter is connected to the bag in such a way that the catheter will not pull out. Terminology Nephrostomy: A surgical procedure to create an artificial opening between the kidney and the skin which allows for urinary diversion directly from the upper part of the urinary system (renal pelvis). Nephrotomy: Surgical incision into a kidney. Tips For the initial nephrostomy procedure, you should report 50040 for an open surgery. To report nephrostomy tube placement, use 50432, Placement of nephrostomy catheter, percutaneous, including diagnostic nephrostogram and/or ureterogram when performed, imaging guidance (eg, ultrasound and/or fluoroscopy) and all associated radiological supervision and interpretation. For retrograde percutaneous nephrostomy, report 52334, Cystourethroscopy with insertion of ureteral guide wire through kidney to establish a percutaneous nephrostomy, retrograde. To report exchange of a percutaneous nephrostomy catheter, use 50435, Exchange nephrostomy catheter, percutaneous, including diagnostic nephrostogram and/or ureterogram when performed, imaging guidance (eg, ultrasound and/or fluoroscopy) and all associated radiological supervision and interpretation. If the provider has to reposition the nephrostomy tube and drain an accompanying hematoma, you should report 50040 only. This code covers the redo of the nephrostomy tube in a different site, both in the kidney and skin exit port. If the patient is still in the global period of the initial nephrostomy tube insertion when the provider performs the redo, you should append modifier 78 to 50040 indicating a problem or complication with the first tube insertion. If the provider explores the retroperitoneal space and drains a hematoma but does not actually remove the nephrostomy tube, report 49010. Read Less

short_description: Nephrolithotomy; complicated by congenital kidney abnormality
lay_term: The provider incises the kidney to remove stones, or renal calculi, with the complicating factor of kidney malformation due to a birth defect. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the patient's back on the side of the affected kidney. He dissects soft tissues, incises the Gerota's fascia, and also dissects perirenal fat overlying the kidney. He inserts an instrument, called a nephroscope, to view the internal structures of the kidney, and then irrigates the area. He then removes any small kidney stones and inserts a tube for drainage. For large stones, he may use an ultrasonic device that uses sound waves to break up the stones or a holmium laser lithotripter, a device that uses light waves to fragment the stones before removal. After stone removal, the provider inserts a nephrostomy tube, a drainage tube placed through an opening in the kidney, to drain urine. He closes the incision with large absorbable sutures. Terminology Congenital: Present at birth. Gerota's fascia: The fascia present just above the surrounding kidney space; also known as renal fascia. Nephrolithotomy: Incision into the kidney for removal of kidney stones. Nephrostomy Tube: A tube which connects the kidney to the skin and allows urinary diversion directly from the upper part of the urinary system. Perirenal: In the area around the kidney. Soft tissue: Supports and surrounds bones, organs and other structures. Read Less

short_description: Nephrolithotomy; removal of large staghorn calculus filling renal pelvis and calyces (including anatrophic pyelolithotomy)
lay_term: The provider removes a large staghorn calculus through an incision in the the kidney. A staghorn calculus is a large branched kidney stone, sometimes referred to as a struvite; this type of kidney stone is formed by spillover of highly acidic urine caused by a bacterial infection that hydrolyzes urine to ammonia. Explanation The patient is placed in a prone position, and the site is prepared with an antiseptic liquid and draped in a sterile fashion. The provider makes an incision into the back on the side overlying the affected kidney. The provider dissects down through overlying tissues and clamps off the artery feeding the kidney. He makes an incision in the kidney over the staghorn calculus. He extracts the calculus, which may require incising the renal pelvis and calyces. An anatrophic pyelolithotomy involves entering the parenchyma (working elements) of the kidney (as opposed to the structural elements), injection of methylene blue dye and imaging to identify the anatrophic plane, and cooling of the renal vessels to induce temporary ischemia (lack of blood flow). The reconstruction of the pelvic structures is more complicated. Once the stones are removed and closure is performed, a nephrostomy tube is placed to drain the fluid from the kidney into a bag. After removal of stones and suturing the kidney structures, the provider closes the incision in layers. Terminology Parenchymal tissue: The tissue that forms the working elements of an organ as opposed to the structural elements. Renal calyx: A cup–shaped structure in the kidney that surrounds the renal pelvis. Renal pelvis: Funnel–like structure of the kidney, where urine collects and drains into the ureter and on to the bladder. Nephrostomy tube: A tube which connects the kidney to the skin and allows urinary diversion directly from the upper part of the urinary system (renal pelvis). Tips Use CPT® code 50070 if the procedure is complicated by congenital kidney abnormality. Read Less

short_description: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy or pyelolithotomy, lithotripsy, stone extraction, antegrade ureteroscopy, antegrade stent placement and nephrostomy tube placement, when performed, including imaging guidance; simple (eg, stone[s] up to 2 cm in single location of kidney or renal pelvis, nonbranching stones)
lay_term: The provider removes one or more stones from the kidney or renal pelvis using an antegrade (“downhill”) percutaneous approach. The provider uses imaging guidance and may place a stent and nephrostomy tube. This is a simple procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider begins the percutaneous antegrade kidney stone or renal stone removal. Antegrade refers to a “downhill” approach, as opposed to a retrograde (“uphill,” against the usual flow) approach. As a percutaneous procedure, the provider uses a minimally invasive access site, such as by using a nephrostomy tube that serves as a tunnel directly into the kidney (or into the renal pelvis with pyelolithotomy). The provider uses imaging guidance to visualize the procedure. The provider may place a ureteral access sheath in the tube to allow for introduction of a ureteroscope. The provider uses endoscopic instruments to break (perform lithotripsy) and remove one or more stones (usually made of mineral salts or other such compounds). The provider may place a stent through this antegrade route to help urine drain after the procedure, and the provider may leave a nephrostomy tube in place at the end of the procedure. Use this code when the documentation indicates this is a simple procedure, such as for one or more stones that measure 2 cm or smaller in a single location of the kidney or renal pelvis. Terminology Endoscope: A stiff (rigid) or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, stomach, or eye; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Nephrostomy tube: A tube which connects the kidney to the skin and allows urinary diversion directly from the upper part of the urinary system (renal pelvis). Percutaneous procedure: A minimally invasive procedure performed through the skin. Renal: Related to the kidneys. Renal pelvis: Funnel–like structure of the kidney, where urine collects and drains into the ureter and on to the bladder. Ureter: One of a pair of ducts that pass urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Tips A common term for this procedure is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL). See 50081 for complex procedures. Coding guidelines indicate that 50080 and 50081 do not include creation of percutaneous access or dilation of the tract, so you may report those separately. Report one unit of 50080 or 50081 per side (kidney), even if the provider removes multiple stones on that side. Read Less

lay_term: The provider makes a donor kidney, from a cadaver, ready for transplantation through a standard back table preparation. Explanation The provider moves the kidney, previously harvested from a cadaver, to a back table basin and places the kidney in cold preservation solution. The provider may use electrolyte solution to cool the kidney. She separates all perinephric fat and surrounding structures of the kidney. She removes the essential structures attached to the kidney, such as the vena cava, aorta, perinephric tissue, and adrenal glands. She incises the renal arteries and ties them tightly. She perfuses all branches separately. She separates the renal vein from its branches. She separates the gonadal, adrenal, and any lumbar vein branches and ties them tightly. She removes the lymphatic tissue surrounding the artery and checks for any lymph fluid leaks. She prepares the ureter taking care to protect any vascular framework. She washes the renal vessels with crystalloid solution to identify any vascular leaks or the need for repair of any part. Once she removes all the important structures of the kidney, the kidney is ready for transplant. Terminology Adrenal gland: A gland located on top of the kidney; produces hormones that are responsible for functions such as heart rate control and blood pressure; they also produce the stress hormone, commonly known as the flight or fight hormone, in addition to many more. Allograft: A tissue graft harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also called allogeneic graft and homograft. Aorta: The main artery that comes out of the top of the left ventricle and carries oxygenated blood to the body; consists of an ascending and descending aorta which serve the upper and lower parts of the body respectively. Cadaver donor: A deceased person whose organs or tissue may be harvested for transplantation. Diaphragm: The membrane dividing the abdominal and chest, or thoracic, cavities. Ligate: Close, tie off, repair, or encircle a vessel or other structure using a material such as sutures, wire, or surgical tape. Perinephric: Tissue including connective tissue and fat around the kidney. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Retroperitoneal: Behind and outside the peritoneum. Ureter: Tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. Venae cavae: The major trunks of the venous circulatory system; the superior vena cava brings blood back to the heart from the upper body circulation while the inferior vena cava brings it back from the lower body circulation. short_description: Backbench reconstruction of cadaver or living donor renal allograft prior to transplantation; ureteral anastomosis, each
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider prepares a renal allograft, which includes joining arteries, from a cadaver or living donor kidney to prepare for transplantation. Explanation Prior to transplantation, the provider removes the entire kidney from a cadaver donor or kidney and upper ureter from a living donor for backbench preparation. First, the provider cleans the kidney with cold solution to remove any remaining blood or tissue from the donor kidney. The provider then begins the ureteral anastomosis. The provider performs ureteral anastomosis when the donor kidney has a kidney or ureteral anomaly, such as double ureters or other anatomical differences. The provider separates the ureter from the surrounding tissue, taking care not to disturb any vascular supply. He then prepares an aortic patch and anastomoses it to the ureter. In the case of double ureters, the provider anastomoses each ureter to the other or each ureter may require separate anastomosis. Once ureteral anastomosis is completed, it is ready to transplant. Terminology Allograft: A graft or tissue received from a donor and transferred to the recipient of the same species, such as person to person. Anastomosis: The uniting between two organs surgically, such as between arteries or veins. Backbench: A sterile environment in the operating room but separate from the operating table where a provider prepares grafts before transplantation. Cadaver: A dead human body. Transplantation: The process of moving a tissue or an organ from donor to recipient or from one part or individual to another. Ureter: Duct that passes urine from the kidney to the bladder. Tips A provider transplants a kidney and performs the backbench reconstruction as well. I know for the backbench I report 50327, 50328 and 50329. The provider feels there should be extra charges for two microvascular repairs that took an extra three hours and were very difficult. I'm having trouble finding the appropriate code and do not feel adding modifier 22, Increased procedural service, to any of the backbench codes would be appropriate and enough reimbursement for his extra time. How would you suggest I code this procedure? There aren't any additional codes that you should report in this case. The surgeon is given extra payment with the backbench codes. You should report 50327, Backbench reconstruction of cadaver or living donor renal allograft prior to transplantation; venous anastomosis, each, 50328 and 50329, Backbench reconstruction of cadaver or living donor renal allograft prior to transplantation; ureteral anastomosis, each, as you suggest. The arterial anastomoses are covered with 50328 and cannot be separately reported with another code. Appending modifier 22 to 50328 would seem appropriate in this particular case to show the extra time and work your urologist had to put in for this complicated procedure. Remember that all of this information should be clearly documented in the medical records and sent to the carrier for review. Read Less

lay_term: Nephrectomy is a surgical procedure for removal of a kidney or part of a kidney. Explanation The patient (recipient) is placed in the supine position, and the site is prepared with Betadine (an antiseptic liquid) and draped in a sterile fashion. With the patient under general anesthesia, the physician makes an incision below the ribcage. The kidney is then exposed. The ureter (connection from the kidney to the bladder) and blood vessels are disconnected, and the kidney is removed. This kidney is removed because it is no longer functioning. Its removal makes room for a donor kidney to be transplanted. Terminology Nephrectomy: A surgical procedure for removal of a kidney or part of a kidney Tips Use CPT® code 50225 if the same surgery has been performed on the same kidney in the past. Use CPT® code 50230 if radical nephrectomy has been performed. Radical nephrectomy involves removal of kidney, a section of ureter, the adrenal gland, and the fatty tissue surrounding the kidney. Use CPT® code 50234 if nephrectomy was performed with total removal of ureter and bladder cuff through the same incision. Use CPT® code 50236 if nephrectomy was performed with total removal of ureter and bladder cuff through separate incisions. Use CPT® code 50240 if the physician only removed the diseased or infected portion of the kidney. Use CPT® codes 50300–50320 for the donor. Use CPT® code 50340 for recipient nephrectomy. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the patient's kidney from the normal anatomic location and reimplants it into a new site by connecting renal and iliac vessels. Explanation First, the provider makes a middle transabdominal incision in the skin. The provider dissects the abdominal organs (viscera) and cuts transversalis fascia to enter the space of retroperitoneum. The provider then incises the Gerota's fascia and also dissects the perinephric fat to expose the kidney. The kidney and the ureter are then exposed. After exposing the kidney, the provider gives attention towards preparation for reimplantation into the other site. For implantation, an incision is made into the lower abdomen. The incision is moved down to the rectus fascia and all the transverse abdominis muscles are exposed with the line of incision. The iliac vessels and bladder are then exposed when peritoneum reflects medially. The surgeon then places vascular clamps, cuts, and ties the iliac vessels and cleanses the kidney with cold solution. The prepared renal vessels are then anastomosed to the other arterial or venous site. Vascular clamps are then released and the anastomosis sites are then analyzed for any leakage or bleeding. The provider then inserts a temporary stent to ascertain an open anastomosis site. The kidney is then placed in the new site while preventing any leaks from the blood vessels or ureter. A plastic tube may be inserted through a separate pierce incision for drainage. The incision is then closed in layers. Terminology Autotransplantation: The process of excision of organs or tissues and relocated it into a new location of the same individual. Transversalis fascia: The very deep layer of fascia lining the anterolateral abdominal wall, which is found between the transverse abdominal muscle and the extraperitoneal fascia. Gerota's fascia: The fascia, which is present just above the surrounding kidney space; also known as renal fascia. Transverse abdominis muscles: Deepest muscle of the abdominal wall that runs from the sides to the front of the abdomen Anastomosis: The uniting between two organs surgically, may be vessels, or between two or more nerves, or between arteries or veins. lay_term: The provider creates a new access route percutaneously (through a small incision made in the patient’s skin) and injects contrast material into the ureters (ureterogram) or kidney (nephrostogram) to analyze the internal structures of the kidneys, renal pelvis, and/or ureters using imaging guidance. The provider typically performs this procedure to assess nephrostomy or pyelostomy tube function, identify blockage in the ureteropelvic junction, or check for urine leakage around the tube insertion site. The procedure covers the complete diagnostic procedure and all radiological supervision and interpretation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, using ultrasound or fluoroscopic guidance, imaging technologies that display live images on a video monitor, the provider makes a small incision in the patient’s skin over the kidneys. He places a needle through the incision and inserts a guide wire through the needle into the ureters and/or renal pelvis, the funnel–like structure of the kidney, where urine collects and drains into the ureter and on to the bladder. He advances a catheter over the guide wire, removes the wire, and injects contrast material through the catheter into the areas he wants to image. The provider then takes images of the kidney, renal pelvis, and/or ureter and interprets the images. Terminology Fluoroscopy: Use of fluoroscopy, a live X–ray where the image appears on a monitor, to view body structures while performing procedures. Nephrostogram: An X–ray image of the kidney after injection of a contrast agent through a nephrostomy tube. Nephrostomy tube: A tube which connects the kidney to the skin and allows urinary diversion directly from the upper part of the urinary system, or the renal pelvis. Ultrasound: The use of high frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Ureter: One of a pair of ducts that pass urine from the kidneys to the bladder. short_description: Symphysiotomy for horseshoe kidney with or without pyeloplasty and/or other plastic procedure, unilateral or bilateral (1 operation)
lay_term: The provider incises anomalous tissue connecting two kidneys so that they become two separate structures. The provider may also perform a reconstruction procedure such as pyeloplasty of the kidney’s renal pelvis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision, typically across the abdomen, to access the kidneys. He separates the isthmus, the band of renal or fibrous tissue connecting the two kidneys, from the surrounding muscles, fat, and other tissue. He then incises the isthmus and sutures the incision site on each side to create two separate kidney structures. If needed, the provider may then perform pyeloplasty on the renal pelvis or perform another plastic repair on one or both sides. He cleanses the operative site with sterile saline solution and controls bleeding. The provider may place a separate drain tube through a separate incision in the skin. He removes all surgical instruments and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Horseshoe kidney: A congenital partial fusion defect of the right and left kidneys resulting in one large horseshoe shape kidney structure. Pyeloplasty: Surgical repair of the kidney’s renal pelvis, such as removal of a blockage between the kidney and ureter, the tube that connects the kidney to the bladder. Renal pelvis: A funnel structure where urine collects in the kidney and drains into the ureter. Symphysiotomy: Incising the meeting point of two structures. Read Less

short_description: Renal endoscopy through established nephrostomy or pyelostomy, with or without irrigation, instillation, or ureteropyelography, exclusive of radiologic service
lay_term: The provider inserts an endoscope through a previously established opening between the collecting system of the kidney and the exterior of the body or a previously established opening between the renal pelvis and the exterior of the body. She examines the kidney, renal pelvis, and ureter. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider disconnects the external urinary drainage bag from the nephrostomy or pyelostomy tube. She then moves a guidewire forward through the nephrostomy tube and pulls the nephrostomy tube out over the wire. The provider may use some surgical instruments to widen the opening passageway. Once she widens the pathway, the provider inserts an endoscope, which is a small, flexible tube with an attached optical system, into the kidney through an established nephrostomy or pyelostomy tract. She uses it to analyze the interior structures of the renal collecting system. For better visual perception, the provider may add sterile saline solution into the area of the renal collecting system. The provider may instill some other therapeutic solutions into the kidney or may use contrast material for separately reportable radiologic examination of the ureter and renal pelvis. Once examination is completed, the provider withdraws all the instruments, replaces the tubes, and reconnects the external urinary drainage bag to the tubes for temporary urine flow. Terminology Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Nephrostomy: The creation of an artificial pathway between the kidney and outside of the body to allow drainage of urine from the renal pelvis. Pyelostomy: An artificial opening in the renal pelvis to create a drainage route for temporarily diverting the flow of urine from the ureter. Renal endoscopy: Process of visual examination of the structures of the renal collecting system with the help of a fiberoptic instrument known as an endoscope. Renal pelvis: A funnel structure where urine collects in the kidney and drains into the ureter. Ureter: The tube that connects the kidney to the bladder. Ureteropyelography: The process of radiologic study of the ureter and renal pelvis performed by injecting contrast agent. Tips Before choosing your final renal endoscopy code, review 50551 to 50580 to be sure you’ve chosen the best option for your case. Read Less

lay_term: The provider ablates, or destroys, one or more small renal masses in one kidney in a minimally invasive surgical procedure using cryotherapy, or extreme cold, applied through a percutaneous needle. Explanation Using percutaneous technique, the physician pulverizes one or more kidney tumors of the right or left kidney by cold therapy. Cryotherapy, also known as cold therapy, uses cold to devastate the abnormal or diseased tissue. The tumor is recognized by using ultrasound, CT, or MRI guidance. First the patient is taken to the operating room and placed in the prone position in the CT or MRI scanner. Local anesthetic may be injected. The physician decides the placement of cryoprobe. The cryoprobes are then inserted into the tumors with the help of real–time ultrasound or CT fluoroscopy taking care not to destroy any other major blood vessels. The entire procedure is visualized using CT, ultrasound, or MRI. Cold is then applied for approximately 10–20 minutes. Depending upon the size and location of the tumor, the applicator may need to be re–adjusted and additional treatments administered. For more than one or very large tumors, more than one needle is repositioned carefully into the multiple locations of tumors to freeze and destroy the tissue cells. Once end of the probe confirms the proper location, the cold ablation unit gets functional and probes freeze at lower temperature. During the freeze cycle, an ice ball develops over approximately 15 minutes to cause tumor destruction. Cold therapy uses multiple freeze–thaw cycles that is initiated by replacing the argon with helium. Complete destruction typically requires two freeze/thaw cycles. Once treatment is finished, the probes are removed and dressing is used to cover the open area of the skin. Terminology Cryotherapy: Cryotherapy, also known as cold therapy, means treatment is done by using low temperatures. It uses cold to destroy the diseased tissue. short_description: Ureterectomy, with bladder cuff (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes all or part of a ureter along with a section of the bladder cuff. He most commonly performs this procedure to treat cancer of the ureter. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the abdomen overlying the urinary bladder. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin and the muscles. He exposes the bladder and the lower portion of the ureter. Next, he mobilizes the bladder and excises as much as necessary off the cuff, including the ureteral opening. The provider also dissects above the site of the defect or diseased portion of the ureter and bladder cuff to ensure he removes the entire affected area. Once he completes the ureterectomy and bladder cuff excision, he places a catheter, closes the opening in the bladder, and places a drainage tube. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the abdominal wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. He removes the drainage tube and catheter after five days. Terminology Bladder cuff: Band like structure that forms a circle around part of the bladder and is shaped like a cuff. Ureter: Tube that carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder. Ureterectomy: Surgical removal of a segment or all of a ureter. Urinary bladder: A hollow organ in the pelvic cavity that collects urine. Tips The descriptor for this code indicates that the procedure can be performed separately but should not be reported when performed along with a related procedure (e.g., same anatomic area or through the same incision, orifice, or surgical approach). lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes an abnormal ureter, or one which is not in its proper position and terminates at a different site. He performs this procedure through a combination of approaches abdominal, vaginal, and or perineal approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the abdomen over the ectopic ureter. He then dissects the muscles, fat, and surrounding fascia to expose the abnormal ureter. Once the provider exposes the abnormal ureter, he examines the urinary system for any other abnormalities or disease along with the terminal point of the ectopic ureter. The provider then makes another incision in the vagina or perineum at the termination site of the ureter. short_description: Ureterolysis, with or without repositioning of ureter for retroperitoneal fibrosis Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 50715 with modifier 50)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically frees the ureter from fibrous bands of inflamed tissues of the retroperitoneum, or the space between the peritoneum and the abdominal wall. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the abdomen over the location of the ureter. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin and the muscles to expose the ureter. The provider then identifies the retroperitoneal fibrous tissues surrounding or adhering to the ureters. The provider dissects all the fibrotic tissues to free the ureter. The provider then reshapes the ureter with the help of sutures, positioning the ureters if possible away from the fibrotic tissue. Otherwise, he divides the ureters and repositions or reattaches the ureters to the kidney. The physician may insert a small catheter in the ureter for healing and to reduce the leakage of urine. The provider may place a drain tube into the abdomen through a separate pierce incision in the abdomen, and he inserts a bladder catheter to precisely monitor the urine output from the kidneys. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the abdominal wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that a provider inserts into a vessel through which he can pass instruments, blood can be withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a provider can insert this flexible tube into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Ureter: Tube that carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder. short_description: Ureterolysis for retrocaval ureter, with reanastomosis of upper urinary tract or vena cava
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider frees a ureter from a ureteral obstruction due to a retrocaval ureter, a rare congenital anomaly in which the ureter passes behind the inferior vena cava. The provider uses one of two approaches to repair the anomaly. He may dissect the ureter to repair the retrocaval ureter or he dissects the vena cava into two ends, repositions the ureter in front, and reanastomoses, or surgically reconnects the vena cava. A retrocaval ureter is also known as a circumcaval ureter. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the skin of the abdomen to expose the retrocaval ureter. He then incises the muscles, fat, and fascia surrounding the ureter. The provider dissects the tissues surrounding the retrocaval ureter and frees the ureter. He then dissects the ureter from both sides of the vena cava. He trims the constricted portion of the ureter and surgically connects the lower end of the ureter to the upper ureter. The provider may alternatively divide the vena cava into two, move the ureter in front of the vena cava, and surgically reconnect the vena cava. The provider may insert a small catheter in the ureter to help with healing and to reduce the leakage of urine. He may place a drain tube into the abdomen, and he inserts a bladder catheter to precisely monitor urine output from the kidneys. Finally, he stops all bleeding and closes the abdominal wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that a provider inserts into a vessel through which he can pass instruments, blood can be withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a provider can insert this flexible tube into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. short_description: Ureterocalycostomy, anastomosis of ureter to renal calyx
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically connects the upper pole of a healthy nondilated ureter to the renal calyx for urinary drainage in a procedure known as ureterocalycostomy. He performs this procedure to bypass a ureteropelvic junction obstruction, or a blockage, in the upper part of the ureter and restore the continuity of the upper urinary tract. He then divides and separates the ureter and moves it away from the area of fibrosis or stricture. Next, the provider exposes the calyx and incises the parenchyma within the calyx. The provider places a stent and creates a surgical tension free connection between the upper pole, or end, of the ureter with the lower pole of the calyces over the stent. The provider then sutures the calyx to the ureter. The provider then closes the area and may cover the repair with adjacent tissue to help with healing. short_description: Ureteroureterostomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises and takes away a blocked portion of the ureter and then rejoins the two ends of the healthy ureter. The provider performs this procedure primarily to remove the blocked or injured part of the ureter. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider typically chooses to make an incision in the midline below the navel. He separates and retracts the rectus abdominis muscle. He then retracts the abdominal contents to gain a view of the ureters. He identifies the large intestine, inferior vena cava, common iliac vessel, and the uterine artery in females, ensuring he does not injure them during the procedure. He identifies the portion of the ureter to work on. He mobilizes the portion to be removed, taking care not to damage the delicate network of blood vessels surrounding the ureter. He then excises the blocked portion of the ureter. He inserts a silastic urethral catheter traversing up to the renal pelvis and down to the bladder to provide support to the site where the provider will rejoin the cut ends of the ureter. The provider then rejoins the two ends of the healthy ureter, taking care that there is no pull or tension at the anastomosis site due to the shortening of the length of the ureter. Because the ureter is very delicate and narrow in diameter, the provider uses fine needles with fine suture material. He stitches together only the fibrous and the muscular layer, not piercing the innermost mucosal layer and also taking care not to occlude the lumen with too many stitches. He then places a drain near the anastomosis site to prevent any collection of urine or fluid there. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the wound in layers. Common iliac vessel: A vessel providing blood supply to the lower limbs. Inferior vena cava: The vessel carrying deoxygenated blood from all over the body to the heart. Layers of ureter wall: The ureter consists of an outer fibrous and muscular layer and an innermost layer lining the lumen known as mucosa. Lumen: The space within an organ or structure. Rectus abdominis: A flat sheath–like muscle in the front of the abdomen. Renal pelvis: The enlarged upper portion of the ureter in between the kidney and the main ureter. Ureter: A very delicate, narrow, tube–like structure that transports the urine produced in the kidney to the urinary bladder for temporary storage. Uterine artery: The blood vessel supplying oxygenated blood to the womb in females. short_description: Transureteroureterostomy, anastomosis of ureter to contralateral ureter Notes: (Codes 50780-50785 include minor procedures to prevent vesicoureteral reflux)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises and takes away a blocked or injured potion of the ureter and then joins the renal end of the remaining portion of the ureter to the healthy ureter on the other side of the body. The provider performs this procedure primarily if the length of the remaining ureter after removing the blocked or injured part is insufficient for anastomosis to the bladder. He separates and retracts the rectus abdominis muscle. He then retracts the abdominal contents to gain a view of the ureters. He identifies the large intestine, inferior vena cava, common iliac vessel, and the uterine artery in females, ensuring he does not injure them during the procedure. He identifies the portion of the ureter to work on. He mobilizes the portion to be removed, taking care not to damage the delicate network of blood vessels surrounding the ureter. He then excises the blocked or injured portion of the ureter. He then goes on to create a tunnel through the sigmoid colon mesentery, which is a thin membranous covering of a portion of intestine, taking care to avoid injury to nearby structures. He gently pulls the donor ureter across the midline through this tunnel to approximate this ureteral end to the healthy ureter on the other side of the body. He then creates a small opening in the healthy recipient ureter and anastomoses the donor ureteral end to the recipient ureter, taking care that there is no pull or tension at the anastomosis site due to the shortening of the length of the ureter. Because the ureter is very delicate and narrow in diameter, the provider uses fine needles with fine suture material. He stitches together only the fibrous and the muscular layer, not piercing the innermost mucosal layer and also taking care not to occlude the lumen with too many stitches. He also inserts a double J stent traversing up to the renal pelvis, of the donor side, through the anastomosis and down to the bladder to provide support to the anastomosis site. He then places a drain near the anastomosis site to prevent any collection of urine or fluid there. After achieving hemostasis, that is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the wound in layers. short_description: Ureteroneocystostomy; anastomosis of single ureter to bladder Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 50780 with modifier 50) (When combined with cystourethroplasty or vesical neck revision, use 51820)

short_description: Ureteroneocystostomy; anastomosis of duplicated ureter to bladder

short_description: Ureterosigmoidostomy, with creation of sigmoid bladder and establishment of abdominal or perineal colostomy, including intestine anastomosis
lay_term: The provider creates a bladder structure out of an excised part of the sigmoid colon, inserts the ureters into it, and attaches the structure to allow passage of the patient’s urine through an artificially created outlet in the abdomen or perineum. Providers typically perform this procedure on patients whose urinary bladder has been taken out due to cancer or other reasons. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a midline abdominal incision cutting through skin, muscles, and fascia. Once he enters into the abdominal cavity, he pulls out the sigmoid colon and ureters. He excises a segment of sigmoid colon, closes that segment on one end, and creates a pouch–like structure. He then makes two small incisions on that structure and stitches one ureter to each of these incisions. This helps create a new passage of urine into the pocket formed with the sigmoid colon. Next, the provider makes another small incision on the abdominal wall to form an opening outside of the body, called a colostomy, and stitches the sigmoid colon segment on the abdominal wall opening; alternatively, the provider could create a similar opening through the perineum. The provider stitches the loose end of sigmoid colon, left after excision of the sigmoid colon segment, back to the intestine. Also called an anastomosis, this connection maintains the continuity of the colon. After irrigating the abdominal cavity with antibiotics, the provider closes the abdominal cavity using sutures, and the team transfers the patient to the recovery room. Terminology Anastomosis: An artificial opening or connection between two structures, most commonly between tubular structures. Perineum: An area between the anus and vulva in the female and between the anus and scrotum in the male. Ureter: Tubular structure that connects and supplies urine from a kidney to the urinary bladder. Ureterosigmoidostomy: Artificial outlet of urine created by inserting ureters into an excised portion of the sigmoid colon; performed in a patient whose urinary bladder has been removed. short_description: Ureteroileal conduit (ileal bladder), including intestine anastomosis (Bricker operation) Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 50820 with modifier 50) (For combination of 50800-50820 with cystectomy, see 51580-51595)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts a portion of the intestine known as the ileum, closes it from one end to form a pouch, sutures the ureter to divert urine into the ileal pouch, and connects the other end of the ileal pouch to the abdominal wall to create an external opening for outflow of urine. He then sutures the cut ends of the intestine together to reestablish bowel continuity. He primarily performs this procedure to facilitate urine excretion following surgical removal of the urinary bladder due to severe trauma or malignancy. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision below the navel in the midline. He separates and retracts the rectus abdominis muscle. He then retracts the abdominal contents to gain a view of the terminal ileum. He then isolates a portion of ileum, sparing at least the last 25cm of the terminal ileum for salt reabsorption. He transilluminates the portion to ensure its vascularity. He then sutures the cut ends of the intestine together to reestablish bowel continuity. He creates a window in the posterior layer of peritoneum, a sheath between the bowels and the genitourinary system beneath. He then draws the distal end of the ureter through the window and cuts and sutures the ureter to the ileal conduit, or passageway, to divert urine into it. He also positions a stent within the lumen of the ureter, running within the conduit to provide support. He goes on to create the stoma, or the external opening, as follows. He makes an incision on a premarked area on the skin of the lower abdomen on one side. He then creates a channel by dividing through the rectus abdominis muscle and drawing the distal open end of the ileal conduit through the channel. He rolls the wall of the tip of the distal end of the conduit back onto itself and sutures it to the abdominal skin, thus creating a raised mouth–like opening for discharge of urine, which can be collected in a stoma bag. The provider then ensures that there is no stretch or tension in the created conduit. He may wrap it with overlying omentum for better revascularization. He then places drains and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Distal: Situated farther from the center of the body. Ileum: A portion of the intestine. Proximal: Situated nearer to the center of the body. Rectus abdominis: A flat sheath–like muscle in the front of the abdomen. Stent: An artificial tubular support placed within the lumen. Transillumination: Holding an object against light to highlight and examine its details. Ureter: A channel that carries urine formed in the kidneys for temporary storage in the bladder. Ureteroileal conduit: A new channel created by joining the ureters to the ileum for outflow of urine. Vascularity: Supply of blood. Depending on payer requirements, you should also attach modifier 51 to 50820 to show that the provider performed more than one procedure during the operative session. short_description: Urinary undiversion (eg, taking down of ureteroileal conduit, ureterosigmoidostomy or ureteroenterostomy with ureteroureterostomy or ureteroneocystostomy)
lay_term: The provider performs this procedure to reestablish the urinary tract following previous operations of ileal conduits, ureterosigmoidostomy, or ureteroenterostomy with ureteroureterostomy or ureteroneocystostomy. The procedure involves reimplantation of the ureters into the bladder through newly created entry points on the bladder. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision below the navel in the midline. He separates and retracts the rectus abdominis muscle. He then retracts the abdominal contents to gain a view of the bladder. The provider identifies the ureters. The provider takes down or removes a urinary diversion such as an ileal or sigmoid conduit and reimplants the ureters into the bladder or into each other and then into the bladder. He opens the bladder on its frontal surface by creating two stomas and stitches the ureters placed through the stomas inside the bladder. The origin of the tunnel should be higher up and more toward the midline, and with a tunnel length that is at least 3 times the diameter of the ureter. For better support he may place a stent within the ureter at the point of its attachment to the bladder. He may connect a urinary catheter for draining urine, and he may attach a drainage tube because urine leakage occurs from the site, which can lead to abscess formation. He then places drains and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Rectus abdominis: A flat sheath–like muscle in the front of the abdomen. Stent: An artificial tubular support placed within the lumen. Stoma: Mouth–like opening. Undiversion: The provider takes down or removes a urinary diversion such as an ileal or sigmoid conduit and reimplants the ureters into the bladder or into each other and then into the bladder. Ureter: A channel that carries urine from the kidneys to the bladder. Ureteroureterostomy: Resuturing the cut ureter onto itself. Ureteroileal conduit: A new channel created by taking a portion of intestine known as ileum, suturing the ureters onto it to drain urine, and connecting the other end of the ileum segment to the abdominal wall to open externally. Ureterosigmoidostomy: The ureters are surgically connected to the sigmoid colon, a part of the large intestine. Ureteroenterostomy: The ureters are surgically connected to a part of the large intestine. Ureteroneocystostomy: The ureters are resutured to the bladder after releasing them from previous operative diversions like a ureteroileal conduit or ureterosigmoidostomy. short_description: Cutaneous appendico-vesicostomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider cuts a portion of the intestine known as the appendix, joins one end to the urinary bladder to divert urine into the bladder, and connects the other end to the abdominal wall to create an external opening for outflow of urine. He then sutures the cut ends of the intestine together to reestablish bowel continuity. He primarily performs this procedure to facilitate urine excretion following neurogenic or congenital dysfunction of the urinary bladder. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision below the navel in the midline. He separates and retracts the rectus abdominis muscle. He retracts the abdominal contents to gain a view of the right colon and appendix. He then isolates a portion of the appendix and ensures its vascularity. He further sutures one end of the appendix to a hole created in the urinary bladder. After this, he sutures the cut ends of the intestine together to reestablish bowel continuity. He goes on to create the stoma or the external opening as follows. He makes an incision on a premarked area on the skin of the lower abdomen on one side or at the umbilicus. He then creates a channel by dividing through the rectus abdominis and drawing the distal open end of the appendix through the channel. He rolls the wall of the tip of the distal end of the appendix back onto itself and sutures it to the abdominal skin, thus creating a raised mouth–like opening for discharge of urine, which can be collected in a stoma bag. The provider then ensures that there is no stretch or tension in the passage created. He may place drains, and then he closes the wound in layers. short_description: Ureterostomy, transplantation of ureter to skin Notes: (For bilateral procedure, report 50860 with modifier 50)
lay_term: The provider creates an artificial opening to attach the ureter to the surface of the body to drain urine. Explanation The procedure may involve one ureter or both. When both are moved, the provider chooses between placing one drainage port on either side of the abdomen, bringing them to the same side, or creating a single stoma linking both ureters to it. The provider also chooses from many different ureterostomy techniques. In a surgical loop procedure, for example, the patient is placed in a flank position. He then locates the ureter and frees it from the connective tissue. He brings a loop of ureter out of the incision and closes the fascia under the loop. The provider then makes a longitudinal incision in the ureter and passes an appropriately sized catheter through the lope into the renal pelvis. He then brings the surrounding edges together with the ureter and anchors it in place to prevent the opening from narrowing. Finally, the provider closes the remaining incision in layers. Renal pelvis: Small funnel–like structure in each kidney into which urine is discharged before passing into the ureter. Transverse incision: An incision that runs across the body to provide access to the abdomen and pelvis. Ureter: duct that passes urine from the kidney to the bladder. short_description: Ureterorrhaphy, suture of ureter (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider stitches a crack or discontinuity in the wall of the ureter. The provider may perform this primarily to regain the patency of the lumen following injury or surgical removal of stones within the ureter. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider typically chooses to make an incision in the midline below the navel. He separates and retracts the rectus abdominis muscle. He then retracts the abdominal contents to gain a view of the ureters. He identifies the large intestine, inferior vena cava, common iliac vessel, and the uterine artery in females, ensuring he won’t injure them during the procedure. He identifies the portion of the ureter to work on. Because the ureter is very delicate and narrow in diameter, the provider uses fine needles with fine suture material. He stitches together only the fibrous and the muscular layer, not piercing the innermost mucosal layer. He may reinforce the suture with a layer of peritoneum, taking care not to occlude the lumen with too many stitches. He then closes the wound in layers. short_description: Closure of ureterovisceral fistula (including visceral repair)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes a ureterovisceral fistula, or an abnormal connection between the ureter and an internal organ of the body near the ureter. He also repairs the defect in the internal organ. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the lower abdomen and exposes the ureter. The provider excises the muscles and surrounding fatty layers overlying the ureter for better visualization of the passageway from the ureter to the visceral organ. short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; ureteroneocystostomy with cystoscopy and ureteral stent placement
lay_term: The provider reimplants the ureter into the bladder using a laparoscopic approach. The procedure includes the use of a laparoscope, and cystoscope, or endoscope, to examine the bladder and lower urinary tract and the placement of a stent. The procedure is done to treat ureteral injury, stricture, and/or obstruction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision near the navel to access the abdominal cavity. She then introduces a disposable trocar. Next, she inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide, and passes a laparoscope through the trocar. The provider then makes other ports, or incisions, to insert other instrumentation as needed. She moves the instrumentation to view the ureter, and bladder through the laparoscope. She then dissects the tissue surrounding the ureter to free it. The provider incises the bladder in a direction which will allow the ureter to lie without kinking in the through. Toward the end of the dissection, she makes a small opening into the mucous membrane of the bladder, and lays the ureter into the trough. She then connects the ureter to the new position, and closes the trough. Still under laparoscopic vision, the provider inserts a cystoscope into the bladder, and she advances a ureteral stent up the ureter to the kidney. The provider then places a urethral catheter. She tests the repair by filling the bladder, and uses the laparoscope to look for any leaks. When no leaks are visible, she removes all instrumentation, and closes the abdominal opening in multiple layers. Terminology Cystoscope: A tubular surgical instrument that is used to examine the interior of the urinary bladder and ureter. Laparoscope: A tubular surgical instrument that is used to view the interior of the abdomen and pelvis. Stent: A tube inserted inside a tubular body part to provide support. Trocar: A sharp–pointed surgical instrument inside a cannula, or tube, used to withdraw fluid, administer a medication or solution, or guide the placement of a soft catheter. Ureter: duct that passes urine from the kidney to the bladder. Ureteroneocystostomy: Surgical procedure to transplant a ureter to a different site in the bladder. Tips Choose between code 50947 and 50948 based on whether the procedure is performed with a cystoscopy and ureteral stent placement. Read Less

short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; ureteroneocystostomy without cystoscopy and ureteral stent placement Notes: (For open ureteroneocystostomy, see 50780-50785)
lay_term: The provider reimplants the ureter into the bladder using a laparoscopic approach to treat ureteral injury, stricture, and/or obstruction. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision near the navel, and dissects down to access the abdominal cavity. She then introduces a disposable trocar. Next, she inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide, and passes a laparoscope through the trocar. The provider then makes other ports, or incisions, to insert other instrumentation as needed. She moves the instrumentation to view the ureter, and bladder through the laparoscope. She then dissects the tissue surrounding the ureter to free it. The provider incises the bladder in a direction which will allow the ureter to lie without kinking in the through. Toward the end of the dissection, she makes a small opening into the mucous membrane of the bladder, and lays the ureter into the trough. She then connects the ureter to the new position, and closes the trough. She tests the repair by filling the bladder, and uses the laparoscope to look for any leaks. When no leaks are visible, she removes all instrumentation, and closes the abdominal opening in multiple layers. Terminology Laparoscope: A tubular surgical instrument that is used to view the interior of the abdomen and pelvis. Trocar: A sharp–pointed surgical instrument inside a cannula, or tube, used to withdraw fluid, administer a medication or solution, or guide the placement of a soft catheter. Ureter: duct that passes urine from the kidney to the bladder. Ureteroneocystostomy: Surgical procedure to transplant a ureter to a different site in the bladder. Tips Choose the between code 50947 and 50948 based on whether the procedure is performed with a cystoscopy, and ureteral stent placement. Read Less

short_description: Ureteral endoscopy through established ureterostomy, with or without irrigation, instillation, or ureteropyelography, exclusive of radiologic service
lay_term: The provider examines the kidney, renal pelvis, and ureters using an endoscope, which is passed through an opening already established between the skin, and ureter. The procedure is done for the diagnosis of ureteral lesions and removal of ureteral stones. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, and anesthetized, the provider inserts an endoscope through a ureterostomy, a previously constructed external opening on the skin, into the ureter. He then passes a guidewire into the opening, and removes the ureterostomy tube that was placed when the artificial opening was created. Next, he passes the endoscope into the kidney, or renal pelvis. The provider may flush the area with saline to clear the visual field. He may also introduce contrast material into the area for X–ray of the structures, called a ureteropyelogram. After the examination is complete, the provider removes the endoscope, and guidewire instruments, and reinserts the ureterostomy tube, or he allows the passage to close by itself. Terminology Endoscope: Medical instrument consisting of a long, thin, flexible or rigid tube which has a light and a video camera used to view or image the inside of the body. Guidewire: A thin, usually flexible wire used as a guide for placement of larger devices, such as a catheter. Renal pelvis: Small funnel–like structure in each kidney into which urine is discharged before passing into the ureter. Ureter: Duct by which urine passes from the kidney to the bladder. Ureterostomy: A surgically constructed external opening from the skin into the ureter. Tips It is important that you determine that the endoscopy is performed through an established ureterostomy. It is equally important that you know the reason for the endoscopy including: biopsy, foreign body removal, etc. Endoscopy procedures include radiological services, but you should report them separately if performed, excluding the ureteropyelogram, which is included with this service. The code requires use of modifier 50 if performed bilaterally, and some payers may require RT and LT modifiers, so check individual payer’s guidelines. Read Less

short_description: Cystotomy or cystostomy, with fulguration and/or insertion of radioactive material
lay_term: The provider makes a surgical incision into the urinary bladder (cystotomy) or creates an opening in the bladder wall (cystostomy) to access the abnormal tissue. The provider then destroys abnormal tissue with fulguration (using high frequency current), by placing a radioactive substance in the bladder cavity, or both. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the lower abdomen and dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue to locate the urinary bladder. The provider checks the bladder by inserting a syringe and drains out any urine. The provider then makes an incision into the urinary bladder and identifies abnormal tissue. This procedure involves cystotomy or cystostomy. Cystotomy is a surgical procedure where an incision is made into the bladder. It is a temporary opening used during surgery to access the bladder’s interior. Cystostomy, on the other hand, involves creating a more permanent opening in the bladder, often to insert a catheter for long–term drainage of urine. This procedure is typically used when normal urination is not possible due to conditions like bladder obstruction. After accessing the bladder’s interior, the provider performs fulguration, radioactive material placement, or both. Fulguration uses an electric current to destroy abnormal tissue by burning it. The electric current generates heat, which cauterizes or destroys the targeted tissue. Alternatively, or in addition, the provider may place a radioactive substance into the bladder cavity to destroy the abnormal tissue. Next, the provider sutures the urinary bladder wall, as appropriate. The provider stops all bleeding and, if a cystostomy was done, the provider may suture a tube in place. Finally, the provider closes the abdominal wound, such as by suturing the soft tissue in layers. Read Less

short_description: Cystotomy, with insertion of ureteral catheter or stent (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision into the urinary bladder to insert a stent or catheter into the ureter. The aim of this procedure is to treat a stricture or blockage in the ureter. He then dissects down through the subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin and the muscles. He identifies the bladder and checks it by inserting a syringe and draining out the urine. He then makes an incision in the urinary bladder. Next, he places a catheter or stent in the bladder and passes it through the ureter, usually to facilitate normal flow of urine from the ureter to the bladder. Stent: A thin expandable tube placed through a narrowed area of a tubular structure, such as the esophagus, small intestine, or a vessel, to prevent obstruction and provide support after dilation. short_description: Cystotomy, with calculus basket extraction and/or ultrasonic or electrohydraulic fragmentation of ureteral calculus
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes an incision into the urinary bladder and removes a ureteral calculus, or stone, using different techniques of extraction, such as a calculus basket extractor and ultrasonic or electrohydraulic fragmentation of the ureteral calculus. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the abdomen overlying the urinary bladder. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin and the muscles. He then identifies the bladder and checks it by inserting a syringe and draining out the urine. He locates the calculus, and then he makes an incision in the urinary bladder wall according to the size of the stone. He removes the calculus from the ureter either with a basket extractor device or with an ultrasonic or electrohydraulic fragmentation method. He inspects the area for other defects then sutures the bladder incision and places a catheter for draining of the urine. This prevents urine leakage from the surgical site, which can lead to an abscess formation. Finally, he stops all bleeding, places a drain tube and closes the abdominal wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. He removes the drainage tube and catheter after five days. Terminology Abscess: Sac or pocket formed due to the accumulation of purulent material, pus, in the soft tissue, caused by infection. Basket extraction: A soft wire multifilament basket like instrument used for extracting calculus. Catheter: A flexible tube that a provider inserts into a vessel through which he can pass instruments, blood can be withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a provider can insert this flexible tube into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Electrohydraulic fragmentation: A method of removing calculus of the ureter using a probe containing two electrodes segregated by an area of insulation; the electric current passes to create a spark between the electrodes, which exerts pressure on the surrounding fluids; this leads to expansion of fluids, creating a shock wave; the shockwave exerts pressure on the calculus causing it to fragment, or break up. Ureter: Tube that carries urine from kidney to the urinary bladder. Urinary bladder: A hollow organ in the pelvic cavity that collects urine. Read Less

short_description: Aspiration of bladder; with insertion of suprapubic catheter Notes: (For imaging guidance, see 76942, 77002, 77012)
lay_term: Aspiration of bladder; with insertion of suprapubic catheter. Explanation Code 51102 is used for punch cystostomy, also known as suprapubic cystostomy. Urinary flow may be obstructed due to several reasons like BPH, kidney stone, cancer, or congenital defects. This procedure is performed to create a connection between the urinary bladder and the skin with a catheter. This procedure is performed for aspiration of bladder and for inserting a suprapubic catheter for passing urine. The provider locates the bladder above the symphysis pubis, sterilizes the area, and injects a local anesthetic 2 cm above the symphysis pubis. Some physicians use ultrasonography to locate the bladder. The provider then identifies the insertion site. The physician uses a 22–gauge needle with a typical 10 or 20 mL syringe attached to it. The physician inserts the needle over the lower abdomen until urine appears within the syringe. After the urine is obtained, the needle is removed, and a guidewire is inserted. A scalpel is used to make an incision near the guidewire. A suprapubic catheter is inserted over the guidewire, and the wire is subsequently removed. The urine in the bladder is aspirated through the suprapubic catheter. The incision is sutured by the physician. short_description: Cystectomy, complete; with bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy, including external iliac, hypogastric, and obturator nodes

He performs this procedure when cancer is present in more than one area of the bladder. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the skin of the abdomen overlying the urinary bladder. He then dissects down through subcutaneous tissue, or just under the skin and the muscles. He locates the bladder and the tumor in the bladder wall and assesses the extent of the disease. short_description: Cystectomy, complete, with ureterosigmoidostomy or ureterocutaneous transplantations
lay_term: The provider completely removes the urinary bladder and adjoining organs. The procedure is most commonly performed as a result of bladder cancer found in more than one area of the bladder, or to treat cancer that has recurred. The procedure also includes a method to reroute urine by surgically implanting a ureter into the colon, or joining the urethra to the skin. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped, and anesthetized, the provider places a Foley catheter in the urethra, and inflates the balloon with sterile saline. The provider then incises the navel to the pubic bone. She enters the peritoneal cavity, and exposes the bladder, and surrounding organs. She examines the tumor, and organs, and assesses the extent of the disease. She then retracts all attached tissues, and excises the entire bladder and surrounding organs. In female patients, the provider typically removes the uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, and possibly part of the vagina. In a male patient, she would usually take the prostate, seminal vesicles, which are the glands that help produce semen, and possibly the vas deferens, the duct that conveys sperm. In this procedure, the provider does not dissect any lymph nodes or nerves. She then creates a method of urinary diversion to remove the urine after the procedure. For example, if she chooses to implant a ureter into the colon, the provider makes an incision into part of the lower colon. She then folds the colon into a U shape, and stitches the edges together with sutures to make a pouch large enough to hold both urine and stool. She then cuts a small hole into this part of the colon, and inserts a ureter into the hole. Next, she secures the ureter to the colon with stitches. She may place a thin tube, called a stent, in the ureter to help widen the ureter so urine can flow through it without difficulty. She repeats the procedure with the ureter on the other side. She then closes the incisions and places a tube into the rectum to carry urine, and stool from the body. She closes the site and inserts a drainage tube, and catheter. Terminology Cystectomy: Surgical procedure to remove the urinary bladder. Foley catheter: Catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder. Retract: Drawn back. Ureter: Duct that passes urine from the kidney to the bladder. Ureterocutaneous: Between the ureter and the skin. Ureterosigmoidostomy: Surgical implantation of a ureter in the sigmoid colon. Urethra: Duct that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Read Less
