short_description: Cystectomy, complete, with ureteroileal conduit or sigmoid bladder, including intestine anastomosis
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes the entire urinary bladder. To maintain the outflow of urine he may create a ureteroileal conduit. In this procedure, he cuts a portion of the intestine known as ileum, sutures the ureters to divert urine into it, and connects the other end to the abdominal wall to create an external opening for outflow of urine. As an alternative approach to maintaining the outflow of urine, he may choose to create a sigmoid bladder. In this procedure, he replaces the bladder with a U or J shaped segment of sigmoid colon. He sutures the ureters onto this. He connects the newly made sigmoid bladder to the urethra for outflow of urine. He then sutures the cut ends of the intestine together to reestablish bowel continuity. He primarily performs these procedures to facilitate urine excretion following surgical removal of the urinary bladder due to severe trauma or malignancy. Explanation After the patient is appropriately draped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision below the navel in the midline. He separates and retracts the rectus abdominis muscle. He then retracts the abdominal contents. He exposes the ureters and divides them distally, tying them with long tailed sutures for identification. He then mobilizes the bladder. He divides the vas deferens in males and the round ligament in females. He ligates the blood vessels and removes the bladder. To create a ureteroileal conduit he then isolates a portion of ileum, sparing at least the last 25 cm of the terminal ileum for salt reabsorption. He transilluminates the portion to ensure its vascularity. He then sutures the cut ends of the intestine together to reestablish bowel continuity. He creates windows in the posterior layer of peritoneum, a sheath between the bowels and the genitourinary system beneath. He then draws the distal ends of the ureters through these windows and cuts and sutures the ureters to the ileal conduit to divert urine into it. He goes on to create the stoma, or the external opening, as follows. He makes an incision on a premarked area on the skin of the lower abdomen on one side. He then creates a channel by dividing through the rectus abdominis muscle and draws the distal open end of the ileal conduit through the channel. He rolls the wall of the tip of the distal end of the conduit back onto itself and sutures it to the abdominal skin, thus creating a raised mouth–like opening for discharge of urine, which can be collected in a stoma bag. The provider then ensures that there is no stretch or tension in the created conduit. He wraps it with overlying omentum for better revascularization. The provider may choose to create a sigmoid bladder instead of a ureteroileal conduit. In this procedure, he replaces the lost bladder with a U or J shaped segment of sigmoid colon. He sutures the distal end of the ureters onto this. He anastomoses the sigmoid bladder thus made to the urethra for outflow of urine. He then places drains and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Anastomosis: Joining of two structures separated previously. Cystectomy: Surgical removal of the urinary bladder that stores urine. Distal: Situated farther from the center of the body. Ileum: The final portion of the small intestine. Lumen: The space within an organ or structure. Omentum: A membrane that encloses the intestines. Proximal: Situated nearer to the center of the body. Rectus abdominis: A flat sheath–like muscle in the front of the abdomen. Round ligament: A fibrous band supporting the uterus or the womb. Sigmoid colon: An S–shaped part of the intestine close to the anal passage. Stent: An artificial tubular support placed within the lumen. Transillumination: Holding an object against light to highlight and examine its details. Ureter: A channel that carries urine formed in the kidneys for temporary storage in the bladder. Ureteroileal conduit: A new channel created by joining the ureters to the ileum for outflow of urine. Urethra: A channel originating from the urinary bladder terminating into an external opening for outflow of urine. Vas deferens: The channel which carries the sperm from the testicle to the urethra. Vascularity: Supply of blood. Tips For a radical cystoprostatectomy with sparing of lymph nodes and ileal conduit diversion, you can report the prostatectomy code in addition to 51590. Read Less

He goes on to create the stoma, or the external opening, as follows. He makes an incision on a premarked area on the skin of the lower abdomen on one side. He then creates a channel by dividing through the rectus abdominis muscle and draws the distal open end of the ileal conduit through the channel. He rolls the wall of the tip of the distal end of the conduit back onto itself and sutures it to the abdominal skin, thus creating a raised mouth–like opening for discharge of urine, which can be collected in a stoma bag. The provider then ensures that there is no stretch or tension in the created conduit. He wraps it with overlying omentum for better revascularization. The provider may choose to create a sigmoid bladder instead of a ureteroileal conduit. In this procedure, he replaces the lost bladder with a U or J shaped segment of sigmoid colon. He sutures the distal end of the ureters onto this. He anastomoses the sigmoid bladder thus made to the urethra for outflow of urine. He then places drains and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Anastomosis: Joining of two structures separated previously. Cystectomy: Surgical removal of the urinary bladder that stores urine. Distal: Situated farther from the center of the body. External and internal iliac vessels: Vessels that provide blood supply to the lower limbs. Ileum: The final portion of the small intestine. Lumen: The space within an organ or structure. Omentum: A membrane that encloses the intestines. Proximal: Situated nearer to the center of the body. Rectus abdominis: A flat sheath–like muscle in the front of the abdomen. Round ligament: A fibrous band supporting the uterus. Sigmoid colon: An S–shaped part of the intestine close to the anal passage. Transillumination: Holding an object against light to highlight and examine its details. Ureter: A channel that carries urine formed in the kidneys for temporary storage in the bladder. Ureteroileal conduit: A new channel created by joining the ureters to the ileum for outflow of urine. Urethra: A channel originating from the urinary bladder terminating into an external opening for outflow of urine. Vascularity: Supply of blood. Read Less

short_description: Cystectomy, complete, with continent diversion, any open technique, using any segment of small and/or large intestine to construct neobladder
lay_term: The provider completely removes the urinary bladder and adjoining organs. The procedure is most commonly performed as a result of bladder cancer found in more than one area of the bladder, or a recurrence of cancer. The procedure also includes the rerouting of urine from the body, through various techniques. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places a Foley catheter in the urethra and inflates the balloon with sterile saline. The provider then incises the navel to the pubic bone. He explores the abdominal and pelvic cavities and continues dissecting to expose the bladder and adjoining organs. He then examines the tumor and organs, and he assesses the extent of the disease. He then retracts all attached tissues, and completely excises the entire bladder, carefully removing it, along with the surrounding organs. In female patients the provider would typically remove the uterus, ovaries, fallopian tubes, and possibly part of the vagina. In a male patient, he would usually take the prostate, seminal vesicles, which are the glands that help produce semen, and possibly the vas deferens, the duct that conveys sperm. In this procedure, the provider does not dissect any lymph nodes or nerves. The provider then decides on the method to reroute the flow of urine out of the body. If he chooses a continent catheterizable stoma, for example, he creates a new urinary pouch to remove the urine after the procedure. He takes a small section of the intestines to make the pouch. He cuts open the bowel and folds and sutures it to create a pouch. The provider uses the large intestine to create the pouch, to act as a bladder to store urine. Where the small intestine joins the large intestine, he inserts a one–way valve to stop urine from draining out of the pouch. He brings the end of the small intestine to the abdominal wall and makes a small opening, called a stoma. This allows for catheterization, meaning the use of a catheter to drain the urine, through the stoma. This permits the urine to empty but also allows it to remain continent between catheterizations. The provider uses the stoma to pass a catheter to drain the pouch. He connects the drainage tube and catheters. Then he sutures the site and closes the wound in layers. Terminology Continent catheterizable stoma: Refers to a surgically created opening, or stoma, that allows the patient to empty his bladder by inserting a catheter through a convenient opening in the abdomen; This gives the patient the ability to retain urine or feces between catheterizations. Cystectomy: Surgical procedure to remove the urinary bladder. Foley catheter: Catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder. Retract: Drawn back. Ureter: Duct that passes urine from the kidney to the bladder. Urethra: Duct that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Tips Unlike 51595, the descriptor for 51596 does not include pelvic lymphadenectomy. If the provider performs a pelvic lymphadenectomy in addition to the 51596 procedure, report the pelvic lymphadenectomy separately using 38770. Append modifier 50 if he performs a bilateral lymphadenectomy. Read Less

short_description: Injection procedure and placement of chain for contrast and/or chain urethrocystography Notes: (For radiological supervision and interpretation, use 74430)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a chain into the urethra and or the bladder during the injection of contrast material for urethrocystography, an X–ray examination of the urethra and bladder using a contrast medium. He performs this examination to identify and diagnose abnormalities in the bladder and or lower urinary tract. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a catheter through the urethra and up into the bladder. He uses this catheter to fill and or empty the bladder so the provider can produce filling, voiding, and post voiding radiological images of the urethra and bladder. A bead chain device consists of a series of metallic beads threaded on a fine chain. Thin nylon threads are tied around the bead chain, which a provider introduces through a catheter. The provider inserts the tip of the catheter into the urethra and he moves the bead chain into the bladder. Next, he injects contrast into the bladder and the urethra and takes radiological imaging of these structures. He then evaluates the bead chain X–rays to study urethral or bladder position and mobility. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that a provider inserts into a vessel through which he can pass instruments, blood can be withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a provider can insert this flexible tube into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Urethra: A tube that drains urine out of the bladder and carries the urine to the outside of the body. Urethrocystography: X–ray examination of urethra and bladder using contrast medium. short_description: Injection procedure for retrograde urethrocystography Notes: (For radiological supervision and interpretation, use 74450)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a catheter through the urethra and injects contrast material into the urethra. The provider then follows the flow of the urine backward to the bladder for urethrocystography, an X–ray examination of the urethra and bladder using contrast medium. He performs this examination to identify and diagnose abnormalities in the bladder and or lower urinary tract. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a catheter into the urethra. Once the catheter is in place, he injects contrast material into the urethra for urethrocystography, an X–ray examination of the urethra and bladder using contrast medium. A retrograde urethrocystography, which the provider performs in this procedure, involves the insertion of the catheter into the urethral opening, but not into the bladder. The provider then injects the contrast through the catheter into the urethra and follows as it flows retrograde, or backward, into the bladder. The provider looks for the presence of abnormalities in the urethra and the bladder as well as any passive reflux of contrast flowing backward into the ureter, which connects the kidneys with the bladder. lay_term: Bladder irrigation and instillation are used to deliver medication directly to the bladder via a catheter. These medications are usually anti–inflammatory agents used to treat infection or conditions like Interstitial Cystitis. Explanation When performing a bladder instillation, the physician uses a catheter to fill the patient's bladder with a therapeutic solution — often called a "bladder cocktail". This "cocktail" is made up of various protective and healing agents. The cocktail stays in the bladder for varying amounts of time, depending on the patient's tolerance to the drugs. The bladder is then drained through the catheter. Irrigation, another common procedure, involves passing a saline or therapeutic solution quickly in and out of the bladder. This "flushes" the bladder of clots or debris. Tips Report CPT® code 51700 for both instillation and irrigation. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of non-indwelling bladder catheter (eg, straight catheterization for residual urine)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider places a non–indwelling catheter into the bladder via the urethra for the purpose of intermittent catheterization or catheterization to obtain residual urine left after voiding. A non–indwelling catheter is one that the provider places temporarily and removes after its purpose is complete, usually on the same day. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider cleans the urethral opening with an antibiotic solution. The provider then positions the catheter at the urinary meatus, the external opening of the urethra. Next, the provider pushes the catheter slowly into the urethra until urine is present. The provider then inflates a balloon at the tip of the catheter using sterile water and a prefitted syringe. The provider then gently retracts the catheter and once the balloon fits snuggly at the bladder neck, the provider fits the catheter tube to the collection bag for drainage of urine. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Urethra: Canal that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Urinary bladder: A hollow muscular organ in the pelvis that receives urine from the kidneys, stores urine, and transmits it to the urethra to be conveyed out of the body. Tips See 51702 when the provider places an indwelling catheter temporarily into the bladder via a simple procedure through the urethra. See 51703 when the provider places an indwelling catheter temporarily into the bladder via a complex procedure through the urethra. The procedure is complicated because of difficult anatomy or other patient–specific conditions. Read Less

short_description: Endoscopic injection of implant material into the submucosal tissues of the urethra and/or bladder neck
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider injects a natural or synthetic material into the submucosal tissue of the urethra and or bladder neck using an endoscope, a stiff or flexible tubular instrument with a camera at its one end that provider uses to examine the interior structures of a body cavity. He performs this injection to treat urinary incontinence, a condition in which there is a loss of bladder control causing urine leakage. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts an endoscope through the external opening of the urethra. The provider uses the endoscope to visualize the interior of the urethra and the neck of bladder. Using a guidewire, he then inserts a needle and injects a natural or synthetic material into the submucosal tissue of the urethra and the bladder neck. This material treats the weakness of the urethral sphincter muscles, which controls the exit of urine in the urinary bladder through the urethra. Terminology Guidewire: A flexible wire that provider inserts through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and stent. Implant material: These are synthetic material that provider uses for treatment of urinary incontinence caused due to weakness of sphincter muscles. Submucosa: A layer of tissue that lies beneath and supports the mucosal layer, moist tissue that lines the inner surface of certain parts of the body. short_description: Insertion of transurethral ablation transducer for delivery of thermal ultrasound for prostate tissue ablation, including suprapubic tube placement during the same session and placement of an endorectal cooling device, when performed Notes: (Do not report 51721 in conjunction with 51701, 51702, 55881, 55882, 72195, 72196, 72197, 77022) (For insertion of transurethral ultrasound transducer and ablation of prostate tissue using thermal ultrasound transducer performed by the same physician, use 55882)
lay_term: The provider inserts a transducer in the urethra for transurethral ultrasound ablation (TULSA) of prostate tissue. The provider may also insert a tube above the pubic bone for bladder drainage and may place an endorectal cooling device to protect surrounding tissues during the ablation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a specialized transurethral ablation transducer through the urethra, the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. This transducer is designed to deliver thermal ultrasound energy, which generates heat to ablate (destroy) prostate tissue. This is also known as transurethral ultrasound ablation (TULSA). During the same session, the provider may place a suprapubic tube by making a small incision in the lower abdomen, just above the pubic bone, to insert a catheter directly into the bladder. This tube allows urine to drain from the bladder during and after the procedure, bypassing the urethra and reducing any potential irritation or swelling in the area. Additionally, to protect surrounding structures, the provider may place an endorectal cooling device. This device is inserted into the rectum (the final portion of the large intestine) and helps maintain a lower temperature in the rectal area to prevent damage from the heat generated during the ablation. Tips See 55881 for the prostate ablation service, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) guidance and monitoring. See 55882 when the same provider performs both the transducer insertion and the MRI–guided ablation services. Read Less

short_description: Simple cystometrogram (CMG) (eg, spinal manometer)
lay_term: A cystometer measures the bladder's capacity, or bladder pressure. It evaluates the contraction and expulsion activities of the bladder, and is used to diagnose certain urinary disorders. Explanation In a simple cystometrogram (CMG), the physician places a small catheter in the bladder, and fills the bladder using gravity to measure the capacity and storage pressures using a spinal manometer. The cystometrogram indicates if the detrusor muscle is functioning properly and detects the capacity of the bladder and any abnormal detrusor sphincter contractions. If the patient's incontinence is due to stress, the cystometrogram will appear normal. Tips Code 51725 describes a simple CMG that uses a spinal manometer to measure bladder pressures at various levels of bladder fullness. Note that if your provider performs a complex CMG using electronic equipment for these measurements you should report 51726. Read Less

short_description: Measurement of post-voiding residual urine and/or bladder capacity by ultrasound, non-imaging
lay_term: Providers perform this ultrasound to measure the volume of residual urine in the bladder. Explanation Before performing this ultrasound, the provider asks the patient to urinate to void the bladder before the exam. The provider then assesses any volume of urine left in the bladder, or post–void residual (PVR). The provider places the patient in the supine position. The provider applies ultrasound gel on the lower abdomen and places the ultrasound probe (transducer) on the skin's surface. The transducer emits sound waves through the skin, which return back to the transducer as echoes. The transducer converts the returning echoes into electrical signals to calculate the volume of urine left in the bladder. Terminology Post–void residual (PVR): Refers to the amount of urine left in the bladder after a single act of urination. Tips If the purpose of the scan was to measure post–voiding residual urine, you should always bill 51798. Generally, you'll use this code when the urologist positions a portable ultrasound scanner over the supra–pubic area to measure the residual urine. Most of these scanners actually print out a tape, which should remain part of the permanent medical record. This tape will be your proof the service was performed, and also justify the necessity for the catheterization, if performed. If the scanner doesn't print out a tape (which is unusual) then the provider must document what he or she did, and the actual results of the test. The portable scanner's built–in software will record the post–void residual urine volume and provide the bladder's capacity based on the patient's actual bladder shape. If this scan shows a large amount of residual urine, indicating retention, then the provider will catheterize the patient. If this happens, you can bill the catheterization separately. You can bill a separate E/M visit on the same day as the ultrasound, but you'll probably need a 25 modifier. Carriers closely scrutinize separate E/Ms billed with 51798, so if there is not a separate diagnostic reason for an E/M visit, you shouldn't bill for it. Because 51798 has no separate professional or technical component, you can't bill only for professional services. There's no interpretation involved, because 51798 is only a measurement. You can bill for interpretation if the provider interprets a pelvic or bladder and kidney ultrasound. short_description: Anterior vesicourethropexy, or urethropexy (eg, Marshall-Marchetti-Krantz, Burch); simple
lay_term: The provider performs a simple anterior vesicourethropexy or urethropexy (elevation and fixation of the bladder neck and urethra) to restore the urethrovesical angle and treat urinary incontinence. Explanation After the patient is prepped and draped, the provider inserts a Foley catheter through the urethra and into the bladder to help guide the procedure and catch urine in an attached bag. The patient is placed on her back (supine) in the lithotomy position (knees bent) and given suitable anesthesia. The provider makes a Pfannenstiel (transverse) incision, or sometimes a vertical incision, over the lower pelvic area, down through tissues and enters the space of Retzius. He identifies the bladder and the Urethrovaginal angle with the aid of the previously placed Foley catheter. He inserts a finger into the vagina to identify the perivaginal and periurethral sites and places sutures in these areas. He palpates the bladder and uses a finger inserted into the vagina to aid in placing the sutures, avoiding blood vessels in the plexus of Santorini. For the MMK procedure, he places the sutures in the periurethral tissues, tents up the anterior vaginal wall with two fingers in the vagina, and ties the sutures to the periosteum (outer covering) of the pubic symphysis. For the Burch procedure, he attaches the periurethral sutures to the conjoined tendons or Cooper’s ligament, leaving a space between the ligament and periurethral tissue of about as wide as his finger. He may place additional sutures if needed. Basically, he has created a pubovesical cervical (PVC) fascia sling that brings the bladder neck and proximal urethra back up into the abdomen, correcting the urethrovesical angle and stabilizing intraurethral and Intravesical pressures. He fulgurates or ties off any bleeding vessels after controlling the bleeding with the finger in the vagina. He closes the incision in layers. The Foley catheter may be left in place until the patient is able to urinate on her own. Terminology Fascia: Fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia lies immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Foley catheter: A thin flexible tube that is put into the bladder to drain urine out of the body. Fulguration: Surgical treatment using high–frequency electric currents to produce heat in a part of the body, to increase blood flow, relieve pain, destroy unhealthy tissue, or cause bleeding vessels to clot. Lithotomy position: A specific patient position during surgical procedures and medical examination involving the pelvis and the lower abdomen where the patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Pfannenstiel incision: A semicircular incision that is made just above the mons pubis (pubic mound); it is often referred to as a bikini incision, since it remains hidden when wearing a two–piece bathing suit; it is considered a cosmetic incision for pelvic surgery. Plexus: A weblike collection of lymphatic vessels, nerves, or veins. Stress urinary incontinence (SUI): Urine leakage that occurs when a patient engages in an activity such as laughing, lifting, or sneezing; these activities place pressure or stress on the bladder and can result from a wide variety of causes, including multiple vaginal deliveries, obesity, pelvic tumors, or chronic constipation. Urethra: Canal that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Vesical neck: Neck of the bladder where the urethra and bladder connect. Urethrovesical angle: The angle between the urethra and the posterior bladder wall, which is usually about 90 degrees; when a patient develops a cystocele (a prolapse of the bladder into the vaginal vault or the vaginal canal at the vagina's internal end), this angle narrows and causes stress incontinence. Tips As noted in the descriptors for 51840 and 51841, you'll use these codes if you see the Marshall–Marchetti–Krantz or Burch procedure names in the urologist's documentation. These are usually referred to as a ‘MMK' or ‘Burch.' You would designate the MMK or Burch surgery as complicated (and therefore use 51841) if the documentation clearly supports these situations: (1) If the procedure takes an excessive amount of time to complete, (2) if the patient has extensive bleeding during surgery; (3) if the patient has adhesions from a previous surgery; (4) if the patient has vaginal prolapse, (5) if the procedure is a secondary repair, and/or (6) if the patient is obese making the procedure more difficult. Urologists also may use a vaginal approach to correct incontinence. In this case, you would report 57240. During this procedure, the surgeon folds redundant prolapsed tissue under the urethra and/or bladder neck to help support the structure. On the other hand, the surgeon may use a combined vaginal and abdominal approach to perform a suburethral sling operation. Here, you would report 57288. During this procedure, via a vaginal approach, the urologist places fascia or other materials at the urethrovesical junction to encircle and suspend the urethra. The surgeon then pulls the ends of the sling toward the symphysis pubis and fastens them to the rectus abdominis sheath via an abdominal approach. In addition to the combined approach, you should use 57288 when the urologist addresses SUI with a tension–free transvaginal tape (TVT). During this procedure, the surgeon places the TVT sling, providing new support to tissue with less morbidity than traditional sling procedures. Because the physician doesn't have to harvest graft material, they are able to minimize the number of incisions. Read Less

short_description: Abdomino-vaginal vesical neck suspension, with or without endoscopic control (eg, Stamey, Raz, modified Pereyra)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider suspends the bladder neck of a female patient by anchoring tissues on each side of the bladder neck and then suturing them to the fibrous tissue of the abdomen. He performs this procedure to treat stress incontinence, or the inability to hold urine during physical activities such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercise. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision in the supra pubic area of the abdomen to access the bladder neck, urethra, and tissues supporting these structures. The provider’s objective is to restore the angle of the vesical neck and the urethra to a normal position and stabilize the supporting pelvic tissue. First, the provider frees the vesical neck from its original position and realigns it by suturing the urethral vesical neck along with pelvic supporting structures to the fibrous tissues covering the pubic bone and the abdomen. Using an endoscope, the provider may perform these steps again to verify the suspension placement. Finally, the provider stops all bleeding, places a drain tube, and closes the abdominal wound by suturing the layers of tissue together. Terminology Endoscope: A stiff or flexible tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source to examine the interior structures of a body cavity such as colon, bladder, or stomach; other instruments can be passed through the channel of the scope. Modified Pereyra procedure: In this procedure, the provider dissects the vagina from underlying tissue at the level of bladder neck; he detaches the endoplevic fascia from the urethra and places sutures in the fascia to suspend the bladder neck. Pubic bone: One of the bones that makes up the pelvis, also known as the pubic symphysis. Raz procedure: In this procedure, the provider corrects urethral and bladder neck hypermobility when there is minimal or no herniation of the bladder into the vagina; he makes an inverted U shaped incision in the vaginal wall and releases the fibrous tissue around the bladder neck and urethra; next, he passes a needle through the incision, and pulls the suspending sutures, lifting the front of the vagina and urethra. Rectus muscle: The muscle in front of the abdomen extending from the rib cage above to the pelvis below. Stamey procedure: The provider performs this procedure vaginally or through a small incision above the pubic bone; the provider uses nylon suture to suspend the urethra on each side and cystoscopy to ensure that the urethra and bladder are not injured during the procedure. Urinary bladder: A hollow organ in the pelvic cavity that collects urine. short_description: Closure of vesicovaginal fistula, abdominal approach Notes: (For vaginal approach, see 57320-57330)
lay_term: A vesicovaginal fistula is an opening between the vagina and the urinary bladder. A urethrovaginal fistula is an opening between the vagina and the urethra. These afflictions often occur following an OB/GYN surgery for an enlarged uterus or other gynecological problem. Explanation The patient is brought to operating room and placed in a supine position. After administration of local anesthesia, a lower midline incision is made. The surrounding vesical space is mobilized, and the peritoneum is detached from the bladder. The bladder is opened by a longitudinal midline incision and then split posteriorly and downward directing towards the fistula. The fistula, fistulous tract and surrounding tissue are excised entirely. The opening of the vagina is closed with absorbable sutures in single or multiple layers. Terminology Vesicovaginal fistula: An abnormal opening between the urinary bladder and vagina. Tips See 57320–57330 to report closure of a vesicovaginal fistula via a vaginal approach. If the provider performs a DaVinci laparoscopic closure of a vesicovaginal fistula, you should not bill an open code (51899) for the procedure; since there is no code for a laparoscopic closure of a vesicovaginal fistula, you would need to report 51999 (Unlisted laparoscopy procedure, bladder). Send a copy of the operative report and a covering letter along with your claim. The letter should explain the what, why, and how of the laparoscopic procedure in layman's terms. Compare the laparoscopic procedure to the open abdominal vesicovaginal repair (51900), stating that the services are similar in surgical technique, time to complete the procedure, anatomy, and prognosis, etc. to ensure appropriate reimbursement. short_description: Closure of vesicouterine fistula

short_description: Enterocystoplasty, including intestinal anastomosis

short_description: Cystourethroscopy with incision, fulguration, or resection of congenital posterior urethral valves, or congenital obstructive hypertrophic mucosal folds
lay_term: Cystourethroscopy is the inspection of the interior of the bladder, the urethra, prostatic urethra, and ureteric openings by a cystoscope that is passed through the urethra and into the bladder. It is a common diagnostic procedure for conditions ranging from urinary tract infections and stress incontinence, to the follow up of bladder cancer treatment. It can take as little as 5–10 minutes of surgical time to complete this procedure. Explanation With the patient under anesthesia, the physician inserts the tip of the cystoscope (a flexible or rigid scope depending on the purposes of the physician) into the urethra and slowly glides it up and into the bladder. The camera attached to the cystoscope allows images of the bladder to be viewed on a monitor. The physician examines the urethra and injects sterile saline water into the bladder to improve the view of the bladder wall. As the bladder reaches its capacity, the patient will feel some discomfort and the urge to urinate if the patient is not under general anesthesia. On examination, the provider discovers that the patient has congenital, or present at birth, posterior urethral valves or obstructive, enlarged mucosal folds at the posterior urethra, either of which causes urinary obstruction. He may treat this condition in a variety of ways. if he chooses, he may incise the valves or mucosal folds to enlarge the internal diameter of the urethra. Alternatively, he may use fulguration, or burn the tissue with a high frequency electric current. He could also choose to resect or remove excess tissue to enlarge the urethral passage. When the procedure is complete, he withdraws the instruments and cystoscope and drains the bladder. Read Less

lay_term: During transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP), the surgeon inserts a resectoscope via the urethra and removes a portion of the prostate. This procedure includes several other urological surgery services, such as cystoscopy, meatotomy, and urethral dilation. Because these procedures are intrinsically part of the TURP procedure, you can't report them separately. Explanation After administration of anesthesia, the patient is placed in a dorsal lithotomy position and prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. A cystourethroscope is inserted to examine the entire bladder properly in all quadrants. If necessary, the provider enlarges the urethral opening (meatus) by incising it and dilates the urethra with a filiform and followers if needed. The provider may also resect the vas deferens. Now, attention is made to the enlarged prostate. Using a resectoscope loop, resection is performed initiating at the bladder neck and further down to the circular capsular fibers. Attention is paid to the left lateral lobe, and it is resected down to the capsular fibers. Next, attention is paid to the right lateral lobe resection, and it is resected in a similar fashion obtaining hemostasis along the way. The resectoscope is then moved to the level of the external sphincter and trimming of the apex is done. Hemostasis is obtained and instruments removed. Terminology Calibration: Measuring a structure, such as the urethra or vaginal canal, to make sure the internal diameter will accept a surgical instrument; also, checking the accuracy of a measuring instrument. Vasectomy: Resection of the tubes (vas deferens) that carry sperm from the testis to the urinary tract. Tips For first stage transurethral partial resection of the prostate, see 52601. For a second stage partial resection of the prostate, use 52601 with appended modifier 58, Staged or related procedure or service by the same physician during the postoperative period. The prostate gland can only be resected or removed once. If the patient develops obstructive symptoms postoperatively it is considered residual tissue from the prostate, but there isn't an actual gland left to be resected. Don't overcode:The TURP procedure, and the definition of 52601, includes several other urological services, including meatotomy and urethral dilation. Because these procedures are intrinsically part of the TURP procedure, you can't report them separately and, therefore, you should report only 52601. Remember: Do not choose a TURP code based on the technique the urologist uses for the procedure or on the amount of prostatic tissue he removes. short_description: Laser coagulation of prostate, including control of postoperative bleeding, complete (vasectomy, meatotomy, cystourethroscopy, urethral calibration and/or dilation, and internal urethrotomy are included if performed)
lay_term: Transurethral resection of the prostate is performed in cases of BPH (benign prostate hyperplasia) which commonly occurs in middle–aged and elderly men. It often causes lower urinary tract symptoms, with urgency, frequency, straining weak flow, infection, and incomplete bladder emptying. Explanation Laser coagulation / vaporization is performed under general anesthesia. During the procedure the physician inserts a cystoscope into the urethra to view the surgical field; if necessary, irrigation is performed for proper visualization of the area. Under visualization, a resectoscope is inserted through the urethra and passed on till the prostate. A laser–emitting fiber optic probe device is inserted; the target tissue is then fired with the laser. The heat energy conducted through the probe coagulates the target tissue, reducing the size of the prostate. In order to attain maximum efficacy, a side–to–side sweep technique is used in a clockwise and counterclockwise movement creating an open cavity. Also, during this procedure the physician can perform a vasectomy, meatotomy, and internal urethrotomy. Once the procedure is finished, a catheter is inserted and the patient is transferred to the recovery room. Report 52647 if the prostate is coagulated. short_description: Insertion of inflatable urethral/bladder neck sphincter, including placement of pump, reservoir, and cuff

This procedure treats incontinence due to a lax urinary sphincter or problems with incontinence caused by prostate surgery in males. Explanation Surgical techniques vary, but this describes one technique. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision to the suprapubic region and enters the pelvic space from the abdomen. The provider then attaches a urinary catheter and places the cuff around the urethra, near the bladder neck, so that the urethra closes tightly when the cuff inflates. He creates a space to hold the balloon in the pubic region, and places a pump in a pouch below the abdomen. The provider instructs the patient on how to use the device. During the resting state, the cuff inflates and the pressure closes the urethra, thereby preventing incontinence. short_description: Periurethral transperineal adjustable balloon continence device; bilateral insertion, including cystourethroscopy and imaging guidance Notes: (Do not report 53451 in conjunction with 52000, 53452, 53453, 53454, 76000)
lay_term: Under cystourethroscopic and imaging guidance, the provider uses a minimally invasive approach through the perineum to place an adjustable balloon on each side of the urethra to treat incontinence. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider performs cystourethroscopy and drains the bladder, leaving the scope in place to visualize and palpate the urethra, the tube that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. The provider makes incisions in the perineum, the area between the anus and external genitalia. The provider dissects through perineal tissues, enlarges the incision enough to allow insertion of a sheath, and advances the sheath toward the bladder neck under imaging guidance. The provider may dilate the tissue on either side of the urethral opening at the bladder neck using a tissue expander to make sure there is space for the balloon. The provider determines the appropriate size of the balloon, inflates it with solution, and removes air bubbles. The provider inserts the balloon through the sheath. Using imaging guidance, the provider ensures that the balloon is in the proper position and pulls back on the sheath. The provider inflates the balloon with more solution and confirms its position and inflation using imaging. The provider performs the same procedure on the opposite side and ensures that the urethra is intact using cystourethroscopy. The provider removes the cystourethroscope and confirms urethral closure by the balloons. Next, the provider creates pockets and places the ports for the balloons under the skin. The provider closes the incisions and, if necessary, inserts a catheter until the patient is able to void. Terminology Cystourethroscope: A flexible or rigid tube with a camera at its one end that is inserted through the urethra into the bladder to examine the urethra and urinary tract. Incontinence: Lack of control; as in inability to control urine or feces. Transperineal: Through the perineum, the area between the anus and scrotum in males and between the anus and vagina in females. Tips Codes 53451–53454 represent different adjustable balloon continence device services. Review the descriptors to ensure proper code choice. Read Less

short_description: Urethrolysis, transvaginal, secondary, open, including cystourethroscopy (eg, postsurgical obstruction, scarring) Notes: (For urethrolysis by retropubic approach, use 53899) (Do not report 53500 in conjunction with 52000)
lay_term: The provider treats postoperative urethral obstruction in a female patient due to prior antiincontinence surgeries and the formation of excessive scar tissue. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a midline U shaped incision in the anterior vaginal wall under endoscopic guidance. He visualizes the fibrous bands and periurethral scar tissue that adhere the urethra to the pubic bone and dissects them. After he dissects the scar tissue bilaterally, the provider uses sharp dissection to reach the retropubic space. He then mobilizes the urethra from the surrounding fibrous tissue until traction on the catheter causes some posterior urethral rotation into the vagina. Finally, the provider controls any bleeding, closes the incision in layers, and removes the Foley catheter before discharge of the patient. The provider performs cystourethroscopy to assess the damage of tissue or the source of the problem and later to examine the urethra after the procedure. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Cystourethroscopy: Endoscopy of the lower urinary tract that includes the urinary bladder and urethra. Endoscopy: Examination of a hollow organ or cavity using an instrument specially designed for the procedure; endoscopes include those designed for examining the upper and lower intestinal, or digestive, tract, the urinary system, and the upper respiratory system. Obstruction: Blockage. Retropubic: The area in the lower abdomen below the pubic bone. Urethra: Duct or tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body; in males, it is also responsible for carrying semen; divided in four parts, preprostatic urethra, which is the initial part of the urethra; prostatic urethra, which crosses through the prostate gland; membranous urethra, which is the small and narrow part of the urethra with bulbourethral gland at its back; and spongy urethra, which runs along the length of the penis and produces a spiral stream of urine. Urethrolysis: Surgical procedure to excise the surrounding tissue from the urethra and the pubic bone, done to treat urinary obstruction. Urinary incontinence: Involuntary leakage of urine due to inability to hold it. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus, or womb, to the external genital opening, or introitus; also known as the birth canal. Read Less

short_description: Urethrorrhaphy, suture of urethral wound or injury; perineal
lay_term: The provider sutures a tear in the urethra due to an injury in the perineal region. He performs the procedure to restore function, prevent infection and fistula formation, and to relieve pain. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, typically by local anesthesia, the provider cleans the wound. Then he pierces the perineal area using a needle and sutures the involved dermal and epidermal tissues in layers. He knots the suture in a manner that minimizes wound tension at the perineum and scrotal area. He does this to prevent future complications and fistula formations. He inserts a catheter for passing the urine until the repair heals. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Dermis: Layer of skin that contains connective tissues, situated immediately below the epidermis, the outermost layer. Fistula: Abnormal passageway between structures such as vessels, vessels and organs, or skin and organs or abdominal cavity. Perineum: Area between the anus and scrotum, or testicular sac, in males and between the anus and vagina, or birth canal, in females. Scrotum: The sac that contains the testes, or testicles, a pair of reproductive organs in males that produce sperm. Urethra: A channel originating from the urinary bladder and terminating into an external opening for outflow of urine. Urethrorrhaphy: Surgical procedure that treats the injury or fistula by suturing of the urethra. Tips To treat a urethral wound and injury in females, use code 53502, Urethrorrhaphy, suture of urethral wound or injury, female. To treat a urethral wound and injury in males, use code 53505, Urethrorrhaphy, suture of urethral wound or injury; penile. To treat urethral wound and injury in the area passing from the prostate to the bulb of the penis, use code 53515, Urethrorrhaphy, suture of urethral wound or injury; prostatomembranous. Read Less

lay_term: The provider performs this procedure for stitching of a urethral wound or injury in prostatomembranous region, the part of the urethra passing from the prostate to the bulb of the penis. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a standard perineal incision at the base of the scrotum. He further extends the incision to the fascia and muscular level to reach the prostate. Then he pierces the perineal area using a needle, proximal to the urethral defect, and stitches the injured ureteral wall to close the defect. After achieving hemostasis, which is stoppage of bleeding, he closes the overlying muscles and skin in layers. A catheter is inserted for passing the urine until the suture heals. Terminology Catheter: A tube that can be inserted into a body cavity, duct, or vessel; catheters thereby allow drainage, administration of fluids or gases, or access by surgical instruments; the process of inserting a catheter is called catheterization. Fascia: A thick fibrous sheath present along with and enclosing the muscles. Perineum: Surface area in between the thighs extending from the external genitals to the anus. Prostatomembranous: The part of the urethra passing from the prostate to the bulb of the penis. Proximal: Nearer to the center of the body. Scrotum: The muscular sac containing the male testes. Urethra: A channel originating from the urinary bladder and terminating into an external opening for outflow of urine. Urethrorraphy: Stitching of a urethral defect or injury. lay_term: The provider closes an opening or fistula between the urethra and penile skin to prevent infection and improve urination. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider closes or repairs a fistula between the urethra and penile skin. He makes an elliptical incision around the opening of the fistula and extends it to the deeper tissues towards the urethra. He excises the epithelialized tract of the fistula and turns the urethral mucosa upside down and does a multilayer repair. Typically, he inserts a catheter for urinary drainage until the area heals. Finally, the provider controls any bleeding and closes the incision in layers. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. short_description: Transurethral destruction of prostate tissue; by microwave thermotherapy
lay_term: Microwave thermotherapy is a treatment method that uses heat to destroy abnormal tissue. It is used to treat benign prostatic hypertrophy (BPH), a condition in which the prostate becomes enlarged due to abnormal growth of the stromal and epithelial cells of the prostate. As a result, the urethra becomes obstructed causing obstruction to the flow of urine and subsequent urinary disorders such as dysuria (painful urination), urinary retention, frequent urination, and urinary tract infection. Microwave energy (heat) is applied to the enlarged prostatic tissue, causing reduction of the enlarged tissue with simultaneous protective cooling of adjacent urethral tissue. Explanation The physician passes an endoscope through the urethra and advances it to the prostate region. A microwave antenna is introduced and under endoscopic visualization the benign hyperplastic tissues are destroyed using the heat generated at more than 44.5 C by the microwave antenna. Electrocoagulation is done to stop any bleeding. The endoscope and the microwave antenna are removed and a urinary catheter is placed to allow flow of urine until the patient recovers. Read Less

short_description: Transurethral destruction of prostate tissue; by radiofrequency generated water vapor thermotherapy Notes: (For transurethral ablation of malignant prostate tissue by high-energy water vapor thermotherapy, including intraoperative imaging and needle guidance, use 0582T)
lay_term: The provider uses a radiofrequency–generated water vapor thermal device to destroy prostate tissue to treat BPH and lower urinary tract symptoms. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized or sedated and in the lithotomy position, the provider inserts the proprietary RF–heated water vapor delivery device into the urethra under direct cystoscopic visualization. The provider positions the needle tip of the device distal to the bladder neck and targets the transition zone between the bladder neck and the prostate. The provider injects RF–generated water vapor into the prostate 1 cm from the proximal edge of where the lateral and medial lobes protrude into the bladder, angling the needle perpendicular to the median lobe tissue. The provider delivers the RF–generated water vapor in 9–second bursts circumferentially to the prostate. The provider retracts the needle after each injection and repositions it 1 cm distal to the previous site. The provider repeats these injections until reaching the prostatic tissue just proximal to the verumontanum, creating contiguous and overlapping zones parallel to the natural angle of the urethra. The total number of treatments varies depending on the size and shape of the prostate. When enough of the prostatic tissue has been destroyed, the provider withdraws the instrument. Terminology Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland, typically in older males, that may compress the flow of urine. Cystoscopy: Process of visualization of the urethra and urinary bladder with the help of a tubular instrument furnished with a light (cystoscope). Lithotomy position: A specific patient position during surgical procedures and medical examination involving the pelvis and the lower abdomen where the patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Radiofrequency (RF): Electrical current from a radio wave (a type of electromagnetic wave) used to transmit signals. Transurethral: Through the urethra. Verumontanum (seminal colliculus): An elevated area on floor of the posterior part of the urethra that marks the border between the membranous and prostatic urethra; it contains the openings of the ejaculatory ducts. short_description: Insertion of a temporary prostatic urethral stent, including urethral measurement Notes: (For insertion of permanent urethral stent, use 52282) (For insertion of prostatic urethral scaffold, use 0941T)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider inserts a sterile, disposable tube–like device in the urethra to prevent its collapse and allow proper flow of urine. The provider primarily performs this procedure to support and keep patent the prostatic urethra following obstructive swelling of the prostate immediately after treatment for benign prostrate hyperplasia. Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider passes a well–lubricated flexible measurement device through the meatus into the urethra. He then measures the length of the urethra from its origin below the bladder neck to its end just above the meatus. The provider selects a stent of accurate length. Using an insertion device, he introduces the stent in the urethra to position the stent’s balloon tip at the base of the bladder. He then inflates the balloon. He ensures that the stent is traversing the entire length of the prostatic urethra and attaches a distal anchor with a suture to the sides of the urinary meatus. He may use a retrieval suture near the meatus that can deflate the balloon when pulled; thereby allowing easy removal of the stent as needed. He slowly withdraws the insertion tool. The provider may place the stent as a short–term option to provide for voluntary passage of urine when there is an obstruction to the prostatic urethra. Terminology Benign prostate hyperplasia: A noncancerous enlargement of the prostate gland, typically in older males; may compress the flow of urine. Distal: Located farther from the center of the body. Meatus: External opening of the urine outflow channel known as the urethra. Patent: Open, for instance to keep the urethra open and unobstructed to allow free outflow of urine while averting the compression in the urethra due to an enlarged surrounding prostate. Prostate gland: A bilobed gland situated around the origin of the urethra in males; secretes an alkaline milky fluid during semen ejaculation that helps in keeping the sperm viable in the slightly acidic female genital tract. Prostatic urethra: The portion of male urethra adjacent to the prostate gland. Urethra: A channel originating from the urinary bladder terminating into an external opening for outflow of urine. short_description: Transurethral radiofrequency micro-remodeling of the female bladder neck and proximal urethra for stress urinary incontinence
lay_term: This is a minimally invasive treatment for stress continence. In this procedure the provider inserts a probe with a balloon tip into the bladder lumen and delivers radiofrequency in a controlled manner. The procedure reduces local tissue elasticity by denaturation of the tissue’s structural proteins called collagen. Explanation After the female patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts the radiofrequency probe with a balloon tip through the urethra to reach the bladder lumen and positions four tiny electrodes in the bladder neck submucosa. The electrodes transmit energy for a 60–second cycle while the provider irrigates the mucosa to avoid local tissue heating up. He then maintains the tissue thus treated at 65 degrees Celsius for 30 seconds. He then rotates and repositions the probe and repeats the procedure three times so that the bladder neck and proximal urethra receive a total of 12 foci of collagen denaturation as treatment. Terminology Denaturation: The process of disrupting the molecular structure of proteins by heating. Lumen: The space within the organ. Submucosa: The layer of tissue just below the membrane lining the lumen. Read Less

lay_term: Use 53899 to report procedures in the urinary system that do not have a specific code. Explanation The provider performs a procedure on the urinary system that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes, and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the operative notes or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial. Your payers will consider claims with unlisted procedure codes on a case by case basis, and they will determine payment based on the documentation you provide. Read Less

lay_term: The provider uses a cystoscope to insert a temporary device into the part of the urethra that runs through the prostate. The device compresses the tissue to induce ischemia (a reduction in blood supply). This process helps to relieve pressure on the urethra and improve urine flow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a cystoscope (a tube–like instrument with a camera) through the urethra (the tube that allows urine to leave the body) to visualize the bladder and prostate. Once the anatomy is assessed, the provider inserts a temporarily implanted device into the prostatic urethra. A typical device springs open like a stent, positioning itself within the prostatic channel, deliberately compressing the tissue to induce ischemia (a reduction in blood supply). Over the next several days, this controlled ischemia triggers tissue remodeling, causing the prostate tissue to erode or form small incisions, similar to the effects of a transurethral incision of the prostate. This process helps to relieve pressure on the urethra and improve urine flow. This code is specific to insertion of the device. Tips See 53866 for catheterization for removal of the temporary device. The provider uses one or more surgical techniques to remove or destroy the lesions. He may locally apply a chemical to destroy the lesions, use a high frequency electric current or laser to burn the lesions, or apply liquid nitrogen to freeze the lesions. He may also perform a surgical excision for which he makes an incision around the area of the lesion and excises it. If he excises the lesion, the provider closes the incision with running absorbable sutures. The chemical, electrodesiccation, cryosurgery, and laser surgery methods require no sutures. Papilloma: A benign tumor of epithelial tissues of the genital organs that the human Papilloma virus causes. short_description: Excision of penile plaque (Peyronie disease); with graft to 5 cm in length
lay_term: The provider excises plaque or abnormal fibrous tissues in the penis and closes the site with a skin graft of up to five centimeters, or cm, in length. The provider performs this procedure to correct Peyronie’s disease in which a patient may experience severe penile curves and pain during erection, or a lump within the shaft of the penis including shortening of the penis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises around the penis and retracts the skin to expose the plaque. He then excises the plaque, or abnormal fibrous tissues underlying the corpus cavernosum region, or the spongy erectile tissues in the penis. During dissection, the provider preserves all the important nerves and small blood vessels. When dissection is complete, he procures a suitable five cm or less skin or tissue graft from another part of the patient's body and places it on the penis to fill in the defect. Any skin graft measuring five cm or less is applicable for this code. The provider finally closes the skin incision with sutures. Terminology Autogenous graft: Tissue harvested from the patient’s own body used to replace diseased, damaged, or missing tissue. Cadaver: Body of deceased person.. Corpora cavernosa: Sponge like tissue in the penile shaft region, which contains most of the blood that is in the penis during an erection. Fascia: Fatty or fibrous connective tissue that covers, protects, and gives support to other structures; superficial fascia is immediately below the skin; deep fascia surrounds deeper structures such as muscles, bones, nerves, and blood vessels. Graft: To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structure with another material; repair of defects in body structures; artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis. Peyronie disease: A medical condition in which plaque or a hard lump forms on the superior or inferior side of the penis; sometimes results in severe curvature of the penis and pain during erection, and or shortening of the penis; cause is commonly uncertain. Tunic of testis: Three layer cover of the testes, the two egg shaped male reproductive organs that enables blood supply to the testes and creates a partition between the sperm producing areas of the testes. Tips Graft harvest may occur from multiple sources, eg, fascia, tunic of testis, and cadaver sources. When the provider obtains an autogenous graft through a separate incision, you should report this procedure separately. Read Less

short_description: Amputation of penis; complete
lay_term: The provider completely removes the penis. The provider performs this procedure to treat a serious injury or disease of the penis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider removes the entire penis due to a severe injury or disease. The provider makes an incision from above the penis to the base of the shaft and carries the incision forward to near the middle of the scrotum. The provider carefully divides the underlying structures and creates a new meatus between the scrotum and anus. The urethra is brought through this opening, and an on–off valve in the urethra above the penis level helps control the urination process. The provider closes the rest of the tissues and skin with sutures and places a drain in the scrotum to allow drainage of any fluid. The provider leaves a catheter in the bladder and closes the incision with sutures. Terminology Amputation: Surgical removal or traumatic loss of a complete or partial appendage of the body. short_description: Amputation of penis, radical; with bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy
lay_term: The provider completely removes the penis along with surrounding lymph nodes in the groin areas. The procedure is typically performed to treat cancer of the penis that is not responding to standard treatment or when the size and depth of a mass are extensive. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and sedated, the provider makes a circular incision around the penis beginning above its base and extending around the shaft to near the midline of the scrotum. He then incises the fascia of the penis and dissects the urethra. He places a vessel loop around the urethra to draw it back while he continues to dissect the penis. The provider locates the suspensory ligaments and vessels of the penis, clamps, cuts, and ties them off. Next, he makes a small circular incision in the perineum at the base of the penis below the scrotum, and he makes a tunnel through the tissue. He incises the urethra and pulls it downward and through the tunnel. He then joins the urethra to the perineum skin. He places a drain in the penectomy incision and closes the incision. He inserts a catheter into the new urethral opening. To remove the surrounding lymph nodes, the provider incises the pubic bone to the pelvic bone. He identifies, isolates, and carefully removes the node packets from the surrounding muscles, blood vessels, and nerves on both sides of the groin. He then rotates the thigh muscles over the defects and secures them with sutures. Finally, he closes and dresses the wounds. Terminology Fascia: Sheet or band of muscle, fat, and fibrous tissue that lies under the skin. Inguinofemoral: Pertains to the groin and thigh area. Lymphadenectomy: A surgical procedure in which the provider removes lymph glands from the body and examines them for the presence of cancer. Penectomy: Surgical removal of the penis. Perineum: Area between the anus and genitals. Urethra: Duct that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Vessel loop: A surgical device used to hold or position an organ to facilitate or improve the visualization of a surgical site. Read Less

short_description: Circumcision, surgical excision other than clamp, device, or dorsal slit; neonate (28 days of age or less) Notes: (Do not report modifier 63 in conjunction with 54160)
lay_term: The provider excises the foreskin of a newborn 28 days old or less; he uses a technique other than a clamp, other devices, or dorsal slit. Explanation The newborn, 28 days old or less, is placed on his back or in a molded plastic seat. His arms and legs are strapped down to prevent any unwanted movement during the procedure. The baby may be given a pacifier dipped in sugar to calm him. The skin of the perineum and thighs is prepared with Betadine® or pHisoHex® liquid antiseptic, and the area is draped in a sterile fashion. A numbing cream or local dorsal penile or ring anesthetic block or both cream and block may be administered. The provider can employ various non–device techniques to remove the foreskin. For example, he can free the prepuce from the glans and pulled it out from the glans, place locking forceps across the prepuce, and excise the skin flush to the forceps. Alternatively, he can retract the prepuce over the glans and make a circumferential incision around the shaft of the penis, then pull the prepuce back over the glans and make another circumferential incision around the shaft in the same position as the first one. He then makes a longitudinal incision between the two circumferential ones, removes the strip of skin, and sutures the raw edges. He may include the frenulum in the original excision or cut it separately. When the procedure is complete, the provider applies petroleum jelly over the wound and wraps the penis in gauze. Newborn circumcision diminishes the risk for cancer of the penis, urinary tract infection, and lowers the risk for cervical cancer in sexual partners. Terminology Corona of the glans penis: The protruding rounded border of the glans, which resembles a crown. Dorsal slit: An incision along the length of the foreskin on the top of the penis from the tip to the corona. Foreskin: Skin covering the end of the penis; this skin is a retractable skin. Frenulum of the penis: A small fold of membrane that attaches to the undersurface of the penis connecting the glans to the shaft and limiting the movement of the glans. Glans penis: Tissue present at the head of the penis; this tissue has erectile properties. Regional anesthesia: Medications administered by local injection used to block sensation in a specific part of the body during and after surgery; spinal and epidural anesthesia are two main types of regional anesthesia. Tips For the same procedure on an infant older than 28 days, see 54161. For circumcision using a clamp or other devices with regional dorsal penile or ring block anesthetic, see 54150. The procedure described by 54150 is likely to be performed using a Gomco® clamp, Mogen clamp, or PlastiBell®, but many new devices have been developed. Some of the newer devices are Zhenxi rings, Tara Klamp, SmartKlamp, Shang Ring®, and PrePex®. Read Less

short_description: Dynamic cavernosometry, including intracavernosal injection of vasoactive drugs (eg, papaverine, phentolamine)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs dynamic cavernosometry, a study to measure the pressure in the blood vessels of the corpora cavernosa. He also injects the corpora cavernosa with vasoactive drugs that dilate the blood vessels. The provider performs this procedure to measure the blood flow rate during erection and identify the severity of venous leakage. Explanation The provider injects vasoactive drugs into the corpora cavernosa to evaluate erectile dysfunction. The provider inserts a needle into the penis and injects a vasodilator like papaverine, prostaglandin E1, or phentolamine, or a combination of these vasoactive drugs. Then the provider measures the vascular pressure in the corpora cavernosum during an erection. The provider may pump fluid into the penis at a known rate and pressure to obtain the erection. The vasodilator drugs increase the diameter of penile blood vessels and the provider assesses and measures the rate of infusion necessary to obtain the rigid erection. He also measures the blood flow rate during erection, which helps determine the extent of the venous leakage. The provider may perform a cavernosography in addition to this procedure where the provider injects a contrast material and then takes X–rays to visualize any leakage. Terminology Corpora cavernosa: Sponge like tissue in the penile shaft region, which contains most of the blood that is in the penis during an erection. Dynamic cavernosometry: A study of the pressure in the blood vessels in the corpus cavernosum. Papaverine: A drug that a provider commonly uses to relieve muscle tightness. Phentolamine: A drug that helps to dilate blood vessels, especially in patients with hypertension. Prostaglandin E1: A drug that helps the blood vessels to dilate in patients with erectile dysfunction. Venous leakage: A condition in which the veins in the penis cannot prevent blood from leaving the penis during an erection; this is called venous leakage which leads to erectile dysfunction. X–ray: X–rays, or radiographs, involve using radiation to diagnose, manage, and treat diseases by examining specific body structures. Tips Erectile dysfunction may no longer be payable for 54230. Many diagnostic tests for erectile dysfunction were payable in the recent past, but may no longer be payable. The above tests may still be payable under certain circumstances, such as if the patient has a lifetime history of erectile dysfunction, a history of perineal trauma, or no response to injection therapy. lay_term: The provider performs nocturnal penile tumescence, or NPT, a procedure that electronically monitors the frequency, rigidity, and or circumferential changes of erections during rapid eye movement sleep, or REM, in the night. This helps the provider determine the extent of the patient’s erectile dysfunction. Explanation The provider places the patient in a comfortable position to conduct the test. An NPT device consists of two loops surrounding the penis that the provider attaches to a small computer. The provider places an elastic loop containing mercury around the shaft of the penis. Strain gauge test measures an increase in circumference of the penis depicted by stretching of the loop and a change in the electrical signal. An absence of erection signals impotence of a probable organic etiology, or cause. Terminology Mercury: A heavy silvery white chemical substance which is liquid at room temperature; it is commonly used in a thermometer to gauge changes in temperature. Rapid eye movement sleep, or REM sleep: The state of sleep where rapid eye movements occur and the person normally dreams. Strain gauge test: An examination that the provider uses to gauge or measure the amount of strain on a body part. Tumescence: Refers to the engorgement, or swelling of the erectile tissues with blood. Tips When the nocturnal penile tumescence and or rigidity test is done at home and not in the clinical setting, report 54250 to Medicare and other payers, for the interpretation of the test only. You should be able to report the code for each night the patient wears the device. Append modifier 26, Professional Component to each instance to indicate that the provider, typically a urologist, only interpreted the test. Since the patient wears the device at home and the urology provider isn't performing the test in the office or hospital, do not report the technical component. Because the provider will interpret each night's test, you should be able to report the interpretation for each night. Most often, each night the test shows slightly different results as the patient gets used to wearing the device. Some insurers and Medicare carriers will only pay for one night, but you should still report 54250 with modifier 26 for each night of testing. Your payer, however, has the option to pay for one, two or three nights based on its own policies or local coverage determinations, or LCD. Check with the payer first for benefit and coverage specifics. Read Less

short_description: Plastic operation of penis for straightening of chordee (eg, hypospadias), with or without mobilization of urethra
lay_term: The provider corrects an abnormal curvature of the penis known as chordee. This deformity commonly occurs in patients with hypospadias. He may also mobilize the urethra during this procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the penis at the area of deformity. The provider may use several techniques to correct the defect like removing extra fibrous tissues by excision, making the length of the penis on both sides equal, even removing normal tissue when necessary. The provider may also correct a urethral defect if any. The provider takes care to spare important nerves and vessels. Then he closes the incision with absorbable sutures and applies a dressing. Finally, the provider may create an artificial erection by placing a band around the base of the penis and using an injection of saline to determine the effectiveness of the procedure in reducing the curvature of the penis following the treatment. Terminology Hypospadias: A medical condition present from birth in some males in which the opening of the urethra is under the penis rather than at the tip of the penis. Mobilize: To make moveable; to move. Plastic procedure: A reconstructive or aesthetic surgery to improve the appearance of the patient; often referred to as cosmetic surgery. Urethra: The duct through which urine passes out of the body from the bladder. Read Less
