short_description: Plastic operation on penis for correction of chordee or for first stage hypospadias repair with or without transplantation of prepuce and/or skin flaps
lay_term: The provider surgically corrects an abnormal curvature of the penis known as a chordee, or he performs the first stage of an operation to repair a hypospadias, a condition where the opening of the urethra is under the penis. He may also transplant prepuce, which is the foreskin, or skin flaps onto the area of the defect he creates during the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider incises the penis at the area of deformity. The provider may use several techniques to correct the defect such as removing extra fibrous tissues, excision of the prepuce, or foreskin, or making the length of the penis equal on both sides. The provider takes care to spare important nerves and vessels in the area. The provider also corrects any hypospadias present. First stage hypospadias correction involves the division of the glans penis deep in the midline to the tip. The provider carefully unfolds the dorsal foreskin and divides it in the midline and performs a midline closure. The provider drains the bladder with a Foley catheter. He may also transplant a free or flap skin graft of foreskin to the operative site to cover the defect he creates while performing this procedure. The provider leaves the urethral opening on the anterior shaft of the penis for final repair in a second stage procedure. Then he closes the incision in layers with sutures and applies a dressing. The provider may create an artificial erection by placing a band around the base of the penis and using an injection of saline to determine the effectiveness of the procedure in reducing the curvature of the penis after the treatment. Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Flap: Tissue for grafting, typically removed from one place on the body and positioned in another; however, it may remain anchored and rotated from one side of an area to another. Foley catheter: A catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder; it is a flexible tube that the provider commonly passes through the urethra into the bladder. Foreskin: Skin covering the end of the penis; this skin is a retractable skin. Glans penis: Tissue present at the head of the penis; this tissue has erectile properties. Hypospadias: A medical condition present from birth in some males in which the opening of the urethra is under the penis rather than at the tip of the penis. Midline: In the middle. Urethra: The duct through which urine passes out of the body from the bladder. Read Less

short_description: 1-stage distal hypospadias repair (with or without chordee or circumcision); with simple meatal advancement (eg, Magpi, V-flap)
lay_term: The provider performs a single stage surgical procedure to correct hypospadias with a meatal advancement or V flap. Providers commonly use this technique to treat glanular hypospadias where the meatus is mobile, which can be pushed to the tip of the glans comfortably. He may perform a circumcision during this procedure and or correction of an abnormal curvature of the penis known as chordee. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision around the glans penis and dissects the skin. He takes special care not to injure the urethra. He produces an artificial erection to assess for chordee. The provider excises the extra fibrous tissue if he needs to correct a chordee. Then the provider creates another artificial erection to check the reduction in the curvature of the penis. He may also perform a circumcision if he finds it necessary. Next, the provider makes an incision in the underside of the glans. He brings the skin up to the glans and creates an opening by suturing in the head of the penis. The provider closes the incision with sutures. short_description: Repair of hypospadias complication(s) (ie, fistula, stricture, diverticula); by closure, incision, or excision, simple
lay_term: The provider repairs one or more complications that may arise because of surgery for hypospadias, a condition in which the urethral opening of the penis is abnormally located. The repair involves simple closure, incision, or excision. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider repairs one or more complications from previous hypospadias surgery. Hypospadias is a condition in which the urethral opening of the penis is abnormally located, typically on the underside. The urethra is the tube that carries urine out of the body. Complications may include fistula (an opening between two structures), stricture (narrowing), or diverticula (outpouching). The provider may fix these defects using techniques like dilation, simple suturing, closing, or incising. For example, to repair a fistula or diverticula, the provider may identify and excise them and then close any defect with sutures. In a stricture repair, the provider may open the narrowed area with dilating catheters. All the techniques which the provider uses are simple ones and do not include any flap or graft placement. The provider controls any bleeding and completes the procedure. Terminology Diverticulum (pl. diverticula): An abnormal pouch that opens in the wall of the intestines, bladder, esophagus, or other hollow organ. Fistula: Abnormal passageway between two structures, such as between two vessels or between an organ or the abdominal cavity and the skin. Flap (tissue flap): A patch of tissue taken from a healthy site of the patient's body and transferred to the site of repair such as a wound or burn; it retains its own blood supply and may be pedicled (still attached in part to the original site) or a free flap (still with blood supply but needing anastomosis, connection, to the blood vessels at the recipient site). Graft: (verb) To repair or replace defective or missing tissue or structures with another material; (noun) Artificial material, skin, part of a vessel, bone, or other tissue harvested and placed over or in a defect or used for anastomosis (joining) of two structures. Hypospadias: A medical condition present from birth in some males in which the opening of the urethra is under the penis rather than at the tip of the penis. Stricture: Narrowing, typically of a tubular structure in the body. Tips CPT® provides multiple codes for repair of hypospadias complications. Review the descriptors to ensure accurate coding. short_description: Corpora cavernosa-saphenous vein shunt (priapism operation), unilateral or bilateral
lay_term: The provider creates a passage for blood movement between the corpora cavernosa and saphenous vein to allow blood to move freely and relieve pain due to priapism. The provider may create this shunt unilaterally or bilaterally. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a shunt, or passage, to correct priapism, an erection of the penis for an unusual long length of time. The shunt channels the blood to the femoral vein in the thigh from the fatty erectile tissue of the penis. The provider makes an incision in the groin area, harvests the saphenous vein, and dissects the vein free of its attachments, creating a free segment about eight to ten cm, or centimeters long. The provider forms an elliptical or oval window through the deep fascia of the penis and the tunica albuginea. The provider pulls the free end of the distal portion of the saphenous vein through a subcutaneous tunnel with hemostats and anastomoses the end of the saphenous vein to the elliptical defect in the corpus cavernosum with sutures. In this manner, the provider creates a channel for the blood to flow from the penis to the femoral vein through the saphenous vein segment. With lesser blood flow through the shaft, the penis tends to lose its rigid state faster, instead of remaining in the erectile stage for a very long time. Report this code only once even if the provider creates the shunt bilaterally. short_description: Corpora cavernosa-glans penis fistulization (eg, biopsy needle, Winter procedure, rongeur, or punch) for priapism
lay_term: The provider creates a passage through which blood flows out of the corpora cavernosa to the head of the penis. A lesser flow of blood in erectile tissue lowers the penile rigidity and averts or treats a priapic condition. The provider may use a biopsy needle, rongeur, or punch instrument to perform the procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider creates a fistula to correct priapism, an erection of the penis for an unusual long length of time. The provider routes blood from the fatty tissue of the corpora cavernosa of the penis to another area called the glans of the penis. The provider punctures the top portion of the penis or glans with a biopsy needle and advances into the tip of the corpus cavernosum. Alternatively, the provider may use a punch needle or rongeurs to gain access. The provider removes a portion of the tissue from the glans until he reaches the corpus cavernosum to create a small fistula or joining path through which blood flows out of the erectile tissue of the cavernosa to the head of the penis. Thus, a lesser flow of blood occurs in the erectile tissue of the cavernosa lowering the penile rigidity and averting or successfully treating the priapic condition. The provider repeats this procedure on the other side. When the procedure is complete, he closes both puncture sites made to reach the corpus cavernosum tissues with sutures. short_description: Plastic operation of penis for injury
lay_term: The provider performs plastic surgery to repair a patient’s penis after an injury due to various causes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider repairs the penile injury, which may occur due to rupture of the tunica albuginea, corpus cavernosum, or even amputation of penis following an accident. The provider performs the plastic surgery repair of the penis using a number of techniques and with the help of skin grafts, or tissue grafts to reconstruct the penis. The provider harvests the tissue and skin flaps usually from the patient's arm, chest, or pubic area. He takes great care so that the nerve bundles and blood vessels remain intact. The provider debrides tissue as necessary and places the graft at the penile location and sutures the layers of tissue. He may also need to repair the urethra or other structures so as to provide a complete repair of the injured or severed penis. Include any suture, intermediate, or complex repair within the scope of this code. This procedure is also known as a phalloplasty. Terminology Amputation: Disability resulting from the loss or surgical removal of one or more limbs. Corpora cavernosa: The sponge like horizontal tissue in the penis, along the penile shaft which holds most of the blood that is present during an erection. Debridement: The procedure of removing damaged tissue or foreign bodies from a wound. Be sure to read the operative notes carefully, because some providers may verbally describe the procedure as a repair of a fractured penis when the written report actually describes something as simple as incision and drainage of a hematoma, 54015, Incision and drainage of penis, deep. short_description: Orchiectomy, radical, for tumor; inguinal approach
lay_term: The provider excises and completely removes one or both testes to treat a tumor. He performs the procedure through an inguinal (groin) approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an incision over the inguinal ligament. He continues down through the tissues and makes a small incision with a scalpel into the external oblique fascia in line with the muscle fibers. Grasping the edges of the fascia, he bluntly frees up the spermatic cord. He then cross–clamps the cord. Next, he removes the testis and all its associated structures through the incision. The provider takes care not to damage important nerves and vessels in the area as he clamps the cord and removes the testis or testes en bloc. He then opens the cord and clamps and removes the individual bundles of the cord to finish the complete testicle removal. The provider stops all bleeding by electrocautery. He then closes the external oblique fascia and the subcutaneous fat and skin. He may place an artificial testis in the scrotum before suturing closed the incision in layers. short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical; orchiopexy for intra-abdominal testis
lay_term: The provider performs a laparoscopic surgical procedure to move an undescended testis into the scrotum. He uses a laparoscope to perform this service, specific to an intra–abdominal testis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a transverse incision slightly above or below the umbilicus, or navel. He inserts the laparoscope through this umbilical port and places an additional trocar into the abdominal cavity through another port near the umbilicus. Looking into the abdominal cavity through the laparoscopic camera, the provider perforates the peritoneum on the lateral side of the umbilical ligament and the medial side of the anterior inferior epigastric vessel. He locates and pulls down the intra–abdominal testis into normal position inside the scrotum, which may require a two–stage process to perform. The provider mobilizes the spermatic cord as necessary so that the testis can return to its normal position in the scrotum. He then fixes the testis in place. He makes a small pouch to secure the testis to prevent retraction of the testis. Finally, he closes the incision with sutures. Scrotum: The sac that contains the testes, or testicles, a pair of reproductive organs in males that produce sperm. Spermatic cord: A group of structures that pass, cordlike, through the inguinal canal and include blood and lymph vessels, nerves, and the vas deferens, the tube through which spermatozoa, male sex cells, pass. short_description: Incision and drainage of epididymis, testis and/or scrotal space (eg, abscess or hematoma) Notes: (For debridement of necrotizing soft tissue infection of external genitalia, see 11004-11006)

Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider examines the scrotum and scrotal space for the location of the fluid collection. Then he incises the scrotum and locates the abscess or hematoma in the scrotal space. Next, using blunt dissection, the provider drains the accumulation of pus. If the location of the fluid is in the testis, then the provider moves the epididymis away and makes a small incision through the skin of the scrotum. He opens and incises the underlying tissues and tunica vaginalis, which exposes the testis. Next, the provider drains the abscess or hematoma. short_description: Excision of spermatocele, with or without epididymectomy
lay_term: A spermatocele is a cyst in the area between the epididymis and the testis. The urologist may excise the spermatocele with or without a partial excision of the head of the epididymis. Answer: According to the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Database (MPFSDB), spermatocelectomy code 54840 (Excision of spermatocele, with or without epididymectomy) cannot be appended with the bilateral modifier –50 (Bilateral procedure). short_description: Prostatectomy, perineal, subtotal (including control of postoperative bleeding, vasectomy, meatotomy, urethral calibration and/or dilation, and internal urethrotomy)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises the prostate gland through an incision in the perineum, along with the vas deferens, or duct that carries sperm. He also incises and enlarges the urethra, or external urinary duct, and takes measures to prevent blood loss after the procedure. He performs the procedure to treat a tumor or persistent enlargement of the prostate that is obstructing urinary flow. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes an inverted U–shaped incision in the perineum. He isolates the rectum from the prostate posteriorly, or toward the back. The provider examines the area and excises a portion of the prostate, taking care not to harm the seminal vesicles, the glands that secrete semen. He excises the vas deferens, the duct that carries sperm away from the prostate. He inserts a catheter, or tube, with a small balloon at its end into the urethra, the tube that runs from the bladder to the outside of the body, to enlarge the opening and ensure adequate urinary flow. If urinary flow is inadequate, he incises the urethra to enlarge it or incises the meatus, the urinary opening at the end of the penis, or male genital organ. The provider then places a drainage catheter in the urinary bladder to allow urine to pass and monitor postoperative bleeding while the wounds heal. The provider then irrigates the area, removes any instruments, and closes the incision. Terminology Bladder: A muscular organ that receives, stores, and transmits fluids; the urinary bladder stores urine; the gallbladder stores bile. Dilation: A widened area; the process of widening. short_description: Prostatectomy, retropubic radical, with or without nerve sparing
lay_term: The provider removes all of the prostate and some of the surrounding structures using a retropubic approach; he may or may not spare the nerve supply. The space of Retzius is entered; dissection is continued further to the urachus, and the bladder is freed. The endopelvic fascia is then opened and the levator ani fibers are pushed away to free the lateral prostate; this reveals the lateral and inferior aspect of the dorsal venous prostatic complex. If necessary, the neurovascular bundles may be removed. An autologous fascial sling may be created by cutting a strip of rectus fascia and placing it underneath the anastomosis with an angled clamp. Finally, incisions are closed. short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical prostatectomy, retropubic radical, including nerve sparing, includes robotic assistance, when performed Notes: (For open procedure, use 55840) (For laparoscopy, surgical prostatectomy, simple subtotal, use 55867)
lay_term: The provider uses laparoscopic technique and removes the prostate and some of the surrounding tissue but spares the nerve supply; he may use robotic assistance and, if so, this is included with this code. Explanation The patient is placed in a supine position, prepped, and appropriately anesthetized. The provider inserts a catheter through the urethra and into the bladder. He makes an infraumbilical incision and inserts the laparoscope followed by several more incisions where he places a Veress needle and trocars for the placement of additional instruments. The bladder is filled with saline to identify the bladder contours. The provider incises the pouch of Douglas and exposes the Denonvilliers' fascia. He divides the vasa deferentia with a bipolar forceps and frees up the seminal vesicles. He enters the space of Retzius and dissects down to the urachus, freeing the bladder. He opens the endopelvic fascia and pushes the levator ani fibers away to free the lateral prostate. This reveals the lateral and inferior aspect of the dorsal venous prostatic complex. The provider then ligates Santorini's plexus with sutures. Next, he dissects out the bladder neck and opens it up. He also opens up Denonvilliers fascia to access the seminal vesicles and vasa deferentia; further maneuvering exposes both the sides of prostatic pedicles. He dissects around the lateral margins of the prostate to preserve the neurovascular bundles. Finally, he transects the prostatic pedicles. He then dissects the apex of the prostate by sectioning the dorsal venous complex and transection of the urethra and the Denonvilliers fascia. He creates a urethrovesical anastomosis with six separate suture ligatures. He places a Foley catheter in the bladder prior to complete closure and instills saline to check for anastomosis leakage. Finally, He removes all instruments and trocars and closes the incisions. Radical retropubic prostatectomy is commonly performed in an individual who has early prostate cancer. This procedure is generally associated with complications such as urinary incontinence and impotence. There are several different ways in which this procedure can be performed, either open or closed. Terminology Laparoscopy: A surgical procedure where the provider makes small incisions into the abdomen or pelvis; inflates the abdomen with carbon dioxide for better exposure; then inserts trocars (ports) into the incisions to keep the incisions open so that he can insert, through one of the incisions, a laparoscope (a camera attached to a lighted tube to visualize the abdominal or pelvic cavity), and uses the other incisions for inserting instruments to perform the procedure; he removes the ports at the conclusion of the procedure, and typically closes the small incisions with staples or sutures. Radical resection: Surgical removal of a structure to include its vascular supply, associated lymph nodes, and a sufficient margin of surrounding tissues, especially around a tumor, to ensure that all diseased tissue is removed. Robot–assisted surgery: A surgical procedure conducted through a laparoscope with the aid of a mechanical (robotic) arm. Tips For nonlaparoscopic radical and subtotal prostatectomy procedures using various approaches, see 55801 through 55845. Read Less

Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes one or more small incisions and inserts laparoscopic tools. The provider uses the laparoscopic tools to excise part of the prostate gland, which is part of the reproductive system in males. This procedure is known as a simple or subtotal prostatectomy. The provider also performs a vasectomy, cutting through and sealing the vas deferens tubes that carry sperm. The provider measures the diameter of the urethra, the tube that runs from the bladder to the outside of the body, and/or dilates the urethra, such as by inserting a catheter with a small balloon at its end to enlarge the opening and ensure adequate urinary flow. The provider incises the urethra to enlarge it and incises the meatus, the urinary opening at the end of the penis. The provider may use robotic assistance during the procedure. The provider may place a drainage catheter in the urinary bladder to allow urine to pass. The provider ensures control of postoperative bleeding, removes any instruments, and closes the incision(s). Terminology Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel or other hollow structure through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; also, a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure for drainage or to instill fluids. Laparoscopic approach or procedure: A surgical procedure in which the provider views and accesses the abdominal and/or pelvic contents with a laparoscope (a tubular instrument with a light source and camera) to examine the interior structures of a body cavity; usually, several incisions are made, one for the laparoscope and additional incisions for surgical instruments. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Urethra: Canal that conveys urine out of the body from the bladder. Vas deferens (pl. vasa deferentia): The channel which carries the sperm from the testicle to the urethra. Read Less

short_description: Cryosurgical ablation of the prostate (includes ultrasonic guidance and monitoring)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider uses a rapid freezing technique to destroy cancerous cells in the prostate. She performs the procedure under ultrasound guidance. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts multiple thin needles along with a guide wire into the perineal region and monitors their placement via transrectal ultrasound. Then, under ultrasound guidance, she makes skin incision and advances dilators over each of the guide wires. She then removes the guide wires and inserts cryoprobes, the cryosurgery applicators, through the dilators into the prostate. She uses the cryoprobes to release super cooled liquid nitrogen into the prostate to free the tissues. The provider places warming catheters in the neighboring structures to prevent damage to them. She alternates the freeze and defrosts cycle to achieve tissue destruction. She monitors the temperature during the process via sensors. She then removes the cryoprobes, checks for bleeding, and sutures the site of incision. Terminology Ablation: Removal of tissue, a body part, or an organ or destruction of its function. Catheter: A flexible tube that can be inserted into a vessel through which instruments can be passed, blood withdrawn, or fluids instilled; a flexible tube inserted into a tubular structure such as the urethra to instill fluids, allow passage of urine, or examine the urethra and bladder. Cryosurgery: Surgical procedure in which a provider destroys abnormal tissue using extreme cold, commonly using liquid nitrogen, to freeze diseased tissue and destroy it. Dilator: An instrument that can be expanded in a vessel, valve, or other structure to widen the opening. Guide wire: A flexible wire inserted through a catheter to assist in positioning the catheter and other items such as stents. Liquid nitrogen: Nitrogen in a liquid state; commonly used to treat skin lesions or cancers in the skin or other organs. Perineal: Referring to the area of the perineum, between the anus and scrotum in males and between the anus and vagina in females. Prostate: Small gland that is a part of the reproductive system in males; secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Transrectal: Through the rectum. Ultrasound: The use of high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips You should not report ultrasound guidance separately, as it is included in the procedure. lay_term: The provider, a urologist or oncologist, places needles or catheters into the prostate for separate placement of radioactive "seeds" to treat prostate cancer; needle or catheter placement may be done independently of or during a concurrent cystoscopy. If cystoscopy is performed, that procedure is included and should not be reported separately. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider, a urologist or oncologist, guides needles or catheters into the prostate through a small incision in the perineum. He may perform a cystoscopy to examine the urethra, prostate, and bladder and to guide needle or catheter placement. If needle or catheter placement is included at the same time that he performs a cystoscopy, the cystoscopy is included and cannot be performed separately. After this procedure, an oncologist will place the radioactive "seeds," through the needle or catheter, which is reported separately. Terminology Brachytherapy: Placement of a radiation source in, on, or near the cancer site to treat the tumor effectively and minimize radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue. Cystoscopy: Process of visualization of the urethra and urinary bladder with the help of a tubular instrument furnished with a light (cystoscope). Interstitial: Situated within parts or interspaces of a tissue or organ. Intracavitary: Within an organ or body cavity, a hollow space within the body. Tips You should report CPT® code 55875 for only the needle or catheter insertions, not for the insertion of the radioactive elements. For ultrasonic guidance, use CPT® code 76965–26. Because this procedure is performed in a hospital or ASC, the facility will bill for the technical component. Cystoscopy is always included in CPT® code 55875, so don't bill separately for cystoscopy to evaluate the seed placement. However, if the urologist X–rays the pelvis and abdomen, report CPT® code 74018–74021 as per the abdominal views performed along with 26 modifier. Link all these procedures to the appropriate diagnosis code for malignant neoplasm of the prostate. CPT® code 55920 is to be used when needles or catheters are placed into pelvic organs and or genitalia for subsequent interstitial radioelements application. short_description: Ablation of prostate tissue, transurethral, using thermal ultrasound, including magnetic resonance imaging guidance for, and monitoring of, tissue ablation Notes: (Do not report 55881 in conjunction with 55882) (For insertion of transurethral ultrasound transducer and ablation of prostate tissue using thermal ultrasound transducer performed by the same physician, use 55882)
lay_term: The provider uses a transducer previously inserted in the urethra for transurethral ultrasound ablation (TULSA) of prostate tissue. The provider uses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) guidance for the service. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider confirms placement of a previously inserted specialized transurethral ablation transducer. Transurethral means the transducer was inserted through the urethra, the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. The transducer will deliver thermal ultrasound energy, which generates heat to ablate (destroy) prostate tissue. This is also known as transurethral ultrasound ablation (TULSA). The ablation system is connected to a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machine, allowing the provider to determine the exact areas of the prostate to ablate and the location of nearby structures to protect. The TULSA system carries out the treatment plan, creating heat to ablate the targeted prostate tissue. The provider can use the MRI machine to see the changing temperature in real–time, which allows the provider to monitor the heating and make changes if needed. The provider also can use the imaging to confirm the intended ablation is complete. Tips See 51721 for insertion of the transducer in the urethra, including placement of a suprapubic tube and endorectal cooling device, when performed. lay_term: The provider inserts a transducer in the urethra for transurethral ultrasound ablation (TULSA) of prostate tissue. The provider may also insert a tube above the pubic bone for bladder drainage and may place an endorectal cooling device to protect surrounding tissues during the ablation. The provider performs the ablation and uses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) guidance for the service. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts a specialized transurethral ablation transducer through the urethra, the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. This transducer is designed to deliver thermal ultrasound energy, which generates heat to ablate (destroy) prostate tissue. This is also known as transurethral ultrasound ablation (TULSA). During the same session, the provider may place a suprapubic tube by making a small incision in the lower abdomen, just above the pubic bone, to insert a catheter directly into the bladder. This tube allows urine to drain from the bladder during and after the procedure, bypassing the urethra and reducing any potential irritation or swelling in the area. Additionally, to protect surrounding structures, the provider may place an endorectal cooling device. This device is inserted into the rectum (the final portion of the large intestine) and helps maintain a lower temperature in the rectal area to prevent damage from the heat generated during the ablation. The ablation system is connected to a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machine, allowing the provider to determine the exact areas of the prostate to ablate and the location of nearby structures to protect. The TULSA system carries out the treatment plan, creating heat to ablate the targeted prostate tissue. The provider can use the MRI machine to see the changing temperature in real–time, which allows the provider to monitor the heating and make changes if needed. The provider also can use the imaging to confirm the intended ablation is complete. short_description: Intersex surgery; male to female
lay_term: The provider performs many staged procedures to convert male anatomy to female anatomy. The procedures include removing the penis, reshaping genital tissue to appear more female and constructing a vagina. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider dissects and removes the penis leaving vital structures intact. Next, he incises the scrotum, removes the testes, and pulls back the flap of skin. He dissects and opens the region between the scrotum and the anus. He then uses the patient’s excess skin to line the opening and create a vagina. He uses skin from the scrotum and surrounding area to fashion the labia. He shortens the urethra and moves the urethral opening to mimic that of a female. He then places a stent or obturator into the constructed vagina. Terminology Obturator: A prosthesis used to block a surgically created opening that helps with healing. Tips Coverage of gender reassignment surgery and the staged procedures considered to be a component of 55970 vary by payer, so check individual payer’s guidelines. Read Less

short_description: Intersex surgery; female to male
lay_term: The provider performs many staged procedures to convert female anatomy to male anatomy. The procedures can include removing the uterus and ovaries and reshaping genital tissue to appear more male and/or constructing a penis. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider removes the uterus and ovaries. He then creates a penis by using the clitoris that hormones have previously enlarged; or he constructs a penis by using free tissue grafts from the arm, thigh, or belly, along with an erectile prosthetic. For the constructed penis, the provider then reroutes the urethra through the fabricated penis to allow for urination. He uses the adjacent skin to form the scrotum, and he inserts prosthetic testicles into the constructed pouch. He then closes, or removes, the vagina. short_description: Partial hymenectomy or revision of hymenal ring
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider either partially removes the hymenal membrane or revises the hymenal ring. Explanation First, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. The provider then injects local anesthetic to block any pain. The provider preps and drapes the perineum and retracts the labia. The provider then uses tissue forceps to grasp the hymenal tags and makes an incision to open the vaginal canal. Once the vaginal canal is opened, the provider excises part of the hymenal membrane and completely removes it from the connection with the vaginal opening. For revision of the hymenal ring, the provider revises the ring of tissue inside the labia and inside the vaginal canal. After he completes the procedure, the provider sutures the cut margins with deep running stitches or sutures. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Hymen: A thin and incomplete membrane of connective tissue at the junction of the vestibule and vagina. It grows out of the perineum region and extends upward, leaving a small opening. It is normally in a half moon shape to allow menstrual blood to pass and is easily torn. Hymenectomy: The removal of all or part of the hymen. A hymenotomy (CPT® code 56642) is performed by placing a hole in the hymen or making a cross cut in the middle of the hymen. Read Less

short_description: Excision of Bartholin's gland or cyst Notes: (For excision of Skene's gland, use 53270) (For excision of urethral caruncle, use 53265) (For excision or fulguration of urethral carcinoma, use 53220) (For excision or marsupialization of urethral diverticulum, see 53230, 53240)
lay_term: Providers perform this procedure for persistent and recurrent Bartholin’s gland abscesses or cysts. Explanation After the provider administers anesthesia, he places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and preps and drapes the perineum. The provider examines the rectal and vaginal area to identify the area of the gland or cyst. The provider retracts the labia and incises the vaginal mucosa directly over the opening into the Bartholin's gland. The provider retracts the surrounding tissue to expose the wall of the gland, which he then carefully excises to avoid excessive bleeding from the pudendal artery. Because of the extensive blood supply in this area, he controls bleeding using either electrocautery or sutures along the bed of the gland. If the provider removes a cyst rather than the gland, he makes a wedge–shaped vertical incision in the vaginal mucosa of the cyst. The provider uses hemostats to grasp the cyst wall, and he uses scissors to dissect it from its bed. He irrigates the cystic cavity with normal saline. He may also insert a small closed suction drain into the wound and suture it in place. He then closes the incisions with sutures. Terminology Bartholin’s glands: Glands which are located on each of the labia, the vaginal lips, near the opening of the vagina. A Bartholin's cyst is a small, fluid filled, sac like growth that forms on the Bartholin's gland. The cysts commonly occur during puberty until menopause. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Hemostats: Instruments the provider uses to control bleeding. Pudendal artery: Artery that supplies blood to the external genitalia. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the providers performs a repair of the damaged area of perineum. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and preps and drapes the perineal area. The provider administers a general anesthetic and marks the area to be removed with a pen. This area is generally in the shape of an upside–down triangle with the base at the vaginal opening. The triangle will encase any scarred areas. The provider then makes an incision starting at the posterior wall of the vagina and following the triangular lines to end at the tip located on the perineum. The provider resects and removes the skin and mucosa within the triangle, along with the scar. The provider then gently stretches the exposed vaginal mucosa to the edge of the remaining perineal skin and sutures it together. The provider then uses two fingers to check the size of the adjusted vaginal opening. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Perineum: The short stretch of skin that starts at the bottom of the vulva and continues to the anal opening. Tips Perineoplasty is the same as perineorrhaphy, and the provider may document either term. Read Less

short_description: Colposcopy of the vulva
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a colposcope, which is an endoscope, into the vulva to examine it for abnormalities or lesions. Explanation First, the provider places the patient in a normal lithotomy position. The provider cleans the vulva several times with a 3 to 5 percent acetic acid solution, such as vinegar. When it dries, it will turn any abnormal areas to white, which is referred to acetowhite areas. The provider positions the colposcope about 30 cm from the vulva and uses several different magnification levels to inspect the entire vulva for any abnormalities or suspicious lesions. The provider may use a green filter to look for abnormal vascular patterns. If the provider finds no lesions or abnormalities, he reassesses the patient but does not perform a biopsy. Terminology Colposcope: A lighted, binocular, magnifying instrument that the ob gyn uses to examine the tissues of the vulva, vagina, and/or the cervix. Colposcopy: Colpo is a prefix that means vagina, and scopy if a suffix that means to view, so colposcopy means to view the vagina using an endoscope. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Vulva: The external genital area of the female. It includes the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, and the vestibule. The vestibule is an almond shaped area that is bounded by the labia minora, and it contains the openings for the urethra, Bartholin’s glands and vagina. Read Less

short_description: Colpotomy; with exploration
lay_term: The provider incises the vaginal wall and explores the pelvic cavity for any abnormalities. Explanation The provider may administer local, regional, or general anesthesia. The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and inserts a speculum to view the cervix, which the provider grasps with a toothed instrument called a tenaculum. This is done to expose the back of the vagina, clinically referred to as the posterior vaginal fornix. After the provider applies an antiseptic solution, he makes an incision into the pelvic cavity and explores the area using instruments. One of the instruments is a thin rod called an intrauterine sound, and it aids in active examination of the cavity to ascertain any conditions. After completing the exploration, the provider closes the incision with absorbable sutures. Terminology Colpotomy: Surgical incision into the posterior wall of the vagina, which is also called a vaginotomy. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure. It has two blades that are hinged, which are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when the speculum is in place. Read Less

short_description: Colpotomy; with drainage of pelvic abscess
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider incises the vaginal wall to drain an abscess in the pelvic cavity. Explanation The provider may administer local, regional, or general anesthesia. The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and inserts a speculum to view the cervix, which he grasps with a toothed instrument called a tenaculum. He punctures the abscess with a long hemostat, and the hemostat may be spread apart to enlarge the opening and allow the abscess to drain. He explores the cavity and may insert a drain to promote continued drainage. Once he successfully drains the abscess, the provider closes the incision with sutures. short_description: Incision and drainage of vaginal hematoma; obstetrical/postpartum
lay_term: The provider incises and drains a hematoma from the vaginal wall of a pregnant patient or one who has recently delivered and places a Foley catheter for continued drainage. Explanation The provider performs an incision and drainage of a vaginal hematoma on a patient who developed the hematoma during pregnancy or after delivery. With the patient appropriately prepped and typically under general anesthesia, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and inserts a speculum into the vagina to facilitate inspection of the hematoma. He cleans the perineum and vagina with an antiseptic solution. The provider incises the vaginal mucosa over the hematoma and drains the hematoma. He ties any bleeding vessels with sutures and irrigates the cavity. He usually places a drain and then closes the incised area with sutures. He then packs the vagina with gauze. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Foley catheter: Plastic or rubber tube used for drainage. Hematoma: A collection of blood outside the blood vessels, usually the result of a hemorrhage. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure. It has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when the speculum is in place. Tips Report 57022 if the provider performs the procedure on an obstetrical or postpartum patient, meaning the provider renders care and treatment related to childbirth and during the period before or after delivery. Report code 57023 when the provider performs this procedure on a nonobstetrical patient. Read Less

short_description: Destruction of vaginal lesion(s); simple (eg, laser surgery, electrosurgery, cryosurgery, chemosurgery)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider destroys one or more small or simple vaginal lesions. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. The provider applies a local anesthetic to the vaginal mucosa. Once the provider identifies the location of the lesion, he destroys it by using laser surgery, electrosurgery, cryosurgery, or chemosurgery. For laser surgery, he vaporizes the lesion tissue using a high beam of light to kill the lesion or lesions. For electrosurgery, the provider uses a monopolar or bipolar instrument to destroy the lesion or lesions. In cryosurgery, the provider uses an instrument called a cryoprobe to apply liquid nitrogen to the lesion or lesions with repetitive freeze and thaw cycles performed. For chemosurgery, the provider applies a chemical to the lesion or lesions and then removes the destroyed tissue. The provider may also use monopolar surgery, where the current passes through the patient to complete the current cycle, or bipolar surgery, where the current only passes through the tissue between the two electrodes of the instrument. Terminology Chemosurgery: Surgical removal of dead or diseased tissue after the application of a chemical agent or stain. Moh’s surgery is referred to as chemosurgery. Cryosurgery: The use of extreme cold to destroy lesions, such as liquid nitrogen. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Electrosurgery: Destruction of a lesion by heat using a high frequency electric current Laser: Acronym for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Laser surgery: use of laser light to heat cells or tissue in the area being treated until they burst Tips The term simple would normally apply to the destruction of small or simple lesions. Report code 57065 for removal of one or more large or complex lesions requiring significant work. Read Less

short_description: Vaginectomy, partial removal of vaginal wall
lay_term: The provider removes either the upper one third or the lower two thirds of the vagina. Explanation In this procedure, the provider removes only part of the vaginal wall. The provider places the patient in a lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider usually places sutures to mark the extent of the planned excision. Because the vagina has so many blood vessels, the provider will usually inject the area with an agent that helps with constriction of the blood vessels to minimize bleeding. If the surgery is performed via the vaginal approach, the provider makes an incision at the lower end of the area to be removed using a scalpel in a circular manner all around the vagina. At the upper edge of the area, the provider will dissect the vagina off the underlying structure with scissors to remove the diseased portion including margins. The provider applies sutures as the work progresses to stop any bleeders. Once the provider successfully removes the portion of vaginal wall, he closes the incision with sutures or packs the vagina with bleached cotton cloth. The provider may perform vaginal reconstruction by grafting at a later time. If the procedure is performed via the abdominal approach, the provider first identifies the vaginal vault with a gauze roll or sponge holder that is placed in the vagina to stretch the vault. The provider incises the area over the vaginal vault and dissects off the vagina. Special care is taken not to injure the ureters, since they are very close to the incision area. The provider then makes an incision into the area of the posterior cul–de–sac and separates the rectum from the vagina and the uterosacral ligament. Once the bladder, ureters, and the rectum are clear, the provider excises the diseased tissue as described by the vaginal approach procedure. The provider normally places drains when performing the abdominal approach procedure. Providers perform this surgery as a treatment for vaginal cancer, but sometimes, they perform it for severe chronic benign conditions that affect the vaginal canal or to biopsy large vaginal lesions where it is not known if cancer is present. Terminology Cul–de–sac: The extension of the peritoneal cavity between the rectum and back wall of the uterus; also known as the rectouterine pouch or the pouch of Douglas; also, any dead–end pouch. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Uterosacral ligament: Ligament of the uterus, extending from the cervix to the posterior pelvic wall. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Tips For a radical partial vaginectomy with excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57107, and for an even more extensive partial vaginectomy procedure that includes bilateral total pelvic lymphadenectomy and para–aortic lymph node biopsy in addition to excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57109. For a complete vaginectomy procedure, see 57110, for complete (radical) vaginectomy with excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57111. Read Less

short_description: Vaginectomy, partial removal of vaginal wall; with removal of paravaginal tissue (radical vaginectomy) with bilateral total pelvic lymphadenectomy and para-aortic lymph node sampling (biopsy)
lay_term: The provider removes the upper half of the vagina along with paravaginal tissue and all the pelvic lymph nodes on both sides of the vagina and biopsies lymph nodes in the para–aortic area. Explanation With the patient appropriately prepped and under satisfactory anesthesia, the provider makes an abdominal incision and enters the peritoneal cavity. After exploration, the provider removes the upper half of the vagina by dissecting the bladder off the anterior vaginal wall and the rectum off the posterior vaginal wall. This dissection will include the paravaginal tissues that surround the removed portion of the vagina. The provider carefully releases the ureters from the surrounding tissue to ensure they are not cut during the surgery. The provider cuts all of the ligament supports of the vagina. He removes the bilateral pelvic lymph nodes either before or immediately after excising the upper half of the vagina. The provider takes a biopsy of the para–aortic lymph nodes. He then cauterizes the bleeding and places closed suction drains. The provider closes the abdomen in layers. Because of the lymphadenectomy performed with this procedure, the surgery will always be an abdominal approach surgery, and the provider will remove the upper half of the vagina. Providers perform this surgery as a treatment for vaginal cancer, removing any adjacent tissue that may be diseased, the pelvic lymph nodes, and biopsying some of the para–aortic lymph nodes in order to assess the extent or the cancer. Terminology Lymphadenectomy: Surgical removal of one or more lymph nodes or glands from the body to examine them for the presence of cancerous cells; also known as lymph node dissection. Paravaginal tissues: The tissues that run along the sides of the vaginal canal and under the vaginal wall; also known as paracolpium. Pelvic lymph nodes: Located above and on each side of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries that work as filters and follow the course of the iliac blood vessels; they include the iliac, hypogastric, and obturator lymph nodes, which surround the iliac artery and branches. Para–aortic lymph nodes: The lymph nodes located near the aorta, in front of several lumbar vertebrae, that receive drainage from the upper gastrointestinal tract and the abdominal organs; the pelvic lymph nodes drain into the para–aortic nodes; if there is cancer present in these nodes, the cancer has spread outside of the pelvic region. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Tips For a partial vaginectomy without excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57106, and for a partial vaginectomy with just excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57107. For a complete vaginectomy procedure, see 57110, and for complete (radical) vaginectomy with excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57111. Read Less

short_description: Vaginectomy, complete removal of vaginal wall
lay_term: The provider removes the entire vaginal wall. Explanation In this procedure, a radical vaginectomy, the provider makes an abdominal incision and enters the peritoneal cavity. After exploration, he dissects the bladder off the anterior vaginal wall, and dissects the rectum off the posterior vaginal wall down to the level of the distal vagina. He carefully releases the ureters from the surrounding tissue and ligaments to ensure they are not cut during the surgery. The provider cuts all of the ligament supports of the vagina at the level of the pelvic sidewall so that the vagina is freely moveable. After clamping and suturing all of vascular connections, he removes the entire vagina. He irrigates the peritoneal cavity and cauterizes the bleeding. He then typically places closed suction drains. The provider may perform vaginal reconstruction at a later time. Terminology Lymphadenectomy: Surgical removal of one or more lymph nodes or glands from the body to examine them for the presence of cancerous cells; also known as lymph node dissection. Paravaginal tissues: The tissues that run along the sides of the vaginal canal and under the vaginal wall; also known as paracolpium. Pelvic lymph nodes: Located above and on each side of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries that work as filters and follow the course of the iliac blood vessels; they include the iliac, hypogastric, and obturator lymph nodes, which surround the iliac artery and branches. Para–aortic lymph nodes: The lymph nodes located near the aorta, in front of several lumbar vertebrae, that receive drainage from the upper gastrointestinal tract and the abdominal organs; the pelvic lymph nodes drain into the para–aortic nodes; if there is cancer present in these nodes, the cancer has spread outside of the pelvic region. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Tips For complete (radical) vaginectomy with excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57111. If the provider removes the uterus and vagina, check to see if a hysterectomy code, such as 58275 or 58280, would be more appropriate. Read Less

short_description: Vaginectomy, complete removal of vaginal wall; with removal of paravaginal tissue (radical vaginectomy)
lay_term: The provider removes the entire vaginal wall with removal of paravaginal tissues. Explanation In this procedure, a radical vaginectomy, the provider makes an abdominal incision and enters the peritoneal cavity. After exploration, he dissects the bladder off the anterior vaginal wall, and dissects the rectum off the posterior vaginal wall down to the level of the distal vagina. He carefully releases the ureters from the surrounding tissue and ligaments to ensure they are not cut during the surgery. The provider cuts all of the ligament supports of the vagina at the level of the pelvic sidewall so that the vagina is freely moveable. After clamping and suturing all of vascular connections, the provider makes a separate incision that takes in tissue that is lateral to the vagina. He extends the vaginal incision to meet the incision made through the abdominal wall. After this, he removes the entire vagina and paravaginal tissues. He irrigates the peritoneal cavity and cauterizes the bleeding. He then typically places closed suction drains. The physician may perform vaginal reconstruction at a later time. Terminology Lymphadenectomy: Surgical removal of one or more lymph nodes or glands from the body to examine them for the presence of cancerous cells; also known as lymph node dissection. Para–aortic lymph nodes: The lymph nodes located near the aorta, in front of several lumbar vertebrae, that receive drainage from the upper gastrointestinal tract and the abdominal organs; the pelvic lymph nodes drain into the para–aortic nodes; if there is cancer present in these nodes, the cancer has spread outside of the pelvic region. Paravaginal tissues: The tissues that run along the sides of the vaginal canal and under the vaginal wall; also known as paracolpium. Pelvic lymph nodes: Located above and on each side of the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries that work as filters and follow the course of the iliac blood vessels; they include the iliac, hypogastric, and obturator lymph nodes, which surround the iliac artery and branches. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Tips For complete (radical) vaginectomy without excision of paravaginal tissues, see 57110. If the patient still has her uterus, and the provider performs a complete vaginectomy, the provider will have to remove the uterus at the same surgery. If the uterus is absent, the provider is more likely to perform a complete vaginectomy with removal of the surrounding paravaginal tissue via a vaginal approach. If the provider removes the uterus and vagina, check to see if a hysterectomy code, such as 58275 or 58280, would be more appropriate. Read Less

short_description: Colpocleisis (Le Fort type)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider closes the vagina to treat vaginal prolapse. It is a vaginal approach procedure. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, usually with the addition of a regional anesthetic such as a pudendal block, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and carefully examines the genitalia and vagina. He then grasps the cervix with a forceps and prolapses the vagina. He removes rectangular or triangular segments of the anterior pubocervical and posterior rectovaginal fascia. After removing the skin, he stitches together the strong underlying supporting layers of the fascia with circular stitches. The prolapse is completely reduced back into the patient's vagina and pelvis, leaving a horizontal space through which uterine and cervical secretions can drain. The completed procedure usually leaves the patient with a shortened vagina, thus making the patient incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse. Terminology Colpocleisis: Surgical closing of the vaginal canal, partial closure or complete. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Pubocervical fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the anterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the bladder. When this tissue is weak, it can cause the bladder or urethra to prolapse into the vaginal canal. Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. When these tissues become weak, they can lead to the prolapse of the rectum into the vaginal canal. Vagina: Canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane. It extends from the vestibule to the area where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault. It is longer on the posterior wall, side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, side located below the bladder. Vaginal prolapse: A condition in which a portion of the vaginal canal protrudes from the opening of the vagina. Tips The bracketed Le Fort type wording gives an example of the type of procedure for which you can use this CPT® code. The descriptor does not, however, mean that you can only use this code for that particular type of procedure. Code 57120 is reported for any colpocleisis, including partial closure of the vagina. Additional Info The Le Fort procedure is often recommended for elderly patients with severe prolapse who are no longer sexually active but still have their uteruses. This surgery closes the vaginal canal so that intercourse is no longer possible. Providers perform a total colpocleisis on patients who do not have a uterus but have complete vaginal vault prolapse. short_description: Excision of vaginal cyst or tumor
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes a cyst or tumor in the vaginal wall. This is a vaginal approach surgery. Explanation The provider administers local anesthesia. The patient is in the dorsal lithotomy position. He cleans the area of the cyst with plain water or dilute vinegar, and the provider carefully examines the cyst/tumor area for excision under local anesthesia. The provider then makes an incision in the vaginal mucosa over the cyst or around the tumor. He excises the whole semisolid material, closed sac, of the cyst or fully excises the vaginal tumor along with supportive healthy tissues around the tumor. He may send a cyst sample to the laboratory for examination. Once the provider successfully excises the cyst or tumor, he closes the incision with absorbable sutures. Lastly, the provider may pack the vagina with bleached cotton cloth. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Vagina: Canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane. It extends from the vestibule to area where the cervix buts up against the vaginal vault. It is longer on the posterior wall, side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, side located below the bladder. Tips Do not use code 57135 to report the drainage of a vaginal cyst. Additional Info There are various types of vaginal cysts, such as Gartner's duct cyst, Bartholin's cyst, small cysts, and benign tumors, which are uncommon and made up of cysts. Vaginal tumors are abnormal growths of tissue in the vagina, and many vaginal tumors are secondary vaginal cancer that spread to the vagina from other sources. Read Less

short_description: Irrigation of vagina and/or application of medicament for treatment of bacterial, parasitic, or fungoid disease
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider washes out the vaginal canal and may also instill medication when the patient has a bacterial, fungal, or parasitic disease. Explanation In this procedure, the provider washes the vagina with a fluid or applies a medicinal drug to treat a bacterial, parasitic, or fungoid disease. The provider places the patient in a normal lithotomy position, meaning the patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and legs spread apart with the heels in stirrups. The provider places a hollow, flexible tube into the vaginal canal. He attaches a syringe with the tube containing antibacterial, antiparasitic, or antifungal solution that he gradually introduces into the vagina. The provider also may administer antibacterial, antiparasitic, or antifungal medication through a vaginal applicator into the vaginal vault to prevent vaginal infection. Terminology Pessary: A device that the provider inserts into the vagina, which gives structural support to the vagina, uterus, bladder, or rectum; a pessary can also be used to administer medication. Tips Report 57150 only when the physician treats bacterial, parasitic, or fungoid disease. Do not report 57150 when the provider washes out the vaginal canal during the removal, cleaning, and replacement of a pessary unless there is documented evidence of a bacterial, parasitic, or fungus infection. Even then, check with the payer to determine whether they will permit reporting 57150 in addition to 57160 for the fitting and insertion of a pessary. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of uterine tandem and/or vaginal ovoids for clinical brachytherapy Notes: (For placement of needles or catheters into pelvic organs and/or genitalia [except prostate] for interstitial radioelement application, use 55920) (For insertion of radioelement sources or ribbons, see 77761-77763, 77770, 77771, 77772)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts devices into the uterus and into the sides of the cervix that will hold radioactive material to treat cancer cells. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and places the patient in a lithotomy position. He performs a complete pelvic examination. The provider places a Foley catheter in the bladder. He places retractors in the vagina and visualizes the cervix. He applies a single tooth tenaculum to the anterior lip of the cervix. With the aid of uterine sounds, he measures the central cavity of the uterus. He dilates the cervix is dilated and selects an appropriately curved uterine tandem based on the patient’s anatomy. The provider adjusts the flange marker on the tandem to match the insertion depth, and he then inserts the tandem into the uterus. The other end of the tandem is left sticking out from the vaginal opening. The provider places a right and left ovoid on either side of the cervix and tests it for the correct fit. Once he determines the fit and makes adjustments, he reinserts the final ovoid assembly and affixes it to the tandem using a locking device. The provider may also place a vaginal pack to widen the distance between the bladder and rectum. The provider takes X–rays to confirm placement and to ensure that the bladder and rectum are far enough away to prevent damage to them once treatment is started. After the provider confirms correct placement, he removes the vaginal pack and performs a perineal suture or places a fixation device to secure the final position. The patient is then sent to recovery and is transferred to the radiation suite for the actual treatment. Terminology Brachytherapy: A form of radiotherapy where a radiation source is placed inside or next to the area requiring treatment. Foley catheter: A tube that the provider places through the urethra and advances into the bladder. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Ovoids: Hollow metal capsules that are small enough to fit in the vagina and up against the cervix. Shields in the ovoids prevent radiation doses to the bladder and rectum. Tandem: A hollow metal tube about 10 inches long and as thin as a pencil that the provider inserts through the cervix into the uterine cavity. Then the provider can also place a tandem in a Smit sleeve which was sewn in place at a separate surgical session. A Smit sleeve is a hollow plastic tube with drainage holes, custom fitted to the uterine cavity, inserted via the cervix, and sutured in place. It permits comfortable and reproducible positioning of the tandem. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum. It bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder. The body of the uterus is the widest part,and it lies above the isthmus. The cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips Removal of the tandem and ovoids is considered part of the procedure and would not be billed separately. According the Society of Gynecologic Oncology, the placement of the Smit sleeve would be reported using 57155 with a –52 modifier. It is placed at a different session than when the tandem and ovoids are placed, and it requires moderate sedation. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of a vaginal radiation afterloading apparatus for clinical brachytherapy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider fits and places into the vaginal canal a device that will hold radioactive material. She performs this service prior to treatment with radiation. Explanation The provider places a patient in a lithotomy position and performs a complete pelvic examination. She then places a Foley catheter in the patient’s bladder and a rectal tube in the rectum. She uses retractors in the vagina and visualizes the vaginal cuff. After she dilates the vagina and releases any post radiation adhesions, if applicable, the provider determines the largest possible size device to accommodate the patient’s anatomy. She puts together a vaginal cylinder in the appropriate width and length. She then inserts this device into the vagina and check for fit and stability. The provider may use vaginal packing at this point if she will use vaginal ovoids. She takes X–rays to confirm placement. Once she determines that the vaginal device is in the correct position relative to the perineum, she attaches the base plate of the cylinder to the end of the procedure table and locks it in place. The provider then transfers the patient to the radiation suite where, in a separately reportable procedure, the cylinder connects to a machine that will insert a low or high dose rate radioactive source, LDR or HDR, into the vaginal cylinder to treat the tumor. Terminology Brachytherapy: A form of radiotherapy where a radiation source is placed inside or next to the area requiring treatment. Foley catheter: Catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Ovoids: Hollow metal capsules that are small enough to fit in the vagina and up against the cervix; shields in the ovoids prevent radiation doses to the bladder and rectum. Perineum: The short stretch of skin that starts at the bottom of the vulva, the external female genital organs, and continues to the anal opening. Retractor: An instrument for drawing aside the edges of a wound or for holding back structures adjacent to the operative field. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Vaginal cuff: The end of the vagina close to the cervix. Vaginal cylinder: A hollow cylinder a provider inserts in a patient’s vagina and then places a radioactive source into the cylinder to treat cancer. Tips The removal of the vaginal device is included in payment for its placement. Additional Info Brachytherapy using this device is almost always performed after a hysterectomy for cancer to reduce the chances of the cancer spreading to the upper vagina. Read Less

short_description: Diaphragm or cervical cap fitting with instructions
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider fits the patient with a diaphragm or cervical cap and educates the patient on self–insertion. The purpose of a diaphragm is to prevent sperm from entering the uterus during intercourse to prevent pregnancy. The purpose of the cervical cap is for collecting menstrual flow or to assist in artificial insemination. The cervical cap is not a contraceptive. Explanation For a diaphragm fitting, the provider inserts a fitting ring into the vagina and covers the opening to the uterus. The largest ring that fits comfortably is usually the one the provider chooses. Different types and sizes of diaphragms are available. A cervical cap is usually fitted to prevent pregnancy; it blocks most sperm from entering the uterus. The provider educates the patient on the proper type and size of diaphragm or cervical cap and provides instructions of how to insert and position the device on her own. Instructions for the diaphragm may include that spermicidal cream or jelly should be used with the diaphragm. Terminology Cervical cap: A soft rubber cap with a rim that fits around the cervix. Cervix: Smaller portion of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal and consists of three areas: the external os opens into the vagina, called the ectocervix, the transformation zone lies just inside the os, and the endocervix, which lies just below the internal os, or opening, into the body of the uterus. Diaphragm: A soft latex or silicone dome with a spring molded into the rim, which creates a seal against the walls of the vagina. Read Less

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider sutures a laceration of the vaginal wall and or perineum that is not related to childbirth or pregnancy. Explanation The physician may use local, regional, or general anesthesia to block any pain and keep the patient sedated throughout the surgery. The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. The physician inserts a vaginal instrument to hold open the vagina during the procedure. The physician then makes an incision into the vagina to identify the open wound area or the defect. Once he identifies the underlying fascial defect, he closes the defect with sutures. The physician then repairs the perineum. The physician identifies the laceration and removes any excess skin. He then sutures the perineal laceration and pleats up the underlying muscle with sutures. Once the provider repairs the vagina and or perineum, he removes the vaginal instrument, may remove any excess amount of vaginal skin, if required, and finally closes the incision with subcuticular stitches. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Enterocele: When the small intestines and perineum protrude into the vaginal canal. Rectocele: A bulge of rectal tissue through a tear between the rectum and vagina. It happens during childbirth or with a hysterectomy. Subcuticular suture: Also called an intradermal suture, a type of suture used in many ob–gyn procedures, which is nearly invisible when complete. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane. It extends from the vestibule to area where the cervix buts up against the vaginal vault. It is longer on the posterior wall, side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, side located below the bladder. Tips A colpoperineorrhaphy is bundled into all rectocele repairs and would also be bundled with the codes that combine the anterior and posterior colporrhaphy and the anterior and posterior colporrhaphy, or vaginal wall repair, with enterocele repair. short_description: Anterior colporrhaphy, repair of cystocele with or without repair of urethrocele, including cystourethroscopy, when performed Notes: (Do not report 57240 in conjunction with 52000)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs the vaginal wall where a prolapsing bladder is pushing through. He uses a vaginal approach. The provider may or may not perform a urethrocele repair and cystourethroscopy, examination of the bladder using a lighted tubular instrument. Explanation After administering regional or general anesthesia, the surgeon inserts a speculum into the vagina to hold it open during the procedure. He makes an incision into the anterior vaginal skin to expose the damaged pubocervical fascia, which supports the bladder and urethra. Using delayed absorbable or permanent sutures, the provider plicates the fascia in the midline. He identifies the weak edges of the deep vaginal wall and sutures the strong tissue next to the edges to each other, raising the bladder up and forming a strong wall below this. The provider removes excess vaginal skin. If there is a urethrocele, he reduces it in a similar manner. He may perform a cystourethroscopy to visualize the bladder and urethra and to make sure that the repair has not injured these structures. Plication: The process of folding and suturing tissues. Pubocervical fascia: Tissue underlying the front vaginal wall that supports the bladder, bladder neck, and urethra. short_description: Combined anteroposterior colporrhaphy, including cystourethroscopy, when performed Notes: (Do not report 57260 in conjunction with 52000)
lay_term: The provider repairs the vaginal tissues over the weakened spots to support the area and return the bladder and rectum to their correct positions. This is a vaginal approach procedure. The provider may or may not perform cystourethroscopy. Patients need this procedure because they have problems with the bladder prolapsing into the vaginal canal and also into the rectum. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. The surgery combines repair of both the anterior and posterior vaginal walls. For the anterior repair, the provider makes an incision into the anterior vaginal skin to expose the damaged pubocervical fascia, which supports the bladder and urethra. Using delayed absorbable or permanent sutures, the provider plicates the fascia in the midline. He identifies the weak edges of the deep vaginal wall and sutures the strong tissue next to the edges to each other, raising the bladder and forming a strong wall below this. The provider removes excess vaginal skin. He then closes the vaginal incision with dissolving stitches. For the posterior repair, the provider performs a rectal exam to check for the extent of the rectocele. He makes an incision in the posterior vaginal wall from the top of the vagina to the levator muscles. He plicates the fascia and then brings the edges together and sutures them, making sure that some of the levator muscle is included in the repair. He removes excess vaginal wall tissue. He may perform a cystourethroscopy to visualize the bladder and urethra and to make sure that the repair has not injured these structures. When the provider performs perineorrhaphy, he also repairs the levator and perineal muscles. The provider also adds vaginal packing. Levator ani: A compound muscle in the pelvis that is formed by the pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus muscles. It helps to prevent pelvic prolapse and bring the anus back up after a bowel movement. Perineorrhaphy: Surgical suturing of the perineum. Plicates, plication, pleats: A technique where a provider makes tucks in a structure and sutures it to shorten it. Rectocele: A bulging of rectal tissue into the vagina through a tear in the rectovaginal fascia or septum. lay_term: In this procedure, the vaginal walls that hold the bladder, the rectum and the small bowel in place are weak, and the provider must repair the areas in the wall to support these structures with sutures. This is a vaginal approach procedure and includes the repair of an enterocele, when the small intestines and perineum protrude into the vaginal canal. The provider may or may not perform cystourethroscopy, examination of the bladder and urethra with a lighted tubular instrument.
