short_description: Insertion of mesh or other prosthesis for repair of pelvic floor defect, each site (anterior, posterior compartment), vaginal approach (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure) Notes: (Use 57267 in conjunction with 45560, 57240-57265, 57285)
lay_term: The provider inserts a prosthetic graft over the anterior and or posterior vaginal wall because of the lack of reasonable tissue strength. This is a vaginal approach procedure. This is an add–on procedure and must be reported in conjunction with a code for the primary procedure. Explanation The surgery for the basic vaginal wall surgery is already underway when the provider performs the graft. He cuts the surgical graft material to size for the area that needs to be reinforced. He places sutures deep into the pelvis to ensure the graft will be held in place. He places extra sutures in the levator muscles, the side of the vagina, and the graft to complete its attachment to the vaginal wall. The provider then removes excess vaginal tissue and irrigates the site. He closes any remaining vaginal tissue with running sutures and packs the vagina with gauze. Terminology Levator ani: A compound muscle in the pelvis that is formed by the pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus muscles. It helps prevent pelvic prolapse and bring the anus back up after a bowel movement. Tips Code +56267 is an add–on code, which means that you must code it with another procedure. It also does not take a modifier, and payers reimburse it based on intraoperative work only. It can be billed once for the insertion of the graft material on the anterior wall and once for insertion of graft material on the posterior wall. It may only be reported with the following procedures codes: 45560, 57240, 57250, 57260, 57265, and 57285. Because this is an add–on code, it must be medically justified in its application just as any other surgical procedure. The purpose of the mesh is to shore up vaginal wall fascia that is weak or attenuated, where sutures are inadequate to complete the repair. Therefore, look for documentation that indicates this. short_description: Repair of enterocele, vaginal approach (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider repairs the vaginal wall where the small bowel is pushing through to the vaginal canal. This is a vaginal approach procedure. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and also places a Foley catheter. The provider grasps the vagina over the enterocele with clamps and sizes the boundaries. The provider makes a midline incision through the vaginal fascia over the enterocele and dissects the vaginal tissue away until the sac is freely mobile. The provider may perform a rectal exam if the enterocele sac is difficult to distinguish from the rectum. After the provider dissects the enterocele sac from the vagina and the rectum, they enter and explore it to make sure that no small bowel or omental adhesions are present. The provider sutures the sac closed and removes any excess vaginal wall. The provider then inserts vaginal packing. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Enterocele: A bulging of the small intestines and perineum into the vaginal canal. Foley catheter: A tube that the provider places through the urethra and advances into the bladder. Omentum: Peritoneal fold that covers the intestines. Tips The descriptor for this code indicates the procedure is a “separate procedure.” This designation means that providers often perform this procedure as an integral part of a more comprehensive service or procedure. You should not report 57268 together with the code for the more comprehensive service or procedure. You may report 57268 when the provider performs the procedure independently. You also may report 57268 when any same–session services and procedures are unrelated or distinct from 57268. You may need to append modifier 59 or another payer–approved modifier to indicate 57268 is a distinct procedure. Another term for a vaginal enterocele repair is a McCall’s culdoplasty. This is an integral part of all hysterectomy procedures, as this represents a prophylactic procedure to prevent an enterocele from forming after the uterus has been removed. Read Less

short_description: Repair of enterocele, abdominal approach (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the physician performs either a Halban or a Moschowitz repair of the vaginal wall over the area where the small bowel is prolapsing into the vaginal canal. This is an abdominal approach procedure. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and appropriately preps and drapes the patient. The provider explores the abdomen through an abdominal incision and locates the enterocele. He isolates the enterocele by dissecting it away from the vaginal wall, and then he opens the sac and enters the peritoneal cavity. After making sure that the small bowel is packed away, the provider repairs the weakness of the vaginal wall by either performing a Halban repair or a Moschcowitz repair to obliterate the enterocele sac. In the Halban procedure, the physician uses longitudinal sutures that go through the covering tissue of the sigmoid, into the deep peritoneum of the cul–de–sac, and up the posterior vaginal wall. He then ties the sutures together. In the Moschcowitz procedure, the physician puts pursestring sutures around the cul–de–sac, including the posterior vaginal wall, the right pelvic sidewall, the covering tissue of the sigmoid, and the left pelvic sidewall. He then ties the sutures so that no small defects are present that could trap the small bowel. The physician controls bleeding and closes the abdominal incision with sutures, placing a Foley catheter to promote drainage. Terminology Cul–de–sac: The extension of the peritoneal cavity between the rectum and back wall of the uterus; also known as the rectouterine pouch or the pouch of Douglas; also, any dead–end pouch. Enterocele: When the small intestines and perineum protrude into the vaginal canal. Foley catheter: A tube that the provider places through the urethra and advances into the bladder. Tips CPT® defines code 57270 as a separate procedure, and it tends to be bundled into most female genitourinary procedures. Repair of an enterocele in conjunction with a vaginal vault suspension procedure should not be billed separately since in suspending the vault, the structures used to suspend the vault will also eliminate the enterocele. The Halban or Moschcowitz procedure can also be done in conjunction with an abdominal hysterectomy to prevent the formation of an enterocele. In that case, it would not be billed separately. If the provider performs this procedure with an unrelated procedure, append modifier 59, Distinct procedural service to the code. Be sure the documentation supports the procedure as a separate procedure and not part of some other related procedure. Do not append modifier 59 when a more specific modifier, such as XE (same date, separate encounter), XP (different practitioner), XS (separate organ or structure), or XU (service does not overlap with the usual components of the main service). Documentation must support the use of the modifier. Do not confuse modifier 59 with modifier 51 for multiple procedures (e.g., same procedure on different anatomic sites, related procedures on same anatomic site, or same procedure multiple times on same anatomic site). short_description: Colpopexy, abdominal approach
lay_term: The provider pulls up the vaginal vault that is prolapsing and attaches it to a strong structure using sutures. The provider performs this procedure through an abdominal incision. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and appropriately preps and drapes the patient. The provider makes an abdominal incision through the skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, and fascia. After exploring the abdominal cavity, he identifies the vagina. He dissects the bladder off the anterior vaginal wall and frees the posterior wall. He incises the peritoneum overlying the sacrum and clears the periosteum. He secures the vagina to the periosteum of the sacral promontory, the most superior portion of the sacrum, with sutures to create a sling. He may also insert mesh material to act as a sling. He then closes the abdomen in layers. Terminology Colpopexy: Also called vaginopexy, suspending a relaxed and prolapsed vagina by fixation to the abdominal wall, attachment to the sacrum, fascial strips, or by use of sturdy ligaments and muscles. Periosteum: The outer membrane covering the entire surface of a bone except where the joints meet, or around the area where the bones meet the ligaments and tendons. Sacral promontory: The most prominent anterior projection of the base of the sacrum. Tips If the provider uses mesh to help support the vaginal vault, do not report it separately. Read Less

short_description: Colpopexy, vaginal; extra-peritoneal approach (sacrospinous, iliococcygeus)
lay_term: The surgeon in this procedure performs a colpopexy, which is the suspension of the vaginal apex via a vaginal approach using the extraperitoneal technique. This procedure, also known as vault repair, is performed with suspension of the vaginal apex by attaching it to the sacrospinous or iliococcygeus ligaments. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and appropriately preps and drapes the patient. In an extraperitoneal vaginal vault suspension, the provider makes a vaginal incision and dissects off the rectovaginal fascia from the posterior vaginal wall, all the way to the pelvic sidewall. This is done bilaterally. The provider identifies the ischial spine and the sacrospinous ligaments. If the provider is to place sutures in the iliococcygeus fascia, he finds it just in front of the sacrospinous ligament. The provider can use blunt dissection to remove tissue from this area. He may also perform a rectal exam to make sure that no rectal injury has occurred. He then places sutures into either the sacrospinous ligament or the iliococcygeus fascia. He brings the sutures out to the apex of the vagina and closes the upper part of the vaginal wall with sutures. If the provider uses a mesh system, he attaches the mesh to the vaginal vault and the supporting structure. He then ties the vaginal vault suspension sutures, which elevates the apex of the vagina to the correct position, which is flush with the sacrospinous ligament or iliococcygeus fascia. Terminology Colpopexy: Also called vaginopexy, suspending a relaxed and prolapsed vagina by fixation to the abdominal wall, attachment to the sacrum, fascial strips, or by use of sturdy ligaments and muscles. Iliococcygeus fascia: It makes up the side part of the levator ani muscle and goes from the tendinous arch of the levator ani muscle, also called the obturator fascia, to the anococcygeal ligament and coccyx. Ischial spine: The bony process that projects backward and medially from the ischial posterior border. Extraperitoneal: The portion of the abdomen and pelvis which does not lie within the peritoneum. Sacrospinous ligament: Ligament that extends from the ischial spines on either side to the lower portion of the sacrum and coccyx. Tips Report code 57282 whether the physician performs a unilateral or bilateral suspension. If the physician uses a mesh system for this repair, do not report an add–on code for vaginal mesh. short_description: Colpopexy, vaginal; intra-peritoneal approach (uterosacral, levator myorrhaphy) Notes: (Do not report 57283 in conjunction with 57556, 58263, 58270, 58280, 58292, 58294)
lay_term: The provider pulls up the vaginal vault that is prolapsing using a vaginal approach and attaches it to a ligament inside the peritoneal lining. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and appropriately preps and drapes the patient. In an intraperitoneal vaginal vault suspension, the provider opens the vaginal mucosa at the apex of the vagina. He dissects away the pubocervical and rectovaginal fascia from the vaginal wall, which exposes the enterocele. He identifies the peritoneum and sharply enters it. He retracts the bowel away and packs it with a laparotomy towel. The provider identifies the ureters and palpates them bilaterally because they come very close to the uterosacral ligament, and the physician wants to be sure he does not suture the ureters. He identifies the uterosacral ligaments on each side. He grasps the uterosacral ligaments with clamps and places them on traction. He then places a series of interrupted sutures through the uterosacral ligaments on both sides and pulls them together to plicate the ligaments. At this point, he places sutures into the top of the anterior and posterior vaginal walls and anchors them into the plicated uterosacral ligaments. If the provider instead uses the levator muscle, he places sutures into this structure to create a shelf above the rectum. He then ties sutures from the vaginal vault into this shelf for support. He performs culdoplasty to obliterate the cul–de–sac, or enterocele. He brings the sutures through the exposed pubocervical and rectovaginal fascia. He then ties the sutures to suspend the vagina deep in the pelvis. He closes the vaginal vault with interrupted sutures. He then places a Foley catheter for bladder drainage and packs the vagina with gauze. Terminology Colpopexy: Surgical suspension of a relaxed and/or prolapsed vagina by fixation to the abdominal wall, attachment to the sacrum, fascial strips, or by use of sturdy ligaments and muscles; also known as vaginopexy. Culdoplasty: Placement of sutures across the uterosacral ligaments to obliterate the cul–de–sac to treat an existing enterocele or prevent one from occurring in the future; also known as a McCall culdoplasty. Enterocele: When the small intestines and perineum protrude into the vaginal canal. Foley catheter: A tube that the provider places through the urethra and advances into the bladder. Interrupted sutures: Sutures where the provider individually places and ties each stitch, so the stitches are not connected. Laparotomy: Incision through the abdominal wall to enter the abdominal cavity. Levator ani: A compound muscle in the pelvis that is formed by the pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus muscles.It helps prevent pelvic prolapse and bring the anus back up after a bowel movement. Levator myorrhaphy: Suture of the levator ani muscle to support the vaginal vault. The use of this muscle group is not often used as opposed to the uterosacral ligament. Plication: The process of folding and suturing tissues. Pubocervical fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the anterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the bladder. When this tissue is weak, it can cause the bladder or urethra to prolapse into the vaginal canal. Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. When these tissues become weak, it can lead to the prolapse of the rectum into the vaginal canal. Uterosacral ligament: A band of fascia that inserts into the sacrum and then connects to the back wall of the uterus at the internal cervical os, or opening. This ligament supports the uterus and holds it in place. Tips This uterosacral ligament fixation procedure repairs not only vaginal vault prolapse, but also an existing enterocele. This procedure is normally performed on both sides, but you should report code 57283 only once. Read Less

short_description: Paravaginal defect repair (including repair of cystocele, if performed); vaginal approach Notes: (Do not report 57285 in conjunction with 51990, 57240, 57260, 57265, 58267)
lay_term: The provider repairs a paravaginal defect by dissecting the tissues between the vagina, the bladder, and the urethra using a vaginal approach. The provider may also perform a cystocele repair as part of this procedure. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider then incises the anterior vaginal wall to access the space of Retzius. He then dissects the bladder way from the vaginal tissue and extends this dissection to expose the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis on both sides. The provider places several sutures along the side of the vagina through the pubocervical fascia and brings them through the obturator internus muscle, which is just above the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis. He then ties all sutures in order to close the defect. He then closes the fascia. If there is a cystocele, the provider adds additional sutures to strengthen and close the anterior vaginal wall. This provides better support to the bladder. Terminology Arcus tendineus fascia pelvis (ATFP): A thick band of the fascia over the obturator internus muscles running in an arching line from the pubis to the ischial spine; it may be used as the attachment point for the pubocervical fascia to support the anterior vaginal walls that have prolapsed; formerly called the white line. Cystocele: Prolapse of the bladder into the vagina that occurs when the tough fibrous wall between a woman's bladder and her vagina weakens. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient lies on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Marshal–Marchetti–Krantz (MMK): A surgical procedure where the bladder neck and urethra are separated from the space of Retzius; sutures are placed on either side of the urethra and bladder neck, which are elevated to a higher position; then the free ends of the stitches are anchored to surrounding cartilage and pubic bone. Obturator internus muscle: A muscle that covers the pelvic surfaces of ischium and ilium and obturator membrane, and also attaches to the femur to allow the thigh to rotate outward. Paravaginal defect: A loss of support of the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis, which forms the lateral attachments of the vagina; without the support of the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis, the bladder and urethra prolapse, which may result in cystocele or urethrocystocele. Peritoneum: The lining of the abdominal and pelvic cavity. Pubocervical fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the anterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the bladder; when this tissue is weak it can cause the bladder or urethra to prolapse into the vaginal canal. Space of Retzius: A space in the pelvis where the bladder and its supporting ligaments are found. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Tips In order to report a paravaginal defect repair, the operative note must refer to the key terms space of Retzius and arcus tendineus fascia pelvis. Because this procedure includes repair of a cystocele, you may not report 57285 with codes for any kind of bladder or urethral repair such as a Marshal–Marchetti–Krantz procedure (58267) or a laparoscopic urethral suspension (51990). This procedure would also be bundled into any of the codes that include an anterior colporrhaphy which is done to repair a cystocele (57240, 57260, or 57265). If the provider documents weakened or attenuated pubocervical fascia in the operative report and uses a mesh to shore up this weak tissue, also report the add–on code +57267. Read Less

short_description: Removal or revision of sling for stress incontinence (eg, fascia or synthetic)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes a sling that was placed under the urethra to correct stress urinary incontinence. The provider removes the sling because it is eroding, has become infected, is causing urinary retention, or is protruding from the site. This surgery includes a vaginal or combination vaginal and abdominal approach. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and appropriately preps and drapes the patient. He places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position. The provider makes a vaginal incision in the anterior vaginal vault to the side of the urethra, avoiding any direct contact with the urethra. The provider then carries the incision down to the graft material. He then releases the graft material from the surrounding tissue to the level of the endopelvic fascia, and he does this on both sides of the urethra. When the provider releases all of the graft or mesh material, he can remove it or adjust it. If the sling has been attached above the urethra, the provider makes a small abdominal incision to reach that area and cut the attachment or adjust the sling. The provider normally performs a cystoscopy to ensure that there was no graft material in the bladder and that the surgery around the urethra did not cause any damage. The provider will then irrigate the incision sites, make sure that there is no bleeding from the sites, and close the incision sites with sutures, as well as pack the vagina. Terminology Cystoscope: A catheter like instrument with viewing lenses or optical fibers at the tip that allows images of the bladder and urethra to be projected through an eye piece. Cystoscopy: An examination using a cystoscope to see inside the urethra and bladder. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Endopelvic fascia: Fascia that covers the muscles on the lateral walls of the pelvis, passes onto the superior surface of the pelvic diaphragm, and extends onto the urethral sphincter and up onto the base of various pelvic organs. Stress incontinence: An involuntary loss of urine or inability to hold urine that may happen especially to elderly patients during a physical activity, such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercise. Incontinence is caused by weakness of sphincter muscles Sling: The sling is made of synthetic mesh or fascia taken from the patient's abdomen and is placed inside the body through small incisions. It provides support to the urethra and restores normal functioning of the bladder. Tips Sometimes, providers can perform this procedure in the office and use scissors to remove excess sling material, with the patient under a local anesthetic, rather than taking the patient to the operating room. The code 57287, according to the CMS database, should only be performed in the hospital setting, and it has very high relative value units, or RVUs. To report simple removal of sling material in the office setting, report the unlisted code 53899 or 58999, and compare the work to a simple excision of a foreign body of the subcutaneous tissues, code 10120. While the Correct Coding Initiative does not bundle cystoscopy with code 57287, many payers will deny it for lack of medical necessity if the documentation clearly shows that it was done to check the provider’s work rather than being used as a diagnostic tool for a condition existing prior to or developing during surgery. short_description: Sling operation for stress incontinence (eg, fascia or synthetic) Notes: (For laparoscopic approach, use 51992)
lay_term: The provider places a sling made of fascia or synthetic material under the urethra to support it in the correct position to treat urinary stress incontinence. The procedure can be performed abdominally or vaginally depending on whether the provider uses a pubocervical or transvaginal sling. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and places the patient in either a dorsal lithotomy or supine position. The surgeon reaches the pelvic area from an abdominal or vaginal approach. He places a sling under the urethra and secures it to the abdominal wall and pelvic bone, adjusting it for the correct tension. The provider can create the sling from a strip of tissue from the patient's own abdominal fascia, or he can use a synthetic sling. The sling can be a transvaginal sling, such as a Monarc® subfascial hammock, transobturator tape (TOT), tension–free vaginal tape (TVT), or a pubocervical sling. If he uses tension–free vaginal tape (TVT), the provider weaves tape through pelvic tissue and positions it underneath the urethra. He then pulls the tape up through two tiny incisions in the skin’s surface just above the pubic area. As it passes through several pelvic tissue layers, friction is created, which initially holds the tape in place, like velcro. Over time, the body tissue grows into the mesh, which permanently secures it. If he uses a pubovaginal sling, he makes an incision above the pubic bone and removes a strip of abdominal fascia. He makes another incision into the vaginal wall, through which the sling is grasped and adjusted around the bladder neck. He secures the sling with two sutures loosely tied to each other above the pubic bone incision, providing a hammock to support the bladder neck. With transobturator tape (TOT), the provider makes a vaginal incision at the level of the mid urethra and makes a small skin incision in front of the obturator membrane. He inserts tape through the obturator foramen either by passing the tape via the skin incision to the vaginal incision bilaterally, called the outside in technique, or by passing it from the vaginal incision to the skin, called the inside out technique. The provider positions the tape without tension beneath the mid urethra in the outside in technique and under the junction of the mid and distal urethra in the inside out technique. The sling compresses the urethra back to its normal position. Finally, the provider closes the incision after irrigating the incision sites. The provider performs a cystoscopy to be sure that the sling is not compromising the bladder in any way. He places a catheter for a period of 24 hours and removes it when the patient is able to urinate with better control. Terminology Cystoscopy: An examination using a cystoscope to see inside the urethra and bladder. Cystoscope: A catheter like instrument with viewing lenses or optical fibers at the tip that allows images of the bladder and urethra to be projected through an eye piece. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Monarc subfascial hammock: Needle kit that inserts a sling mesh through vaginal incisions via needles. The mesh supports the urethra. Obturator foramen: A hole that the ischium and pubis bones create, and blood vessels and nerves move through the hole. Obturator membrane: A thin sheet of fibers that almost closes the obturator foramen, which is a hole that the ischium and pubis bones create, and blood vessels and nerves move through the hole. Pubocervical: From the pubis to the cervix. Sling: The sling is made of synthetic mesh and is placed inside the body through small incisions. It provides support to the urethra and restores normal functioning of the bladder. Supine: The patient is lying on her back. Urinary incontinence: The inability to hold urine during physical activities such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercise. Incontinence is caused by weakness of sphincter muscles. Tips Although several types of sling procedures exist, you can only report code 57288 for various sling procedures. Cystoscopy is always bundled with a sling procedure. Read Less

short_description: Pereyra procedure, including anterior colporrhaphy
lay_term: This procedure treats both a cystocele and stress urinary incontinence by repairing the vaginal wall. Providers perform it through a vaginal incision. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position. He makes an incision in the vaginal tissue over the bladder and dissects the bladder off of this tissue. The provider then makes two small lower abdominal incisions and puts a suture in the retropubic fascia and loops it around the neck of the bladder so it can join up with the urethra. The provider anchors this suture to the abdominal wall fascia, which suspends the urethrovesical angle. The provider then plicates the tissue over the bladder in the midline and closes the vaginal mucosa over this, which completes the anterior colporrhaphy. The provider inserts a Foley catheter, places a gauze pack in the vagina, and closes the small abdominal incisions. Terminology Colporrhaphy: Surgical repair of a defect or laceration in the wall of the vagina. Cystocele: A prolapse of the bladder into the vagina due to weakened supportive tissue between the bladder and the anterior vaginal wall. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Foley catheter: A tube that the provider places through the urethra and advances into the bladder. Pereyra: A vaginal approach procedure where the provider ties sutures above the rectus fascia to elevate the urethrovesical angle. Plication: It is a process of folding and suturing tissues. Rectus fascia: Fascia of the anterior abdominal wall. Stress urinary incontinence: The inability to hold urine during physical activities such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercise. Incontinence is caused by weakness of sphincter muscles. Urethrovesical angle: The angle between the urethra and the back of the bladder wall, which is normally about 90 degrees. This angle narrows when there is a cystocele and can lead to stress incontinence. Read Less

short_description: Construction of artificial vagina; without graft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider constructs an artificial vagina without use of a graft to treat patients with congenital absence of a vagina or vaginal agenesis. Explanation After the provider places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position and administers anesthesia, he makes an incision in between the urethra and rectum. The provider then prepares a cavity by using blunt dissection. The cavity preparation depends upon whether uterus is present. If uterus is present, the provider creates the cavity to the level of the uterine cavity. If uterus is absent, then the provider creates a cavity to the peritoneum only. Once the provider successfully creates the cavity, he uses electrocautery for hemostasis to control bleeding. He then inserts stents or a catheter to keep the cavity open. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Stent: A mesh tube. Vaginal agenesis: The failure of the vagina to develop during embryonic growth. Read Less

short_description: Construction of artificial vagina; with graft
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider constructs an artificial vagina with application of a graft. Providers can construct an artificial vagina in various ways, and providers perform the procedure mostly to treat a congenital absence of a vagina or vaginal agenesis. Explanation The provider administers anesthesia and preps and drapes the patient. He prepares a mold on which to place the graft. He may leave a cleft in the mold to avoid urethral pressure. The physician drills two holes for insertion and retention of sutures. The physician then harvests a split thickness graft from the patient's thigh area and cuts it from the mold patterns to aid the graft. Once he completes the graft preparation, the physician makes an incision between the urethra and rectum. The physician then prepares a cavity by using blunt dissection. The cavity preparation depends upon the presence or absence of the uterus. If uterus is present, he creates the cavity to the level of the uterine cavity. If uterus is absent, he creates the cavity to the peritoneum only. Once he successfully creates the cavity, the physician inserts the prepared graft into the cavity. The physician then sutures the graft's surface lines with the skin at the vaginal opening and passes two silk sutures through labial musculature. The physician then washes the mold with saline and inserts a catheter into the bladder. He leaves the catheter in place for several days. He also covers the graft sites with a bleached cotton cloth. Terminology Vaginal agenesis: The failure of the vagina to develop during embryonic growth. Tips According to the Society for Gynecologic Oncology, if anything other than a skin graft is performed, e.g. myocutaneous flaps, you should code it separately, e.g., code 15734. Append modifier 51 for each additional procedure. Read Less

short_description: Revision (including removal) of prosthetic vaginal graft; open abdominal approach Notes: (For laparoscopic approach, use 57426)
lay_term: The provider revises or removes, through an abdominal incision, a prosthetic vaginal graft that was previously placed because it has eroded or the tissue over the mesh has thinned and the mesh is now exposed. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the abdomen and enters the pelvis. He then elevates the vaginal tissue by using his free hand or by placing an instrument into the vaginal cavity to help identify the graft. He then opens the peritoneum over the graft and dissects all or part of the graft material. The provider then removes the graft with the attached tissue. After ensuring that the small bowel, rectum, and bladder are not attached to the graft or tissue, the provider sews together the edges of the endopelvic fascia and closes the vaginal tissue in layers. The provider then identifies where the graft attaches to a ligament and completes the dissection by removing this attachment and the sutures that held the graft in place. He then removes the graft and sutures the area where the graft previously lay. Finally, he closes the abdominal incision, and he may apply vaginal packing with gauze to stop any bleeding. Terminology Endopelvic fascia: Fascia that covers the muscles on the lateral walls of the pelvis, passes onto the superior surface of the pelvic diaphragm, and extends onto the urethral sphincter and up onto the base of various pelvic organs. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Tips If the provider chooses to replace the graft with a new graft held in place with sutures, this would be included as part of the revision. Read Less

short_description: Closure of rectovaginal fistula; vaginal or transanal approach
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider closes a fistula tract between the rectum and the vagina using either a vaginal approach or closing it through the anus. Providers only use these approaches for small fistula tracts. An ob gyn normally uses the vaginal approach, while a gastrointestinal surgeon normally uses the transanal approach. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. The physician makes an incision around the fistula within the vaginal wall and completely excises it to allow free movement of the vagina, rectum, and rectovaginal septum in order to allow for a tension free closure. The physician inserts his index finger into the rectum to help with the repair. The physician first frees the vagina and rectum in a circular fashion so that he can get traction on the edges of the fistula. He then excises the entire tract and any scar tissue that is near the fistula to get clean edges that contain fresh, viable tissue. The physician then inverts the anterior rectal wall by placing interrupted or purse string sutures above and below the fistula. He then places a second layer of sutures in the muscle of the anterior rectal wall. The physician then pulls together the pararectal fascia or muscle to provide an added layer of closure. Finally, the physician closes the vagina mucosa. The physician then inserts a vaginal pack into the vagina to absorb any seepage from the wound. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Episiotomy: The provider incises the area between the anus and vagina to increase the size of the opening to allow for delivery of a newborn. Interrupted sutures: Sutures where the provider individually places and ties each stitch, so the stitches are not connected. Pararectal: Close to the rectum or pararectus muscle. Purse string sutures: The provider makes a circular suture that is continuous, and he pulls it together to close a defect. Rectocele: A bulge of rectal tissue through a tear between the rectum and vagina. It happens during childbirth or with a hysterectomy. Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. When this tissue becomes weak, it can lead to the prolapse of the rectum into the vaginal canal. Rectovaginal fistula: An abnormal passage between the rectum and the vagina. It is usually caused by obstetric injuries, incomplete healing of an episiotomy, rectocele repair, radiation therapy, or uterine cancer. Rectovaginal septum: A layer of fascia between the vagina and the lower part of the rectum. Read Less

short_description: Closure of rectovaginal fistula; abdominal approach
lay_term: In this procedure the provider excises a rectovaginal fistula through an abdominal incision. Explanation The provider places the patient in a supine position and administers anesthesia. The physician makes a skin incision in the lower abdomen and carries it down until the peritoneal cavity is entered. The physician then explores the abdominal cavity and packs the bowel away from the operative site. He then makes sure that the sigmoid colon is released from the surrounding tissue. He then enters the rectovaginal fascia (sometimes called the rectovaginal septum), and he dissects the vagina from the rectum. He then identifies the fistula and excises it. The physician then closes the defect created by removing the fistula by using staples or sutures. He then closes the vaginal incision and inserts a drain that is secured either to drain into the vaginal canal or outside the body through the abdominal wall. He then puts the bowel back into the pelvis and closes the abdominal incision with suture. Terminology Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. When these tissues become weak, they can lead to the prolapse of the rectum into the vaginal canal. Rectovaginal fistula: An abnormal passage between the rectum and the vagina. It is usually caused by obstetric injuries, incomplete healing of an episiotomy, rectocele repair, radiation therapy, or uterine cancer. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Read Less

short_description: Closure of rectovaginal fistula; abdominal approach, with concomitant colostomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises the rectovaginal fistula, and cuts one end of the colon and brings it out of the body so that stool is excreted through this new artificial opening in the abdominal wall. This is an abdominal approach procedure. Explanation The physician places the patient in a supine position and administers anesthesia. The physician makes a skin incision in the lower abdomen and carries it down until the peritoneal cavity is entered. The physician then explores the abdominal cavity and packs the bowel away from the operative site. He then makes sure that the sigmoid colon is released from the surrounding tissue. He then enters the rectovaginal fascia (sometimes called the rectovaginal septum), and he dissects the vagina from the rectum. He then identifies the fistula and excises it. The physician then closes the defect created by removing the fistula by using staples or sutures. He then closes the vaginal incision. Because the fistula is large, the physician creates a colostomy to divert feces outside the body. First, the physician isolates a loop of large bowel that is close to the fistula repair site, and he makes a separate skin incision into the abdominal wall. He then brings the loop of bowel out of the body through this incision, and he sutures it in place. He then makes an opening into the loop of colon so that feces will be able to exit the body. The physician may or may not put the collecting device in place at the time he performs this surgery. He then inserts a drain that is secured, either to drain into the vaginal canal or to drain outside the body through the abdominal wall. Finally, the physician moves the bowel that was packed away back into the pelvis and closes the abdominal incision with sutures. Terminology Colostomy: A surgical procedure that involves cutting the end of the large intestine (colon) and inserting this end through an incision in the anterior abdominal wall where it is sutured in place. Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. When these tissues become weak, they can lead to the prolapse of the rectum into the vaginal canal. Rectovaginal fistula: An abnormal passage between the rectum and the vagina. It is usually caused by obstetric injuries, incomplete healing of an episiotomy, rectocele repair, radiation therapy, or uterine cancer. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Read Less

short_description: Closure of rectovaginal fistula; transperineal approach, with perineal body reconstruction, with or without levator plication
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider closes the rectovaginal fistula but makes an incision through the perineum. The provider must repair the perineum afterward and may shorten the levator muscle, when necessary, during this procedure. Explanation The provider places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position and administers anesthesia. The physician starts the surgery by making an upside–down U incision in the perineum and exposes the external anal sphincter. He then places a probe into the fistula to locate the exact tract it is taking. The physician then separates the fistula tract from the anal sphincter and he cuts away any of the vaginal and rectal mucosa that are part of the fistula. He then identifies the tissue under the anal sphincter and repairs it with suture. He then covers the sphincter with rectovaginal fascia and sutures the area closed. The physician then closes the original perineal incision using sutures. If there was any perineal laxity before the surgery, the physician shortens the levator ani muscle by making folds or tucks on its walls and incorporates this muscle into the surgical closure. Terminology Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Levator ani: A compound muscle in the pelvis that is formed by the pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus muscles.It helps prevent pelvic prolapse and bring the anus back up after a bowel movement. Perineal body: An area of fibrous tissue and muscle that lies below the skin portion of the perineum. It is the insertion point for bulbocavernosus, external anal sphincter and the superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles. A midline episiotomy will extend into this structure. Perineum: Short stretch of skin starting at the bottom of the vulva and extending to the anus. Plication: The process of folding and suturing tissues. Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. When these tissues become weak, they can lead to the prolapse of the rectum into the vaginal canal. Rectovaginal fistula: An abnormal passage between the rectum and the vagina. short_description: Colposcopy of the entire vagina, with cervix if present
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider performs a diagnostic examination of the vagina and cervix, if present, using a colposcope. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. He then inserts a speculum and inspects the vagina completely for visible abnormalities using a bright light. He then applies a 3 to 5 percent solution of acetic acid, such as vinegar, to the entire vagina and the cervix to clean the area and highlight lesions. When the solution dries, it will turn any abnormal areas to white, referred to acetowhite areas. Once the acetic acid dries, the provider positions the colposcope and inspects all of the vaginal surfaces for abnormalities, going from one quadrant of the vagina to the next, and using various levels of magnification. A green filter may be used to look for abnormal vascular patterns. If the cervix is present, the provider turns the scope toward the cervix and inspects the cervix in its entirety. Once the provider inspects the vagina and the cervix, if present, he withdraws the scope and the speculum. Terminology Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal. It consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix. Menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out of the vaginal canal. Colposcope: A lighted, binocular, magnifying instrument that an ob gyn provider uses to examine the tissues of the vulva, vagina, and/or the cervix. Colposcopy: Colpo is a prefix that means vagina, and scopy if a suffix that means to view, so colposcopy literally means to view the vagina. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure. It has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane. It extends from the vestibule to area where the cervix buts up against the vaginal vault. It is longer on the posterior wall, side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, side located below the bladder. Tips If the primary reason for the colposcopy is suspected lesions of the vagina, but the cervix is also examined at the same time, a separate code for colposcopy of the cervix would not be reported. Physician work in examining the entire vagina is significantly more involved than that of examining just the cervix. Therefore, if the cervix is present and examined, this would be included in code 57420. Colposcopy of the vulva (CPT® codes 56820 and 56821) may be reported in addition to 57420 by adding a modifier –51 to the lower valued procedure. Read Less

short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical, colpopexy (suspension of vaginal apex)
lay_term: The provider uses a laparoscopic approach to suspend the top of the vagina to a strong structure to treat vaginal vault prolapse using sutures or mesh. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider makes a small incision in the abdominal cavity near the belly button or uses a specialized access needle to place a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with gas to expand the abdominal cavity, creating a pneumoperitoneum. The provider makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars (access devices) to view the operating site and insert surgical tools. If the provider performs robot–assisted surgery, the provider docks the robot arm to the laparoscope at this time to be able to manipulate it during surgery. If the provider is going to use mesh to suspend the vaginal vault, the provider will prepare the mesh to the correct size. The provider will then explore the abdominal cavity and place a vaginal probe into the vagina to manipulate the vaginal vault as needed during the procedure. The provider then lyses any adhesions that have formed and need to be separated for access to the vaginal vault. The provider makes an incision into the peritoneum (membrane) that is covering the vaginal vault, and excises tissue surrounding the bladder to create a space that exposes the pubocervical fascia (supportive layer of the vaginal wall). The provider then excises tissue surrounding the rectum to loosen it from the rectovaginal fascia (this structure separating the rectum and vagina). The provider then performs a procedure such as a Halban or Moschcowitz culdoplasty to obliterate the cul–de–sac to prevent an enterocele (intestinal protrusion into the vaginal canal). The provider then secures the graft material to the pubocervical and rectovaginal fascia. The provider secures the mesh to the sacrum or other sturdy structure, such as the uterosacral ligament, and closes the peritoneum over the entire graft. The provider removes the laparoscope, all trocars, and the docked robot arm, if used. The provider then closes the small incisions with sutures. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands that form between tissues and organs, which typically result from inflammation or injury during surgery; they may be thought of as internal scar tissue. Colpopexy: Surgical suspension of a relaxed and/or prolapsed vagina by fixation to the abdominal wall, attachment to the sacrum, fascial strips, or by use of sturdy ligaments and muscles; also known as vaginopexy. Enterocele: A bulging of the small intestines and peritoneum into the vaginal canal. Halban culdoplasty: A procedure done to obliterate an enterocele sac by placing longitudinal sutures that go through the covering tissue of the sigmoid, into the deep peritoneum of the cul–de–sac and up the posterior vaginal wall. Laparoscopic approach or procedure: A surgical procedure in which the provider views and accesses the abdominal and/or pelvic contents with a laparoscope (a tubular instrument with a light source and camera) to examine the interior structures of a body cavity; usually, several incisions are made, one for the laparoscope and additional incisions for surgical instruments. Lyse: To break down a structure, free up adhesions, separate tissues by cutting and dividing, or to destroy cells using an agent or substance. Moschcowitz culdoplasty: A procedure done to obliterate an enterocele sac by placing purse string sutures around the cul–de–sac including the posterior vaginal wall, the right pelvic sidewall, the covering tissue of the sigmoid, and the left pelvic sidewall. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pneumoperitoneum: The presence of gas or air in the peritoneal (abdominal) cavity; when laparoscopic procedures are performed, typically carbon dioxide gas is pumped into the abdominal cavity to expand the viewing space. Prolapse: The dropping, falling, sinking, or sliding of an organ or structure from its normal position or location in the body. Pubocervical fascia: The underlying supporting tissue of the anterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the bladder; weak tissue can cause the bladder or urethra to prolapse into the vaginal canal. Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. Rectum: The terminal portion of the large intestine, extending from the sigmoid colon to the anal canal. Robot–assisted surgery: A surgical procedure conducted through a laparoscope with the aid of a mechanical (robotic) arm. Sacrum: Large, triangular bone at the end of the vertebral column. Trocar: A hollow, pointed puncturing device, typically part of a cannula and trocar combination. Uterosacral ligament: Ligament of the uterus, extending from the cervix to posterior pelvic wall. Vagina: The muscular canal extending from the uterus (womb) to the external genital opening (introitus); also known as the birth canal. Vaginal vault: Area of the vaginal canal located at the internal end of the vagina. Tips When robotic surgery is performed, the physician can bill only for the code that describes the laparoscopic approach. This is because the robot is a surgical tool, not a separate surgical procedure. You may report S2900 for informational purposes to let the payer know that a robot was used or for tracking purposes for your organization. Read Less

lay_term: As an add–on procedure, the provider uses specially designed computer–aided mapping to identify potential abnormalities of the cervix uteri during colposcopy (endoscopic exam). The service measures and maps light–scattering characteristics of the cervical epithelium (outer layer of tissue) treated with acetic acid. A typical device provides a high–resolution digital view of the cervix that can be displayed real–time, or stored, printed, or manipulated by a computer. Explanation In addition to a primary colposcopy procedure, the provider uses a special device that provides images of the uteri cervix to detect any hidden abnormality. After spraying acetic acid on the cervix, the provider uses the device to capture images, possibly for several minutes. Software calculates changes in reflectance over time for every pixel (roughly one cell per pixel). The acetic acid causes the color change by the acetowhitening effect, meaning the acid turns abnormal epithelium white by changing its light scattering characteristics. The software produces a color–coded map with acetowhitening data overlaid onto an image of the cervix. Areas of interest typically can be enlarged, enhanced, marked, or measured to help identify any false findings and to inspect the minute details. Computerized digital image processing may facilitate a more quantitative method for assessing acetowhitening effects. lay_term: In this procedure, the physician performs conization of the cervix using a scalpel or a laser and may use electrical current, called fulguration. The provider places the patient in a lithotomy position and inserts a weighted speculum and retractors into the vagina. He marks the area of excision and injects the cervix with a vasoconstrictor to minimize bleeding. He uses a long–handled scalpel, called a cold knife, or a laser to make a circular incision just to the side of the outer limit of the transformation zone. The provider holds the scalpel at the same depth and angle throughout the cutting. This creates a cone like excision, which will include the exocervix, all of the transformation zone, and some or all of the endocervix. The provider may remove the specimen in more than piece, and scissors are usually required for complete removal of the cone. short_description: Trachelectomy (cervicectomy), amputation of cervix (separate procedure)

short_description: Radical trachelectomy, with bilateral total pelvic lymphadenectomy and para-aortic lymph node sampling biopsy, with or without removal of tube(s), with or without removal of ovary(s) Notes: (For radical abdominal hysterectomy, use 58210)
lay_term: In this procedure, the physician performs radical surgical removal of the uterine cervix, called a trachelectomy, along with removal of bilateral total pelvic lymph nodes. He also performs a biopsy of para aortic lymph nodes. The procedure may include removing the ovaries. Explanation The provider preps and drapes the patient for abdominal surgery and administers a general anesthetic. He makes an incision in layers until he enters the peritoneal cavity. He explores the abdominal and pelvic cavities. The provider excises the cervix and upper third of the vagina and removes them by dissecting the ureters from the parametria. He also cuts, clamps, and sutures all bleeders and bisects all ligaments that keep the cervix in place. He performs a bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy either before or immediately after the radical excision of the cervix. The provider takes care not to disturb the infundibulopelvic and tubo–ovarian ligaments, which connect the ovaries to the abdominal wall and the uterus, as they will be the main supply of blood to the uterus, which is being preserved. He may also use closed suction drains. He then closes the abdomen in layers. short_description: Excision of cervical stump, abdominal approach
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider excises the cervical stump, remaining after a previous subtotal hysterectomy, where the provider removes the uterus but leaves the cervix intact. The procedure includes amputation through the abdominal approach. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers anesthesia. short_description: Excision of cervical stump, vaginal approach; with anterior and/or posterior repair
lay_term: In this procedure, the physician excises the cervical stump remaining after a previous subtotal hysterectomy, through a vaginal approach and also performs anterior and or posterior repair. Explanation The provider places the patient in a lithotomy position and inserts a speculum into the vagina. The provider uses retractors to hold the labia out of the way. He injects the cervical stump with a local anesthetic mixed with a vasoconstrictor to minimize bleeding. He makes a circular incision around the stump, which he dissects away from the vaginal tissue using scissors. He places clamps on the cardinal ligaments and uterosacral ligaments to further detach the cervical stump, and if the round ligaments are attached to the stump, he transects them. He removes the cervical stump. The physician then performs anterior and or posterior repair. For anterior repair, the physician makes an incision into the anterior vaginal skin to expose the damaged pubocervical fascia, which supports the bladder and urethra. Using delayed absorbable or permanent sutures, he plicates the fascia in the midline. He identifies the weak edges of the deep vaginal wall and sutures the strong tissue next to the edges to each other raising the bladder and forming a strong wall below this. The provider removes excess vaginal skin. He then closes the vaginal incision with dissolving stitches. For the posterior repair, the provider makes an incision in the posterior vaginal wall from the top of the vagina to the levator muscles. He plicates the fascia and brings the edges together and sutures them, making sure that some of the levator muscle is included in the repair. He removes any excess vaginal wall tissue. He performs repair of the perineum including repair of the levator and perineal muscles when perineorrhaphy is also performed. The incision made by removing the cervical stump is closed with sutures. Rectocele: A bulging of rectal tissue into the vagina through a tear in the rectovaginal fascia or septum. Rectovaginal fascia: Underlying supporting tissue of the posterior wall of the vagina between the vagina and the rectum. When these tissues become weak, they can lead to the prolapse of the rectum into the vaginal canal. short_description: Cerclage of uterine cervix, nonobstetrical
lay_term: In this procedure, the physician performs cerclage, which is using stitching to repair a defect in the cervix, prior to the patient becoming pregnant. Explanation The provider places the patient in the lithotomy position and places a speculum into the vaginal canal. The provider administers a general anesthetic. The cervix is exposed, and the provider places a uterine sound in the opening of the cervix to verify the location of the defect in the cervical wall. He makes a transverse vaginal incision where the vaginal wall and cervix meet. He dissects the bladder from the cervix. He exposes the defect in the cervix and excises the unhealthy cervical tissue with a knife. He closes the opening in two layers with sutures. He again uses a uterine sound to make sure that the vaginal canal was not closed during suturing of the defect. He then brings the vaginal mucosa back on top of the repaired area and sutures it in place. The provider may also insert a vaginal pack. Terminology Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix. Menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Tips This procedure, called a Lash cerclage, is more difficult than a cerclage performed during pregnancy. Providers perform it on patients who have had previous miscarriages due to cervical incompetence to try and prevent this from happening in a future pregnancy. Usually, there is evidence of trauma to the cervix or an anatomical abnormality. It is a permanent cerclage, and women who have this procedure must deliver any baby via a cesarean delivery. Because of this, some payers may require specific documentation of the current state of the patient’s cervix and history before payment will be made. Always check with your payer before billing. short_description: Dilation of cervical canal, instrumental (separate procedure)

short_description: Insertion of intrauterine device (IUD)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider places a contraceptive intrauterine device (IUD) in the uterine cavity. Explanation The provider places the patient in the lithotomy position and performs a vaginal exam to check for the position of the uterus. The provider then inserts a speculum and cleans the cervix with an antiseptic solution. He then grasps the lip of the cervix with a tenaculum and places a numbing gel into the cervical canal. The physician inserts a uterine sound into the uterus to check for the depth of the cavity. If the uterus is greater than 6 cm, he inserts the IUD. The provider prepares the IUD for insertion, and with an inserting tube, he places it into the uterus so that the device can expand into the cavity. Once he inserts the IUD, the tube is withdrawn and he trims the IUD string to 3 cm. He checks bleeding areas and stops any bleeding that he finds. He removes the speculum. The provider then documents in the patient record the depth of the uterine cavity and the length of the IUD string. Intrauterine device (IUD): Birth control device available in various shapes, such as coiled, loop, and T; usually a small, T–shaped flexible device that the provider inserts within the uterus; an IUD can be made of plastic or copper and may have a drug in it. Lip of the cervix: The edge of the ectocervix, the portion of the cervix that projects into the vagina. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure; it has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Tenaculum: A surgical clamp designed to hold or grasp tissue during dissection, commonly used to grasp the cervix. Uterine sound: An instrument used to probe the uterus through the cervix, to measure the length and direction of the cervical canal and uterus, or to determine the level of dilation, and or to induce further dilation. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. short_description: Endometrial ablation, thermal, without hysteroscopic guidance Notes: (For hysteroscopic procedure, use 58563)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider removes the lining of the uterus using a device that produces heat in a procedure known as thermal endometrial ablation. The provider does not use a hysteroscope for guidance during the procedure. This service is done to stop or reduce excessive or abnormal uterine bleeding. Explanation The provider places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position and places a speculum in the patient’s vagina. He dilates, or widens, the cervix, if necessary, and uses a long, flexible instrument called a uterine sound to determine the depth of the uterus. He inserts a balloon catheter into the vagina, through the cervix, and into the uterus. Once it is correctly placed, he fills it with fluid so that it expands to fill the entire uterine cavity. He then heats the fluid, which takes about four minutes. He then leaves the balloon in the uterus for eight minutes to ensure he destroys the uterine lining. The provider lets the fluid cool for about thirty seconds, withdraws the fluid, and then he removes the balloon from the uterus. Alternatively, the provider may use a triangular mesh electrode that uses radiofrequency energy to heat the lining of the uterus, or other devices that can produce heat, such as microwave energy or heated fluid. Terminology Ablation: A surgical technique that removes a body part or destroys its function. Catheter: A flexible or rigid hollow tube placed into the body for administration of medication or fluids, to remove a fluid, or to keep a passage open. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Curettage: Scraping with a curette, a spoon–shaped instrument. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Endometrium: The mucous membrane that forms the inner layer of the uterine wall. Hysteroscopy: Viewing the uterine cavity using a hysteroscope inserted through the cervix; the hysteroscope, or endoscope, used to view the uterus, has a light and camera, and allows the provider to magnify any images. Radiofrequency ablation: Therapeutic destruction of body tissue with the help of radiant energy. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure; it has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Tips Some providers like to perform a suction curettage of the uterus before performing the endometrial ablation to collect a biopsy sample and to somewhat thin the lining. This additional procedure is always bundled because you cannot bill for removing the uterine lining using two different methods at the same session. Read Less

short_description: Uterine suspension, with or without shortening of round ligaments, with or without shortening of sacrouterine ligaments; with presacral sympathectomy Notes: (For anastomosis of tubes to uterus, use 58752)
lay_term: In this procedure the provider suspends the uterus, pleating and suturing the stretched ligaments that normally hold the uterus in place so that the uterus and cervix return to their normal positions. The stretched ligaments that are pleated could include the round ligaments or the sacrouterine ligaments. This procedure includes a presacral sympathectomy. This service is done for uterine prolapse where a woman's uterus sags or slips from its normal position. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider then makes a low transverse abdominal incision and exposes the uterus and the round and sacrouterine ligaments. Or he makes an incision in the vagina. Once he exposes the ligaments, the provider utilizes different methods, such as Gillian suspension, Olshausen operation, Baldy Webster procedure; all procedures where the provider plicates or sutures the ligaments to shorten them. During any of these procedures, the provider will also perform a presacral sympathectomy where the provider removes or destroys a portion of the presacral nerve to relieve pelvic pain usually from a condition known as dysmenorrhea, or extremely painful menstruation. In the Olshausen operation, the provider sutures the round ligaments to the abdominal fascia with non–absorbable suture material. In Gillian suspension, the provider takes out each round ligament in the peritoneum through an opening and brings each ligament below the anterior rectus sheath. Similarly, in the Baldy–Webster procedure the provider passes round ligaments through the anterior and posterior broad ligaments and sutures them to the posterior surface of the uterus. The provider may fold and tack the sacrouterine ligaments to shorten them. He then closes the abdomen with sutures. Terminology Anterior rectus sheath: portion of the rectus abdominis muscles, the two parallel vertically aligned muscles on each side of the anterior wall of the abdomen surrounded by layers of flat broad tendons. Broad ligaments: A large fold of peritoneum that is attached to each side of the uterus and extends to the walls of the pelvis; these ligaments encase the ovaries and fallopian tubes. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Laparoscope: A tubular surgical instrument that is used to view the interior of the abdomen and pelvis Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Plicates or pleats: Making tucks in a structure to shorten it. Round ligaments: Bands of muscle and fiber that are attached to the top of the uterus on each side and travel through the inguinal canal to end at the labia majora. Sacrouterine ligament: Another term for the uterosacral ligament which is a band of fascia that inserts into the sacrum and then connects to the back wall of the uterus at the internal cervical os, or opening; this ligament supports the uterus, and holds it in place. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Transverse incision: An incision that runs across the body to provide access to the abdomen and pelvis. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips A provider may also use a laparoscopic approach for uterine suspension. Do not confuse this procedure with a laparoscopic colpopexy, which is the suspension of the vaginal vault, not the uterus. If the provider performs a uterine suspension laparoscopically, report the unlisted code 58578, Unlisted laparoscopy procedure, uterus, and use 58410 as your comparison code to let the payer know the amount of the physician work involved. short_description: Hysteroplasty, repair of uterine anomaly (Strassman type) Notes: (For closure of vesicouterine fistula, use 51920)
lay_term: The provider corrects a uterine anomaly such as a uterus with two horns to create a single uterine cavity. The provider performs this procedure via an abdominal approach. A hysteroplasty repair can be quite an extensive surgery depending upon the amount of plastic repair necessary. Explanation The provider places the patient in a supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider then makes a Pfannenstiel incision and exposes the uterus. Next, he makes a transverse incision across the top of the uterus from one uterine horn to the other. He then injects a hemostatic solution, a solution that minimizes blood loss, at the incision site. The provider then sutures the front part of the incision to itself connecting the tissue to make one long piece and the back part of the incision to itself in the same manner. This is done so that there is now one long uterine incision and one cavity instead of two. He then sutures closed the now single incision in layers and closes the abdominal incision. Terminology Anomaly: Deviates from standard or normal; abnormal. Hysteroplasty: A plastic surgery procedure to correct an anomaly or defect in the uterus; also referred to as a metroplasty or an uteroplasty. Pfannenstiel incision: A semicircular incision that is made just above the mons pubis, or pubic mound; it is often referred to as the bikini line incision, as it remains covered when wearing a two piece bathing suit and is considered a cosmetic incision for pelvic surgery. Strassman procedure: Procedure performed to correct a double uterus using a transverse incision. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Transverse incision: An incision that runs across the body to provide access to the abdomen and pelvis. Uterine horn: Points where the uterus and the fallopian tubes meet. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vesicouterine fistula: An abnormal connection between the bladder, or vesico, and the vagina that allows the continuous involuntary discharge of urine into the vaginal vault. Tips Code 58540 reports other types of hysteroplasty, such as the Jones metroplasty for a wedge of the uterus that contains a vaginal septum, a partition in the vagina that requires removal, or a Tompkins metroplasty, where the uterus is cut in the middle and the provider removes and sutures the roof of each horn. short_description: Laparoscopy, surgical, ablation of uterine fibroid(s) including intraoperative ultrasound guidance and monitoring, radiofrequency Notes: (Do not report 58674 in conjunction with 49320, 58541-58554, 58570, 58571, 58572, 58573, 58580, 76998) (For transcervical radiofrequency ablation of uterine fibroid[s], including intraoperative ultrasound guidance and monitoring, use 58580)
lay_term: The provider ablates, or destroys, one or more uterine fibroids, benign tumors made of fibrous tissue, using radio waves. The provider performs the procedure under ultrasound guidance, via a laparoscopic approach. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider inserts two laparoscopic ports into the abdomen through small incisions, one for the laparoscope and one for an ultrasound probe, and then makes another small skin incision to insert the radiofrequency device. She places the ultrasound transducer directly on top of the uterus while looking through the laparoscope and locates the fibroids. She inserts a radiofrequency device into the fibroid and heats the device to the desired temperature. She applies heat to the center of the fibroid for a few minutes to destroy the fibroid tissue, which will be reabsorbed into the body. She then seals the puncture site in the uterine wall using the radiofrequency device. She destroys one or more fibroids in this same manner. The provider then removes the laparoscope, radiofrequency device, and ultrasound transducer and closes all incisions with sutures. Terminology Laparoscopic approach: A surgical procedure in which the provider views and accesses the abdominal and or pelvic contents with a laparoscope, a tubular instrument with a fiberoptic light source and camera to examine the interior structures of a body cavity. Radiofrequency ablation (RFA): Use of heat produced by focused radio waves, a type of electromagnetic wave, to destroy areas of abnormal, damaged, or diseased tissue. Transducer: A small hand–held device that resembles a microphone, attached to the scanner by a cord; the transducer sends out high frequency sound waves into the body and then listens for the returning echoes from the tissues in the body. Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips Some payers consider the treatment of uterine fibroids with radiofrequency ablation investigational or not medically necessary and it may not be covered. Check with Medicare or other payers to determine their coverage policies. Read Less

lay_term: The provider removes the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries using a laparoscope but leaves the cervix. The uterus is larger than normal, usually due to the presence of fibroids, which means it weighs more than 250 g. Explanation First, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. He then preps and drapes the abdomen and administers a general anesthetic. The provider enters the abdominal cavity near the belly button using a Veress needle or an open incision and places a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with CO2 gas to create a pneumoperitoneum and then puts the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He then makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and insert surgical tools. If he is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. The provider opens the peritoneum over the bladder and dissects the bladder off the lower uterine segment. He then finds and moves the ureters out of the way and opens up the sides of the broad ligament. He identifies the infundibulopelvic ligament on both sides and cuts it to remove the ovaries. The provider then cuts the attachments of the uterus (the round ligaments), and if there are any fibroids, he removes them or tags them for separate removal before removing the uterus along with the fallopian tubes and ovaries. He then identifies the uterine artery, clamps, and cuts it. Because he is leaving the cervix in place, the provider does not cut the cardinal or uterosacral ligaments. He separates the fundus of the uterus from the cervix using a scalpel and treats any bleeding from the cervical stump. The provider now uses a morcellator to cut the uterus into small pieces, which he removes from the abdominal cavity though one or more of the trocar sites.
