Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Carbon dioxide (CO2): A colorless and odorless gas produced as a result of respiration; it is naturally present in air and is absorbed by plants; in laparoscopic surgical procedures, CO2 is insufflated into the abdomen to distend it. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Fallopian tubes: A set of two fine tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringe like ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also referred to as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges, or salpinx if singular. Fascia: Sheet or band of muscle, fat, and fibrous tissue that lies under the skin. g: Abbreviation for gram, a metric unit of measure of mass or weight; in pharmacology, a gram is equal to 1000 mg; the previous abbreviation for grams (gm) is outdated. Infundibulopelvic ligaments: Also knows as the suspensory ligaments of the ovary, these ligaments hold the ovary to the pelvic wall and must be cut in order to remove the ovaries. Insufflates: To blow a medicated powder, gas, or vapor into a bodily cavity. Laparoscopy: An operation a provider performs to view the abdominal and pelvic contents through small incisions with the aid of a camera; a provider uses it to inspect and diagnose a condition or to perform surgery for a problem; a fiberoptic instrument a provider inserts through an incision in the abdominal wall and uses to examine visually the interior of the peritoneal cavity; the provider also inserts trocars to allow for the addition of surgical tools. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Pneumoperitoneum: The presence of gas or air in the abdominal cavity; when laparoscopic procedures are performed, carbon dioxide is pumped into the abdominal cavity to expand the viewing space. Robot–assisted surgery: An operation that is started with the laparoscope, but a robot arm is docked with the laparoscope and the surgeon completes the operation while sitting at a console that is next to the operating table. Round ligaments: Bands of muscle and fiber that are attached to the top of the uterus on each side and travel through the inguinal canal to end at the labia majora. Uterine fundus: The top rounded portion of the uterus, above the openings of the fallopian tubes and is where an egg usually implants; a provider measures the fundus to determine the growth of the fetus. Uterosacral ligament: A band of fascia that inserts into the sacrum and then connects to the back wall of the uterus at the internal cervical os, or opening; this ligament supports the uterus, and holds it in place. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Veress needle: A spring–loaded needle used during a laparoscopic procedure to create a pneumoperitoneum. short_description: Hysteroscopy, surgical; with sampling (biopsy) of endometrium and/or polypectomy, with or without D & C
lay_term: The provider either biopsies the lining of the uterus (endometrium) or removes polyps, or both, through a hysteroscope ; he may or may not perform a dilation and curettage (D&C). He sends all samples he obtains to the laboratory for pathological analysis. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a local or regional anesthetic. The provider performs a bimanual pelvic exam so that he knows the size, position, and movement of the uterus. He inserts a Foley catheter to drain the bladder. The provider then places a speculum into the vagina, and dilates (widens) the cervix if needed so he can insert the hysteroscope into the uterus. He next uses a long, flexible instrument called a uterine sound to determine the depth of the uterus and inserts the hysteroscope. Next, he removes the speculum and distends the uterine cavity by introducing air or fluid. While taking videos with the hysteroscope in place, the provider examines the entire uterine cavity and the endocervical canal. If the provider identifies polyps, he dilates the cervix more so he can insert a resectoscope to remove them. Once he resects the polyps, he coagulates the bleeding points. The provider then takes a biopsy or scrapes the uterine cavity (or both) using a sharp curette to obtain tissue for pathologic study. The provider removes the hysteroscope from the uterus and checks the cervix for bleeding from a possible puncture or laceration. If he identifies any bleeding, he controls it using sutures, pressure, or cautery. He then removes all instruments from the vagina and cervix. Terminology Bimanual pelvic exam: Insertion of two fingers into the vagina to isolate the cervix. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Curette: A surgical spoon or scoop shaped instrument designed to scrape tissue or debris from a body cavity or other surface. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Endocervical canal: A spindle like shaped canal extending from the uterus to the vagina; the neck of the uterus; also known as cervical canal, canal of the cervix, or the cavity of cervix. Foley catheter: Catheter with an inflatable balloon tip for retention in the bladder. Hysteroscope: A thin, lighted, flexible tube that is inserted through the vagina to view the inside of the uterus; the scope has channels that allow fluid to be introduced into the uterus to distend it, and to introduce instruments that will be used to perform a procedure; it also has a camera that allows the physician to view in real time the uterine cavity. Polyp, uterine: Growths attached to the inner wall of the uterus that extend into the uterine cavity; they form from an overgrowth of cells in the lining of the uterus; they may also be referred to endometrial polyps, and they are usually benign. Resectoscope: A surgical instrument used to remove tissue from the uterus, which includes a wide angle microscope and an attached wire loop that is electrically activated; when the loop is turned on, it is dragged over the tissue to be removed; the loop cauterizes the site as it moves so sutures are not needed. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure; it has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Tips Polyps are not the same as fibroids. Be certain what the pathology results identify before coding either 58558 (for polyps) or 58561 (for leiomyomata). short_description: Hysteroscopy, surgical; with endometrial ablation (eg, endometrial resection, electrosurgical ablation, thermoablation)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider totally destroys the lining of the uterus in a procedure known as an endometrial ablation. He uses a hysteroscope to perform this procedure, which treats abnormal uterine bleeding. Explanation The provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a local or regional anesthetic. The provider performs a bimanual pelvic exam so that he knows the size, position, and movement of the uterus. Next, he inserts a Foley catheter to drain the bladder. The provider places a speculum into the vagina, and then he dilates, or widens, the cervix and performs curettage to thin the endometrial lining. He next uses a long, flexible instrument, called a uterine sound, to determine the depth of the uterus, and inserts the hysteroscope. He removes the speculum and distends, or expands, the uterine cavity by introducing air or fluid. While taking videos with the hysteroscope in place, the provider examines the entire uterine cavity and the endocervical canal. Once the examination is complete, he may insert a balloon catheter in a thermoablation procedure. He inflates the catheter, and once he knows it is correctly inflated, he fills it with fluid so that the balloon expands to fill the entire uterine cavity. He then heats the fluid, which takes about four minutes. He then leaves the balloon in the uterus for eight minutes to ensure he destroys the uterine lining. The provider lets the fluid cool for about thirty seconds, and then he removes the balloon from the uterus. Alternatively, the provider may coagulate the entire cavity using a rollerball, a resectoscope, or laser. When he destroys all of the lining, the provider removes the hysteroscope from the uterus, and he checks the cervix for bleeding from a possible puncture or laceration. If he identifies any bleeding, he controls it using sutures, pressure, or cautery. He then removes all instruments from the vagina and cervix. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Endocervical canal: A spindle like shaped canal extending from the uterus to the vagina; the neck of the uterus; also known as cervical canal, canal of the cervix, or the cavity of cervix. short_description: Ligation or transection of fallopian tube(s), abdominal or vaginal approach, unilateral or bilateral
lay_term: The provider ligates (ties off) or transects (cuts in two) one or both fallopian tubes to prevent a future pregnancy. The provider performs this service through an abdominal or a vaginal approach. Explanation For the vaginal approach, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider exposes the cervix and grasps the lip of the cervix with a tenaculum. He uses a retractor to expose the posterior cul–de–sac, one of the two small pouches on either side of the uterus in the vaginal canal. He then incises the vaginal wall using scissors or a scalpel. He widens the incision with the scissors and places a retractor toward the back of the cervix just inside the incision, so that he can move the uterus out of the way. He then grasps a fallopian tube with a clamp and brings it out into the operative field. He folds the tube in the middle and sutures below the loop he creates by the fold. The provider then incises the loop and removes a small section of the tube. Next, he sutures the cut ends closed. The provider then repeats this procedure for the other fallopian tube if he wants to perform the procedure bilaterally. Finally, he removes the retractors and closes the vaginal wall incision with sutures. For an abdominal approach, the provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider makes an incision in the umbilical area (the area around the belly button or navel) to expose the fallopian tube. Once he exposes the tube, the provider inserts a clamp to bring the fallopian tube into view. He ligates (ties off) and incises the fallopian tube in the same manner as the vaginal approach. After he sutures the fallopian tube ends closed, he repeats the procedure for the other fallopian tube if he wants to perform a bilateral procedure. Finally, he removes the retractors and closes the abdominal incision with sutures. short_description: Tubouterine implantation
lay_term: In this procedure, known as a tubouterine implantation, the provider sutures the fallopian tube directly into the upper part of the uterus to reestablish the patient’s ability to become pregnant. The provider performs this procedure via an abdominal incision. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the lower abdomen just above the pubic bone. He then incises the peritoneum and explores the abdomen. The provider inspects the abdominal cavity, uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. Once he completes his inspection, the provider elevates the uterus and the tubal segments with packing and lyses adhesions if present. The provider then frees the far end of the fallopian tube segment and incises into the top side of the uterus to make an opening. He then repairs the opening in the fallopian tube and removes any part of the tube that was ligated, or tied off, during the previous sterilization procedure. The provider then sutures the now–open tube into the opening in the uterus. He then performs chromotubation to establish that the fallopian tube is open and the opening in the uterus permits the dye to pass. Finally, he removes the packing and closes the abdominal incision with sutures. Terminology Adhesions: Fibrous bands of internal scar tissue that connect tissues not normally connected, often as a result of injury during surgery; when they develop in the uterus, they are referred to as uterine synechiae. Chromotubation: An injection of dye into the fallopian tube to diagnose tubal problems, or to check that the tubes are open after lysis or fimbrioplasty. Fallopian tubes: A set of two fine tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringe like ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also referred to as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges, or salpinx if singular. Lysis of adhesions (adhesiolysis): Freeing up adhesions by cutting and dividing, typically with a combination of sharp and blunt dissection. Ovaries: Female reproductive organ where eggs are produced. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips Code 58752 is a unilateral procedure. If the provider reconnects both fallopian tubes, add modifier 50, Bilateral procedure, to this code. Keep in mind that coverage may be an issue with this procedure as not all payers reimburse for this reconstructive surgery. Read Less

short_description: Fimbrioplasty Notes: (For laparoscopic approach, use 58672)
lay_term: In this procedure, known as a fimbrioplasty, the provider removes adhesions that form around the end of the fallopian tube to open it up so that eggs from the ovary can pass down to the uterus. Once he completes his inspection, the provider meticulously performs lysis of adhesions of the fimbriae using laser, electrosurgery, or scissors. After he completes the lysis procedure, he flowers back each of the flaps using a laser or sutures to ensure that the tube stays open. The provider then performs chromotubation on the tube to ensure that it is open. He then irrigates the abdominal cavity. short_description: Salpingostomy (salpingoneostomy) Notes: (For laparoscopic approach, use 58673)

lay_term: In this procedure, the provider surgically removes part or all of one or both ovaries depending on the extent of the malignancy, in a procedure known as an oophorectomy. He also takes biopsies of lymph nodes and takes tissue samples. The provider may or may not remove one or both fallopian tubes and the omentum. The provider uses an abdominal approach to perform this procedure. This service is done for ovarian, tubal or primary peritoneal cancer. Explanation The provider places the patient in the lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider incises the lower abdomen just above the symphysis pubis. The provider then continues the incision down through the underlying tissue, and peritoneum. The provider takes samples of the pelvic lymph nodes and sends them to a laboratory for testing. The provider then completely examines the peritoneal cavity for any spread of cancer cells. Once he completes his examination of the peritoneal cavity, the provider washes the peritoneum with a saline solution. The solution, along with tissue samples of the peritoneum that the provider obtains, is sent to the laboratory for examination. The provider then exposes the aortic lymph nodes and takes a biopsy of this lymph tissue located near the aorta. He also examines the diaphragm and takes tissue samples to examine for spread of the disease. To remove the ovary and or fallopian tube, if necessary, the provider identifies the ovarian vessels and the infundibulopelvic ligaments. The provider then frees the ovary from where it lies on the broad ligament and incises the infundibulopelvic ligament. He then sutures closed the end of the ligament. lay_term: The provider removes recurring cancer of the ovaries, fallopian tubes, peritoneum, or uterus, and removes the omentum if necessary. In addition, the provider removes the pelvic lymph nodes and samples the para–aortic lymph nodes. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider accesses the intra–abdominal and retroperitoneal spaces, where the tumors are located. The goal of this procedure is to remove as much of the malignant tissue as possible, a process known as tumor debulking. This involves identifying and excising visible tumor masses that have recurred in areas such as the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, or peritoneum (the lining of the abdominal cavity). During the procedure, the provider also may perform an omentectomy, which is the removal of the omentum, a fatty layer of tissue that drapes over the intestines. Tumors often spread to this area, so its removal can help reduce the cancer load. The provider also performs a pelvic lymphadenectomy. This step involves the removal of lymph nodes from the pelvic region to check for cancer spread and prevent future recurrence. Lymph nodes are part of the immune system and act as filters for harmful substances, including cancer cells. In addition to the pelvic lymph nodes, the provider performs a limited para–aortic lymphadenectomy, which involves removing lymph nodes near the aorta (the major artery in the body) to further assess and reduce potential cancer spread. After removal of cancerous tissue and lymph nodes, the provider closes the surgical site. Read Less

short_description: Amniocentesis; therapeutic amniotic fluid reduction (includes ultrasound guidance)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a needle through the patient’s abdominal wall into the fetal amniotic sac to withdraw excess amniotic fluid to treat a condition known as polyhydramnios. The provider uses real time ultrasound scanning to perform this service. Explanation The provider first drapes and preps the patient’s abdominal area. Using ultrasound guidance, he identifies the needle insertion site, and he slowly inserts a needle into the amniotic sac. The provider, working with an assistant, attaches the needle to tubing. While the provider holds the needle in place, the assistant attaches the needle to a drainage system. Using continuous ultrasonic guidance, the provider removes the fluid until a normal amount of amniotic fluid is seen on the ultrasound. The provider remains in constant communication with the ultrasound technician regarding the status of the fetus or fetuses and the fluid level. He does this because continual monitoring of the needle location is necessary to avoid injury to the fetus or placenta because the uterine shape changes as the he removes the fluid. Once he obtains a normal fluid level, the provider removes the needle. Terminology Amnion: Inner membrane of the sac that surrounds the fetus. Amniotic fluid: A clear, slightly yellowish liquid that surrounds the fetus during pregnancy and helps to protect it from mechanical injury. Amniotic sac: A bag of fluid inside the uterus where the fetus develops and grows; it is sometimes called the membranes because the sac is made of two membranes called the amnion and the chorion. Chorion: Outer membrane of the sac that covers the fetus and, which develops hair like structures that attach to the uterine wall. Placenta: A special layer developed during pregnancy to protect and nourish the fetus. Polyhydramnios: An excess of amniotic fluid; it is seen in about 1 percent of pregnancies, and a provider typically diagnoses when the amniotic fluid index, or AFI, is greater than twenty four cm. Real time imaging: The instantaneous display on a monitor of X–ray images of the internal structures or body parts. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips Unlike code 59000, Amniocentesis; diagnostic, code 59001 includes ultrasound guidance so do not report code 76942, Ultrasonic guidance for needle placement, eg, biopsy, aspiration, injection, localization device, imaging supervision and interpretation, in addition to 59001. The provider may need to reduce the amniotic fluid volume on a regular basis, so he will repeat the procedure on an ongoing basis as necessary. Read Less

short_description: Fetal contraction stress test
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider evaluates fetal responses to inducing contractions in the mother to determine if the fetus can tolerate labor. Explanation The provider first drapes and preps the patient, then places a transducer on the abdomen in the area of the baby's heart. Next, he places a pressure gauge around the patient’s abdomen to measure the uterine contractions. The provider asks the mother to stimulate her nipples for several minutes to cause her body to release oxytocin. If there are no contractions after this, the provider administers a dilute solution of oxytocin intravenously to the mother until three contractions occur within ten minutes. He then evaluates the data the monitors’ record and prepares a written report of the findings. Terminology Oxytocin: A naturally occurring hormone that the body produces in the hypothalamus and secrets to the bloodstream through the posterior pituitary gland; the primary purpose of this hormone is to stimulate contractions of the uterus during childbirth and lactation; a provider administers synthetic oxytocin intravenously during labor to stimulate contractions, to control bleeding following delivery, and to stimulate the secretion of breast milk. Transducer: A device that converts one form of energy to another; an ultrasound transducer produces sound waves, captures the echoes created when those waves bounce off body structures, and transfers that data to a computer to create the ultrasound image. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips As the result of the contraction stress test, or CST, the provider will document one of four findings. A positive, or nonreassuring, test means that there were late decelerations following fifty percent or more of the contractions. A negative, or reassuring, test means that the fetus has no late or significant variable decelerations. An equivocal suspicious pattern means there were intermittent late or significant variable decelerations, while an equivocal tachysystolic pattern means that the fetal heart rate decelerations occur with contractions more frequent than every two minutes or lasting longer than 90 seconds. An unsatisfactory test means that the tracing is uninterpretable or contractions are fewer than three in ten minutes. If the provider performs this test in the hospital setting, add modifier 26, Professional component to 59020 because the hospital will bill separately for the technical component of this procedure. short_description: Fetal non-stress test
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider measures the fetal heart rate of the fetus in response to its own movements. Explanation First the patient lies down on the bed with her back raised. The provider attaches one belt to the mother's abdomen to measure fetal heart rate and another belt to measure fetal movements and contractions. The provider then evaluates the fetus via an external monitor that records the heart rate and reactivity of the heart rate to fetal heart movement. In some cases, the mother is given a buzzer and is instructed to push it each time she feels the baby move. The provider may also use sound to induce acceleration in the heart rate. This procedure usually takes 20 to 40 minutes to accomplish. The provider then interprets the result in a written report. Tips The results of the NST can be reassuring or non–reassuring. If there are two or more fetal heart rate accelerations within a 20–minute period (with or without the use of sound), the test is considered reactive (or reassuring). This is true whether or not the mother detects fetal movement during this time period. The test is considered nonreactive (or nonreassuring) if there were insufficient fetal heart rate accelerations in a 40–minute period. If the provider performs this test in the hospital setting, you should add modifier 26 (Professional component) to CPT® code 59025 because the hospital will be billing for the technical component. Note that an NST is a test that measures fetal well–being which is not the same thing as monitoring contractions during labor. This latter type of monitoring is integral to labor management. short_description: Fetal monitoring during labor by consulting physician (ie, non-attending physician) with written report; supervision and interpretation
lay_term: In this procedure, a consulting provider performs imaging supervision and interpretation for a fetal monitoring service at the request of the attending provider. The consulting provider monitors the fetus during labor by supervising or personally attaching an electrode to the fetus and performing the monitoring and interpretation of the results in a written report to the attending provider. Report this code to represent the imaging supervision and interpretation for this procedure. Explanation The consulting physician’s opinion is requested by the attending physician with regard to fetal well–being during labor. The physician supervises nursing staff in the placement of external fetal monitors that detect both uterine contractions and the fetal heat rate. He then evaluates the data from the monitors over a specified period of time for the baseline rate, the baseline fetal heart rate variability, the presence of accelerations, periodic and episodic decelerations, changes or trends of the fetal heart rate patterns over time, and the frequency and intensity of uterine contractions. The physician then interprets the result and makes a recommendation for delivery options to the attending physician via a written report. Terminology Baseline fetal heart rate, or FHR: The pattern of fetal heart rate between uterine contractions. Baseline variability: Fluctuations in the fetal heart rate. short_description: Laparoscopic treatment of ectopic pregnancy; without salpingectomy and/or oophorectomy
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider makes a hole or incision into the fallopian tube and or ovary to remove a small ectopic pregnancy from that location, or removes a fetus that is within the pelvic cavity or imbedded within the cornu of the uterus, or the points where the uterus and fallopian tubes meet, also known as the uterine horns. The provider performs this procedure using a laparoscope. The provider does not remove the fallopian tube or ovary. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized, the provider places the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position. The provider then performs a pelvic examination and places a uterine manipulator through the cervix so the uterus can be manipulated during the surgery. The provider enters the abdominal cavity near the belly button by using a Veress needle or an open incision to place a laparoscope. The provider insufflates the abdomen with CO2, or carbon dioxide gas to create a pneumoperitoneum, and then puts the patient into the Trendelenburg position. He then makes small incisions around the abdominal area to insert trocars to better view the operating site and add surgical tools. If he is performing robotic surgery, he docks the robot to the laparoscope at this time. The provider then inspects the abdominal cavity and locates the ectopic pregnancy. Once he completes his inspection, the provider infiltrates the lining of the fallopian tube or top part of the uterus with vasopressin, a drug that reduces blood loss. He then aspirates any products of conception, blood clots, or free blood that may be present. The provider then makes a small incision in the fallopian tube or ovary, and removes the embryo manually, or removes the fetus that he finds elsewhere. He then washes out the pelvic cavity with saline, checks for bleeding, and repairs the fallopian tube or ovary. Finally, he deflates the abdominal cavity and removes all of the instruments, and trocars. He closes the trocar site, fascia and skin, and removes all instruments from the vagina. Terminology Aspiration: To withdraw fluid from a body cavity or a mass, such as a cyst, with a needle and a syringe. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Ectopic pregnancy: Any gestation outside of the uterine cavity; these can occur in the interstitial portion of the tube, in the rudimentary horn of the uterus, the fallopian tube, the abdomen, the cervix or the ovary. Fallopian tubes: A set of two fine tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringe like ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also referred to as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges, or salpinx if singular. Fascia: Sheet or band of muscle, fat, and fibrous tissue that lies under the skin. Insufflates: To blow a medicated powder, gas, or vapor into a bodily cavity. Laparoscopy: An operation a provider performs to view the abdominal and pelvic contents through small incisions with the aid of a camera; a provider uses it to inspect and diagnose a condition, or to perform surgery for a problem; a fiberoptic instrument a provider inserts through an incision in the abdominal wall and uses to examine visually the interior of the peritoneal cavity; trocars are also inserted to allow for the addition of surgical tools. Oophorectomy: The surgical removal of one or both ovaries. Ovaries: Female reproductive organ where eggs are produced. Pneumoperitoneum: The presence of gas or air in the abdominal cavity; when laparoscopic procedures are performed, carbon dioxide is pumped into the abdominal cavity to expand the viewing space. Robot assisted surgery: An operation that is started with the laparoscope, but a robot arm is docked with the laparoscope, and the surgeon completes the operation while sitting at a console that is next to the operating table. Salpingectomy: The surgical removal of one or both fallopian tubes. Trendelenburg position: The patient is laid flat on her back with her feet higher than her head; this position moves the bowel and upper organs away from the operative site when a laparoscopic procedure is performed. Trocar: A medical device that is made up of an obturator, which may be a metal or plastic, sharpened or nonbladed tip, a cannula, or hollow tube, and a seal; trocars are placed through the abdomen during laparoscopic surgery, and they function as a portal to place other instruments such as graspers, scissors, staplers, and a laser needed during the surgical procedure. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Veress needle: A spring loaded needle used during a laparoscopic procedure to create a pneumoperitoneum. Read Less

short_description: Insertion of cervical dilator (eg, laminaria, prostaglandin) (separate procedure)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider inserts a drug or device that dilates the cervix prior to a gynecological procedure that requires entry into the uterus or to dilate the cervix prior to delivery. The provider performs this procedure using a vaginal approach. Explanation First the provider places the patient in a lithotomy position and inserts a speculum into the vaginal canal. If he places prostaglandin, the provider opens the package, and places the end of the woven applicator behind the cervix before inducing labor. If he places laminaria, the provider grasps the cervix with a tenaculum and inserts the sterile applicator into the opening of the cervix. Once in place, the device absorbs moisture, expands, and slowly dilates the cervix. The provider removes the instruments. Laminaria: Tampon like device that absorb moisture and gradually expands within the cervical canal. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Posterior fornix: The arched recess in the upper part of the vagina. Prostaglandin: A drug laced strip that is introduced into the posterior fornix of the vagina, and causes the cervix to soften. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure; it has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted, and then opened when they are in place. Tenaculum: A surgical clamp designed to hold or grasp tissue during dissection, commonly used to grasp the cervix. short_description: Episiotomy or vaginal repair, by other than attending
lay_term: The provider, other than the attending physician, incises the perineum with scissors or a scalpel, in a procedure known as an episiotomy, to ease the passage of the baby’s head during birth. Explanation With the patient in the lithotomy position, the provider applies a local anesthetic into the area of the perineum. The provider then makes a midline or mediolateral incision into the skin area between the vagina and rectum. Once she incises this area, the vagina enlarges, which helps facilitate delivery of the baby’s head and body. Once the provider delivers the baby and removes the placenta, she examines the birth canal and repairs any first–, second–, third–, or fourth–degree vaginal tears that need repair. The provider then closes the episiotomy incision with absorbable sutures. Terminology First–degree laceration: A laceration that is limited to the area where the labia minora and majora meet at the bottom of the vaginal opening and the superficial perineal skin or vaginal mucosa. Fourth–degree laceration: A laceration that extends from the area where the labia minora and majora meet at the bottom of the vaginal opening, and includes the perineal skin, vaginal mucosa, muscles, anal sphincter, and the rectal mucosa. Lithotomy position: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Perineum: The short stretch of skin that starts at the bottom of the vulva, the external female genital organs, and continues to the anal opening. Placenta: A special layer developed during pregnancy to protect and nourish the fetus. Second–degree laceration: A laceration extends beyond area where the labia minora and majora meet at the bottom of the vaginal opening, the perineal skin and vaginal mucosa to the perineal muscles and fascia, but not to the anal sphincter. Third–degree laceration: A laceration that includes the tissues of a second degree laceration, but also the anal sphincter. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. short_description: Cerclage of cervix, during pregnancy; abdominal
lay_term: The provider closes off a cervix that is damaged by trauma, a previously failed cervical cerclage, or when there is a very short cervix. The provider performs this procedure via an abdominal approach. Explanation The provider places the patient in the supine position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider makes a transverse or vertical incision into the abdominal cavity and exposes the area where the cervix meets the isthmus of the uterus. The provider then chooses an area that has no blood supply and passes a band of mesh from the front to the back of the cervix at the point where the cervix and uterus meet. The provider then wraps the mesh band around the isthmus of the cervix so it lies flat against the uterus and secures it in place with a knot. When the compression of the cervix is complete, the provider checks for bleeding and closes the abdomen with sutures. Terminology Cerclage: Surgical procedure a provider performs through the vagina or abdomen where he uses sutures to close the cervix to prevent the premature delivery of a fetus; also called a cervical stitch. Isthmus of the uterus: A narrow portion of the uterus that connects the cervix to the body of the uterus. Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Transverse incision: An incision that runs across the body to provide access to the abdomen and pelvis. short_description: Vaginal delivery only (with or without episiotomy and/or forceps)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider provides admission to the hospital for delivery, labor management, including induction of labor, fetal monitoring, use of low forceps, and episiotomy, vaginal delivery of the fetus and placenta on the same date of service. Explanation Intrapartum Care: Management of labor usually begins when the patient informs the provider that she thinks she is in labor or presents to the hospital in apparent labor. If the patient calls the provider about labor, he advises the patient when to come to hospital, alerts hospital personnel of the patient’s arrival, and provides initial instructions for the patient's care. The provider then performs an initial history and physical examination at the time of admission to determine that labor has indeed begun. He then assesses the condition of mother and fetus, develops a treatment plan, and communicates with nursing staff, anesthesia, and pediatric staff as necessary. When his initial evaluation is complete, the provider periodically reevaluates the condition of his patient and her fetus throughout the course of labor and alters the treatment plan as necessary. The provider may induce or augment labor, but this is inclusive of labor management no matter if he performs this service using, IV drugs, or rupture of membranes. During the first stage of labor, which starts with contractions and ends with complete dilation of the cervix, the provider evaluates the patient usually every thirty minutes. During the second stage of labor, which lasts from complete dilation of the cervix through the birth of the baby, the provider usually evaluates the patient at 5 to 15–minute intervals. During labor, the provider may administer regional or local anesthesia to ease labor pains. He then continually monitors uterine contractions and the fetal heart rate using external monitors he places on the mother’s abdomen. The provider may instruct the patient on breathing technique, check the uterine contractions for regularity, and perform a vaginal examination to determine position of the fetal head. When he sees the dilation of the cervix is fully or nearly fully complete, he moves the patient to the delivery room, and the patient is prepped and draped. The provider instructs the patient to begin pushing the baby at this stage, and when the baby’s head begins to show through the vaginal opening, called crowning, the provider may perform a few maneuvers with the baby's emerging body to facilitate a smooth and better delivery. He may use low forceps to assist in the delivery of the head and shoulders or apply a vacuum extractor in some cases. He may also perform an episiotomy when the perineum does not stretch adequately and obstructs delivery. Once the head comes out, the provider gently supports the whole body with his hand so the body can rotate and come out through the birth canal. After the delivery is complete, the provider removes the placenta and incises the umbilical cord. The provider inspects the cervix and vagina for lacerations, repairs the episiotomy incision, and repairs any minor vaginal or cervical lacerations as well. Terminology Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Episiotomy: An incision made in the perineum to allow passage of the baby’s head and to prevent ragged tearing of the perineal tissues. Forceps: A two bladed instrument used to compress or grasp. Forceps delivery: One of three types of delivery with forceps may occur, but they are still part of intrapartum care; a provider uses outlet forceps when the baby’s scalp is visible at the vaginal opening; low forceps when the baby's head is at +2 station or lower; and midforceps when the baby’s head is above +2 station, but the head is engaged. Intrapartum period: Period from the onset of labor to the complete expulsion of the placenta. Perineum: The short stretch of skin that starts at the bottom of the vulva, the external female genital organs, and continues to the anal opening. Placenta: A special layer developed during pregnancy to protect and nourish the fetus.Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vacuum extraction: Placement of a bell shaped cup on the baby’s head and application of vacuum pressure to create suction on the baby’s head; the provider then pulls on the device he attaches to the cup at the same time as the mother indicates a contraction is beginning, and he continues throughout the full contraction; at the end of the contraction the provider stops pulling and waits for the next contraction, continuing until the baby’s head begins to exit the vaginal opening. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Tips Add a modifier 22, Increased procedural services, to 59409 when the provider performs work greater than normal. This may occur because the labor management, or delivery was significantly more work than for routine care. The provider must provide detailed documentation to get additional reimbursement. If the provider who delivers the baby also provides inpatient postpartum care, he may bill for this in addition. However, if the provider will perform the outpatient postpartum care as well, report 59410, Vaginal delivery only, with or without episiotomy and or forceps; including postpartum care. Read Less

short_description: Vaginal delivery only (with or without episiotomy and/or forceps); including postpartum care
lay_term: In this global service, the provider admits the patient to the hospital for delivery, labor management, including induction of labor, fetal monitoring, use of low forceps, and episiotomy, vaginal delivery of the fetus and placenta, and inpatient and outpatient postpartum care. Typical postpartum care ends after one or more outpatient visits up to six weeks following delivery. Explanation Intrapartum Care: Management of labor usually begins when the patient informs the provider that she thinks she is in labor or presents to the hospital in apparent labor. If the patient calls the provider about labor, he advises the patient when to come to hospital, alerts hospital personnel of the patient’s arrival, and provides initial instructions for the patient's care. The provider then performs an initial history and physical examination at the time of admission to determine that labor has indeed begun. He then assesses the mother's and fetus’ condition, develops a treatment plan, and communicates with nursing staff, anesthesia, and pediatric staff as necessary. When his initial evaluation is complete, the provider periodically reevaluates the condition of his patient and her fetus throughout the course of labor and alters the treatment plan as necessary. The provider may induce or augment labor, but this is inclusive of labor management no matter if he performs this service using IV drugs or rupture of membranes. During the first stage of labor, which starts with contractions and ends with complete dilation of the cervix, the provider evaluates the patient usually every thirty minutes. During the second stage of labor, which lasts from complete dilation of the cervix through the birth of the baby, the provider usually evaluates the patient at 5 to 15–minute intervals. During labor, the provider may administer regional or local anesthesia to ease labor pains. He then continually monitors uterine contractions and the fetal heart rate using external monitors he places on the mother’s abdomen. The provider may instruct the patient on breathing technique, check the uterine contractions for regularity, and perform a vaginal examination to determine position of the fetal head. When he sees the dilation of the cervix is fully or nearly fully complete, he moves the patient to the delivery room, and the patient is prepped and draped. The provider instructs the patient to begin pushing the baby at this stage, and when the baby’s head begins to show through the vaginal opening, called crowning, the provider may perform a few maneuvers with the baby's emerging body to facilitate a smooth and better delivery. He may use low forceps to assist in the delivery of the head and shoulders or apply a vacuum extractor in some cases. He may also perform an episiotomy when the perineum does not stretch adequately and obstructs delivery. Once the head comes out, the provider gently supports the whole body with his hand so the body can rotate and come out through the birth canal. After the delivery is complete, the provider removes the placenta and incises the umbilical cord. The provider inspects the cervix and vagina for lacerations, repairs the episiotomy incision, and repairs any minor vaginal or cervical tears as well. Inpatient Postpartum Care: The provider transfers the patient to recovery. He writes orders for aftercare including monitoring vital signs, pain management if necessary, patient diet, and ambulation. The provider visits the patient several hours after delivery to check on her progress and follows up with additional visits until the day of discharge, which is normally 48 hours for a vaginal delivery. At discharge, the provider discusses care of the breasts and vulva, diet, exercise with the patient, when the patient should present for her first visit, and when to come in if there are problems such as excessive bleeding or cramping. Outpatient Postpartum Care: Typical outpatient postpartum care includes ongoing evaluation of the mother’s physical and mental status following birth, a physical examination to ensure that the mother is recovering normally, discussion of lactation, nutrition, and exercise after delivery, review or initiation of birth control options, evaluation of immunizations, and collection of a screening Pap smear specimen if necessary. The provider schedules the first visit four to six weeks following delivery but may only order one visit at six weeks instead of two. The provider performs a physical examination, which includes measuring the patient’s weight and blood pressure, examination of the breasts and abdomen, and a pelvic exam. The provider will also incorporate preconception counseling to prepare the patient for a future pregnancy. Terminology Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Episiotomy: An incision made in the perineum to allow passage of the baby’s head and to prevent ragged tearing of the perineal tissues. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Forceps delivery: One of three types of delivery with forceps may occur, but they are still part of intrapartum care; a provider uses outlet forceps when the baby’s scalp is visible at the vaginal opening; low forceps when the baby's head is at +2 station or lower; and midforceps when the baby’s head is above +2 station, but the head is engaged. Global care: A single code and related reimbursement for all care usually associated with a procedure; the packaging is based on three phases of a surgical procedure: preoperative evaluation, the intraoperative procedure, and postoperative care for either zero, ten, or ninety days. Intrapartum period: Period from the onset of labor to the complete expulsion of the placenta. Perineum: The short stretch of skin that starts at the bottom of the vulva, the external female genital organs, and continues to the anal opening. Placenta: A special layer developed during pregnancy to protect and nourish the fetus. Postpartum period: Period from the termination of labor to complete reduction of the uterus to its normal nonpregnant size and state, usually about forty two days. Umbilical cord: The connecting stalk between the fetus and the placenta, normally containing two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein; the umbilical vein supplies the fetus with oxygenated, nutrient rich blood from the placenta and the umbilical arteries transport deoxygenated, nutrient depleted blood from the fetal heart back to the placenta. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. This may occur because the labor management or delivery was significantly more work than for routine care. The provider must provide detailed documentation to get additional reimbursement. Read Less

short_description: External cephalic version, with or without tocolysis Notes: (Use 59412 in addition to code[s] for delivery)
lay_term: In this procedure, the provider attempts to turn the fetus into the head first position prior to delivery. The provider may use drugs to suppress contractions while he performs the procedure. The provider maneuvers the fetus with his hands on the woman’s abdomen. Explanation After monitoring the patient for at least thirty minutes to assess fetal wellbeing, the provider puts the patient in the supine position, and performs a limited ultrasound sound to verify the baby’s position, the position of the placenta, and the amniotic fluid volume. The provider then administers a drug to stop or prevent uterine contractions. After he confirms the fetal heart rate is optimal and there are no contractions, the provider uses both hands on the surface of the mother’s abdomen, one is put by the baby’s head and the other by the baby buttocks, and then he pushes and rolls the fetus to a head down, or cephalic, position. The provider monitors the baby’s heart rate continuously and uses the ultrasound transducer to continue to check on progress. After the fetus is in the head down position, the provider performs one last ultrasound to verify the position. Ultrasound: Ultrasound is when the provider uses high frequency sound waves to view tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. short_description: Routine obstetric care including antepartum care, cesarean delivery, and postpartum care
lay_term: In this global service, the provider provides all of the antepartum care, admission to the hospital for delivery, delivery of the fetus and placenta via an abdominal incision, and inpatient and outpatient postpartum care. These services include evaluation of the health status of both mother and fetus, estimation of the gestational age, identification of the patient at risk for complications, anticipation of problems before they occur and prevention of problems if possible, and education and communication with regard to all issues that relate to the pregnancy such as the pregnancy plan, counseling for antenatal testing, lactation, and nutritional counseling. A provider will complete a comprehensive initial history and physical of the mother as well, with subsequent examinations at each visit thereafter that include both maternal and fetal markers to identify if the pregnancy is progressing normally. These markers include a urinalysis to measure protein and glucose, recording of the fetal heart rate, measurement of the uterine fundus, examination for maternal edema, maternal blood pressure, position of the fetus, cervical status, and ruling out labor. In some cases, the provider will collect a screening Pap smear specimen, and in that case, the collection is part of the antepartum visit. The frequency of visits is usually monthly up to 28 weeks gestation, then biweekly visits to 36 weeks gestation, and then weekly visits until delivery. Antenatal screening tests, care for conditions unrelated to pregnancy, injections, surgical procedures, and ultrasound examinations are generally not included in normal antepartum care and the provider can report them separately based on payer policy. Complications of pregnancy in the antepartum period are rarely paid at the time of the complication, but a provider may bill them at the time of service for later appeal to avoid timely filing issues. The provider performs an initial history and physical examination at the time of admission to assess the mother's and fetus’ condition, develops a treatment plan, and communicates with nursing staff, anesthesia, and pediatric staff as necessary. The provider monitors the fetal heart rate and for possible uterine contractions. The patient is taken to the operating room, and the provider places the patient in a supine position. A spinal anesthetic is administered so that the patient can be awake during the birth in most cases. The provider makes an incision in the lower abdomen and exposes the lower uterine segment. He then dissects the bladder away from the uterus and makes a transverse incision into the lower uterine segment. The provider ruptures the membranes to release the amniotic fluid and delivers the baby manually, with a vacuum cup, or forceps. He then administers a drug to help the uterus contract and manually removes the placenta and membranes. He examines the uterine cavity, closes the uterine wall in one or two layers, and covers the uterine incision with peritoneum. Finally, the provider closes the abdominal incision. Despite a cesarean delivery, the provider inspects the cervix and vagina for lacerations, repairs the episiotomy incision if one was made, and repairs any minor vaginal or cervical tears as well. If the patient is presenting for labor that later fails, intrapartum management usually begins when the patient informs the provider that she thinks she is in labor or presents to the hospital in apparent labor. If the patient calls the provider about labor, he advises the patient when to come to hospital, alerts hospital personnel of the patient’s arrival, and provides initial instructions for the patient's care. The provider then performs an initial history and physical examination at the time of admission to determine that labor has indeed begun. He then assesses the mother's and fetus’ condition, develops a treatment plan, and communicates with nursing staff, anesthesia, and pediatric staff as necessary. When his initial evaluation is complete, the provider periodically reevaluates the patient's and fetus' condition throughout the course of labor and alters the treatment plan as necessary. The provider may induce or augment labor, but this is inclusive of labor management whether he performs this service using IV drugs or rupture of membranes. The provider may give the patient a regional or local anesthesia to ease labor pains during labor. Despite a cesarean delivery, the provider inspects the cervix and vagina for lacerations, repairs the episiotomy incision, and repairs any minor vaginal or cervical lacerations as well. The provider will also incorporate preconceptual counseling into postpartum care, when appropriate, to prepare the patient for a future pregnancy. Edema: Excessive swelling due to fluid retention, usually in the subcutaneous tissues or lungs. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Placenta: A special layer developed during pregnancy to protect and nourish the fetus. Postpartum period: Period from the termination of labor to complete reduction of the uterus to its normal nonpregnant size and state, usually defined as 42 days Supine position: Patient lying on her back with her legs extended. Transverse incision: An incision that runs across the body to provide access to the abdomen and pelvis. Explanation After a cesarean delivery and through the existing abdominal incision, the provider grasps the top of the uterus with a clamp and enters the retroperitoneal space. He incises the round ligaments, separates them from the surface of the broad ligament, and then extends the incision along the broad ligament to loosen the area around the uterus. He then locates the ureters and moves them away from the uterus. If the provider is not removing the fallopian tubes or ovaries, he incises the fallopian tubes and the ovarian ligaments as close as possible to the uterus. If the provider is removing the fallopian tubes or ovaries, he incises the infundibulopelvic ligaments instead. The provider then releases the bladder from where it attaches to the cervix. He then identifies the uterine artery, incises, and clamps it. Next, the provider clamps, cuts, and suture ligates the cardinal ligament. The provider then incises, clamps, and suture ligates the uterosacral ligament and anchors it to the cardinal ligament. Then, he incises the vagina in a circular fashion and removes the uterus with the cervix, tubes, and ovaries, if removing, in one piece. He closes the vaginal cuff with sutures and attaches the cuff to the uterosacral ligaments on the right and left sides. He does this to prevent the small bowel from prolapsing into the vaginal canal. Finally, the provider closes the peritoneum, muscle, and fascia and the abdominal skin incision using sutures. If the provider performs a subtotal hysterectomy instead, the provider leaves the cervix in place. He follows the procedure for the total hysterectomy described above but does not incise the cardinal or uterosacral ligaments. He separates the fundus of the uterus from the cervix using a scalpel and removes the uterus from the abdominal cavity. To prevent cancer from developing, the provider may core out a part of the cervical canal. He closes the top of the exposed cervix with sutures. Finally, the provider closes the peritoneum, muscle, and fascia and the abdominal skin incision using sutures. Terminology Broad ligament: A large fold of peritoneum that attaches to each side of the uterus and extends to the walls of the pelvis; these ligaments encase the ovaries and fallopian tubes. Cardinal ligament: A ligament found at the base of the broad ligament that contains the uterine arteries and veins, and attaches to the pelvic sidewall at the ischial spine; it holds the uterus in its normal position at the level of the cervix. Cervical canal: A spindle like shaped canal extending from the uterus to the vagina; the neck of the uterus; also known as endocervical canal, canal of the cervix, or the cavity of cervix. Cesarean section (C section): A surgical procedure to deliver an infant through an abdominal incision rather than vaginally; also known as a surgical birth or a cesarean delivery. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Extraperitoneal: The portion of the abdomen and pelvis which does not lie within the peritoneum. Fallopian tubes: A set of two fine tubes that begin at the upper body of the uterus and lead to the ovaries; the ovaries lie very close to the fringe like ends of the fallopian tubes; they are also referred to as the oviducts, uterine tubes, or salpinges, or salpinx if singular. Fascia: Sheet or band of muscle, fat, and fibrous tissue that lies under the skin. Hysterectomy: Surgical removal of the uterus. Infundibulopelvic ligaments: Also knows as the suspensory ligaments of the ovary, these ligaments hold the ovary to the pelvic wall and must be cut in order to remove the ovaries. Ovarian ligaments: Cords of muscle tissue that lie on the broad ligament and start at the lower part of the ovary and attach to each side of uterus that is just below the fallopian tubes. Ovaries: Female reproductive organ where eggs are produced. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Retroperitoneal space: Behind and outside the smooth transparent thin membrane that lines the cavity of the abdomen, called the peritoneum. Round ligaments: Bands of muscle and fiber that attach to the top of the uterus on each side and travel through the inguinal canal to end at the labia majora. Ureter: Duct by which urine passes from the kidney to the bladder. Uterine fundus: The top rounded portion of the uterus, above the openings of the fallopian tubes and is where an egg usually implants; a provider measures the fundus to determine the growth of the fetus. Uterosacral ligament: A band of fascia that inserts into the sacrum and then connects to the back wall of the uterus at the internal cervical os, or opening; this ligament supports the uterus, and holds it in place. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear–shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vaginal cuff: The end of the vagina close to the cervix. Tips Because 59525 is an add–on code, do not add a modifier to this code. short_description: Routine obstetric care including antepartum care, vaginal delivery (with or without episiotomy, and/or forceps) and postpartum care, after previous cesarean delivery
lay_term: In this global service, the provider provides all of the antepartum care, admission to the hospital for delivery, intensive labor management, including fetal monitoring, use of low forceps, and episiotomy, vaginal delivery of the fetus and placenta, and inpatient and outpatient postpartum care. The patient has had a previous cesarean delivery but was able to deliver vaginally at this delivery. Typical global services begin at eight to ten weeks gestation, with a full term vaginal delivery at thirty–nine to forty weeks gestation, and routine outpatient postpartum care at six weeks following delivery. Explanation Antepartum care: The care given to the mother at each antepartum visit varies with the requirements of the pregnancy, but there are some basic services a provider performs. The provider integrates these services into the antepartum care no matter when they occur or which level of provider, such as an MD, NP, PA, CNM, or RN, performs them. These services include evaluation of the health status of both mother and fetus, estimation of the gestational age, identification of the patient's risk for complications, anticipation of problems before they occur and prevention of problems if possible, and education and communication with regard to all issues that relate to the pregnancy such as the pregnancy plan, counseling for antenatal testing, and lactation and nutritional counseling. In addition to providing routine prenatal services to the pregnant patient who has undergone a previous cesarean delivery, the provider must also extensively review the patient's delivery records to ascertain whether she is a candidate for a trial of labor and counsel the patient regarding her options for attempting VBAC and the risks and potential benefits of VBAC compared to a repeat cesarean. A provider will complete a comprehensive initial history and physical of the mother as well, with subsequent examinations at each visit thereafter that include both maternal and fetal markers to determine if the pregnancy is progressing normally. These markers include a urinalysis to measure protein and glucose, recording of the fetal heart rate, measurement of the uterine fundus, examination for maternal edema, maternal blood pressure, position of the fetus, cervical status, and ruling out labor. In some cases, the provider will collect a screening Pap smear specimen, and in that case, the collection is part of the antepartum visit. The frequency of visits is usually monthly up to 28 weeks gestation, then biweekly visits to 36 weeks gestation, and then weekly visits until delivery. Antenatal screening tests, care for conditions unrelated to pregnancy, injections, surgical procedures, and ultrasound examinations are generally not included in normal antepartum care, and the provider can report them separately based on payer policy. Complications of pregnancy in the antepartum period are rarely paid at the time of the complication, but a provider may bill them at the time of service for later appeal to avoid timely filing issues. Intrapartum Care: Management of labor usually begins when the patient informs the provider that she thinks she is in labor or presents to the hospital in apparent labor. If the patient calls the provider about labor, he advises the patient when to come to hospital, alerts hospital personnel of the patient’s arrival, and provides initial instructions for the patient's care. With a vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC), the provider usually must be at the hospital soon after the patient arrives. The provider performs an initial history and physical examination at the time of admission to determine that labor has indeed begun, assesses the mother's and fetus’ condition, develops a treatment plan, and communicates with nursing staff. After the initial evaluation, the physician periodically reevaluates the condition of his patient and her fetus throughout the course of labor and alters the treatment plan as necessary. Monitoring of the VBAC patient occurs with greater frequency and is more intense than monitoring of other patients in labor because of the risk of uterine rupture and often requires the constant presence of the provider. In addition to bedside evaluation of the patient, the physician consults with anesthesiologists, operating and delivery room staff, and a pediatrician or neonatologist. The provider may administer regional or local anesthesia to ease labor pains during labor. He then continually monitors uterine contractions and the fetal heart rate using external monitors he places on the mother’s abdomen. The provider may instruct the patient on breathing technique, check the uterine contractions for regularity, and perform a vaginal examination to determine position of the fetal head. When he sees the dilation of the cervix is fully or nearly fully complete, he moves the patient to the delivery room, and the patient is prepped and draped. The provider instructs the patient to begin pushing the baby at this stage, and when the baby’s head begins to show through the vaginal opening, called crowning, the provider may perform a few maneuvers with the baby's emerging body to facilitate a smooth and better delivery. He may use low forceps to assist in the delivery of the head and shoulders or apply a vacuum extractor in some cases. He may also perform an episiotomy when the perineum does not stretch adequately and obstructs delivery. Once the head comes out, the provider gently supports the whole body with his hand so the body can rotate and come out through the birth canal. After the delivery is complete, the provider removes the placenta and incises the umbilical cord. The provider inspects the cervix and vagina for lacerations, repairs the episiotomy incision, and repairs any minor vaginal or cervical tears as well. Inpatient Postpartum Care: The provider transfers the patient to recovery. He writes orders for aftercare including monitoring vital signs, pain management if necessary, patient diet, and ambulation. The provider visits the patient several hours after delivery to check on her progress and follows up with additional visits until the day of discharge, which is normally 48 hours for a vaginal delivery. At discharge, the provider discusses care of the breasts and vulva, diet, and exercise with the patient, when the patient should present for her first visit, and when to come in if there are problems such as excess bleeding or cramping. Outpatient Postpartum Care: Typical outpatient postpartum care a provider performs includes ongoing evaluation of the mother’s physical and mental status following birth, a physical examination to ensure that the mother is recovering normally, discussion of lactation, nutrition, and exercise post delivery, review or initiation of birth control options, evaluation of immunizations, and collection of a screening Pap smear specimen if necessary. The provider schedules the first visit four to six weeks following delivery but may only order one visit at six weeks instead of two. The provider performs a physical examination, which includes measuring the patient’s weight and blood pressure, examination of the breasts and abdomen, and a pelvic exam. The provider will also incorporate preconception counseling to prepare the patient for a future pregnancy. Terminology Antenatal testing: Tests a provider offers a mother to check on the health of the baby and mother. Antepartum period: Period from confirmation of pregnancy to delivery of the baby. Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal. Cesarean delivery: A surgical procedure to deliver an infant through an incision rather than vaginally; also known as a surgical birth or a cesarean section (C section). Episiotomy: An incision made in the perineum to allow passage of the baby’s head and to prevent ragged tearing of the perineal tissues. Forceps: Pincers or tongs used for grasping; also surgical forceps. Forceps delivery: One of three types of delivery with forceps may occur, but they are still part of intrapartum care; a provider uses outlet forceps when the baby’s scalp is visible at the vaginal opening; low forceps when the baby's head is at +2 station or lower; and midforceps when the baby’s head is above +2 station, but the head is engaged. Gestational age: The period of time between conception and birth. Global care: A single code and related reimbursement for all care usually associated with a procedure; the packaging is based on three phases of a surgical procedure: preoperative evaluation, the intraoperative procedure, and postoperative care for either zero, ten, or ninety days. Intrapartum period: Period from the onset of labor to the complete expulsion of the placenta. Perineum: The short stretch of skin that starts at the bottom of the vulva, the external female genital organs, and continues to the anal opening. Peritoneum: Membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Placenta: A special layer developed during pregnancy to protect and nourish the fetus. Postpartum period: Period from the termination of labor to complete reduction of the uterus to its normal nonpregnant size and state, usually defined as 42 days. Umbilical cord: The connecting stalk between the fetus and the placenta, normally containing two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein; the umbilical vein supplies the fetus with oxygenated, nutrient rich blood from the placenta and the umbilical arteries transport deoxygenated, nutrient depleted blood from the fetal heart back to the placenta. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear–shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Vacuum extraction: Placement of a bell shaped cup on the baby’s head and application of vacuum pressure to create suction on the baby’s head; the provider then pulls on the device he attaches to the cup at the same time as the mother indicates a contraction is beginning, and he continues throughout the full contraction; at the end of the contraction the provider stops pulling and waits for the next contraction, continuing until the baby’s head begins to exit the vaginal opening. Vagina: A canal made up of muscle lined with a mucous membrane that can stretch due to folds in the membrane; it extends from the vestibule area to where the cervix butts up against the vaginal vault; it is longer on the posterior wall, the side located above the rectum, than the anterior wall, the side located below the bladder. Vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC): The practice of delivering a baby vaginally after a previous baby has been delivered through caesarean section. Tips If the provider performs less than normal global care, add modifier 52, Reduced Service to 59610; this may include providing fewer than normal antepartum visits or not being present for labor management or the delivery of the baby. Add modifier 22, Increased procedural service, to 59610 when the provider’s work is greater than normal; this may occur because the patient was seen many more times than expected in the antepartum period due to complications or the labor management or delivery was significantly more work than for routine care; detailed documentation is necessary to get additional reimbursement. short_description: Treatment of incomplete abortion, any trimester, completed surgically
