short_description: Induced abortion, by 1 or more vaginal suppositories (eg, prostaglandin) with or without cervical dilation (eg, laminaria), including hospital admission and visits, delivery of fetus and secundines; with hysterotomy (failed medical evacuation)
lay_term: In this global procedure, the provider terminates a pregnancy by inserting vaginal suppositories to induce labor contractions and may also insert a laminaria to dilate the cervix. In this service, the patient fails to abort the fetus and the provider performs surgical removal of the fetus and the placenta via an incision into the uterus, like a cesarean delivery. The provider admits the patient to the hospital, inserts the drug and cervical dilator, manages the labor that follows, and then performs the incision into the uterus. The provider then follows the patient in the hospital until discharge. Providers use this method usually after the first trimester, fourteen weeks and zero days gestation or more. Explanation The provider admits the patient to the hospital and performs an admission history and physical. The provider takes the patient to the procedure room and places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position. The provider inserts a laminaria into the cervix and then places a medicated suppository into the vaginal canal every three to four hours until labor begins. Once labor begins, the provider monitors the patient as he would for any vaginal delivery up until the point that he decides that the induction has failed and a hysterotomy is necessary. The provider takes the patient to the operating room, places the patient in the supine position, and administers a general anesthetic. The provider makes a vertical or horizontal incision in the lower abdominal wall, and he enters the uterus through the lower uterine segment by making an additional incision in that location. He removes the fetus and placenta from the uterine cavity. After ensuring that all bleeding is under control, the provider sutures the uterine and abdominal incisions. The provider then provides all of the hospital care to the patient through discharge. short_description: Multifetal pregnancy reduction(s) (MPR)
lay_term: The provider reduces a higher order multifetal gestation pregnancy to either a twin or singleton pregnancy to increase the chances of a successful pregnancy for the remaining fetuses and to help prevent the serious complications that can occur with higher order gestations. Explanation Before beginning the procedure, the provider performs an ultrasound to identify the viability of all the fetuses and selects the ones to reduce. The ultrasound is a separately reportable procedure from 59866. When the ultrasound is complete, the provider preps and drapes the abdominal area. Then, he identifies the needle insertion site and injects the site with a local anesthetic. The provider then inserts a needle into the thorax of the selected fetus using ultrasound guidance. He injects potassium chloride and waits for the fetal heartbeat to stop. He then removes the needle from the thorax and moves it into the amniotic sac where he removes the fluid surrounding this fetus. The provider repeats the procedure for each fetus to be reduced. When the procedure is complete, the provider removes the needle from the mother’s abdomen. The provider performs a follow–up ultrasound to verify that the remaining fetuses have a heartbeat, and this ultrasound is also reported separately from 59866. Terminology Amniotic sac: A bag of fluid inside the uterus where the fetus develops and grows; it is sometimes called the membranes because the sac is made of two membranes called the amnion and the chorion. Multifetal: More than two fetuses. Singleton pregnancy: A single fetus. Thorax: Part of the body between the neck and the abdomen. Ultrasound: The use of high–frequency sound waves to view internal tissues to diagnose or manage conditions. Tips Ultrasound guidance during the procedure is included as part of 59866 since a provider cannot perform the procedure without using it, but the pre– and post–procedure ultrasounds are separately reportable. short_description: Removal of cerclage suture under anesthesia (other than local)
lay_term: The provider removes a cerclage suture, which was placed to hold the cervix closed. The provider normally performs this service via a vaginal approach with the patient under general anesthesia Explanation The provider places the patient in a dorsal lithotomy position and administers a general anesthetic. The provider places a weighted speculum into the vagina and uses a retractor to expose the cervix and the knot of the originally placed Shirodkar cerclage. The provider then elevates the suture, which may have become buried in the cervical mucosa and cuts the knot to allow him to gently pull the suture line from around the cervix. He then closes the cervical mucosa and checks for bleeding. Terminology Cervix: Fleshy end of the uterus that juts into the vaginal canal, which consists of an outer opening, called the exocervix or ectocervix, middle section, called the transformation zone, where the squamous and columnar cells meet, and inner portion that opens into the body of the uterus, called the endocervix; menstrual blood passes from the uterine lining into the cervix and out into the vaginal canal Dorsal lithotomy: The patient rests on her back with knees bent, positioned above the hips, and spread apart through the use of stirrups. Retractor: An instrument for drawing aside the edges of a wound or for holding back structures adjacent to the operative field. Shirodkar cerclage: Placement of purse string sutures through the walls of the cervix so they're not exposed; this type of cerclage is more difficult to do than the McDonald, and sometimes involves a permanent stitch around the cervix which will not be removed so a cesarean will be required to deliver the baby. Speculum: An instrument used to hold the vaginal walls apart during a vaginal or cervical procedure; it has two blades that are hinged and are closed when the speculum is inserted and then opened when they are in place. Tips Normally, the removal of the cerclage suture by the same provider who placed it in is not separately reportable. The exception to this is when the suture knot has become buried into the cervical mucosa and requires surgery to remove it. The provider generally performs this from a vaginal approach, but 59871 does not specify the approach. Given that an abdominal approach would be more work, if the provider must remove the suture via an abdominal incision, ensure there is documentation to support this approach and add a modifier 22, Increased procedural services, to code 59871.
